An earlier version proposed to model RNN dependencies as a partially ordered set (poset) and to retain the meet-irreducible elements of its dependency lattice. By Birkhoff's representation theorem, the meet-irreducible ideals of a finite poset are in bijection with its elements, so retaining them retains everything; the critical-set criterion used earlier selects precisely the elements comparable to all others, of which a dense recurrent layer has none. Condensing a thresholded dependency graph into strongly connected components yields a well-defined dependency order, a graded order score and an acyclic pruning rule; for Cohen-Grossberg networks and LSTMs, acyclic pruning makes local stability decompose over modules. For a 128-unit LSTM pruned at matched sparsity on row-wise and chunked sequential MNIST (three seeds, equal training budgets), the original rules remove every recurrent weight or equal random column pruning; the order score is no better than degree, PageRank or norm; trained weights show little directional bias; and imposing acyclicity from initialisation costs 2.1 and 10.5 percentage points at 50% and 90% sparsity. In the networks studied, order structure must be imposed rather than discovered.

items.title: Sub-Voxel Displacement and Ipsilateral Territory Decoupling for 3D Bilateral Coronary Artery Tree Reconstruction in Cardiac CT Angiography
items.summary: Bilateral coronary tree (LCA/RCA) reconstruction in cardiac CT angiography (CCTA) faces $64^3$ discretization, territory ambiguity, and ostium drift. Within GT-foreground $128^3$ ROIs ($\pm 15$-voxel margin, 9.8--12.0 mm; seed-free in ROI; whole-volume localization upstream), we propose a canonical $(Z_{IS},Y_{PA},X_{LR})$ multi-task network and scalar-potential arborescence solver. Volumes, centerlines, and thick-stem ostia map to $(Z_{IS},Y_{PA},X_{LR})$, extending a 3D pyramid encoder and tubular decoder with a $128^3\to 64^3$ skip, stop-gradient $128^3$ residual branch, 3D sub-voxel displacement head $Δ\hat{u}(x)$, ipsilateral head $(P_{LCA},P_{RCA})$, and $32^3$ ostium head. From a recall-balanced anchor, 327,385 active parameters (398,843 total) are fine-tuned in a 30-epoch AdamW loop ($ε=10^{-8}$, 7 groups) with L2-SP/anchor blending. Our solver couples Valsalva-STJ calibration, $128^3$ rooting, contralateral inhibition, radius-ratio pruning, normal-plane pullback, and collision reduction. On OOS-50 (Cases 251--300, 50 volumes, 100 trees; 201--250 isolated) vs. 3D U-Net (skeleton/$M_3$--$M_5$) and 5 proxies, it reaches $2.7671\pm 1.1385$ mm $CD_{CL}^{union}$ (SD 0.0415), $3.2338\pm 1.3557$ mm $CD_{CL}^{arc1mm}$, and $3.2926\pm 2.6253$ mm $CD_{ipsi}$ (arc1mm 3.7460 mm, node $p_{Holm}\le 0.0400$ vs. Ext-0b [arc1mm $p=0.1629/0.2187$]; 76.33% junction [23.04% 1-to-1], 79.65% branch F1). On Dev-14 (14 volumes, 28 trees), it reaches $2.1362\pm 0.5041$ mm $CD_{CL}^{union}$ (SD 0.0369), $2.3798\pm 0.5725$ mm $CD_{CL}^{arc1mm}$, and $2.2480\pm 0.6835$ mm $CD_{ipsi}$ (arc1mm 2.4951 mm, node $CD_{CL}^{union}$ $p_{Holm}=0.0494$ vs. Ext-0b [$CD_{ipsi}$/arc1mm $p_{Holm}=0.1353/0.0676$--$0.0906$]; 56.76%/77.74% F1@1/2mm; 79.95% junction [21.06% 1-to-1], 83.80% branch F1, 4.6880/4.9298 mm ostia), and $N=64$ $CD_{CL}^{union}=2.6291\pm 1.0629$ mm (arc1mm 3.0470, $CD_{ipsi}$ 3.0641).

items.title: Structural identifiability of partially-observed stochastic processes: from single-particle trajectories to total particle density data
items.summary: The increasing availability of experimental data has intensified interest in calibrating stochastic models, raising fundamental questions about parameter identifiability. Structural identifiability determines whether parameters can be uniquely recovered from idealised data, a prerequisite to allow for parameter estimation in real-world scenarios. However, there is a lack of methodologies generally applicable to analyse the structural identifiability of such stochastic processes. Therefore, we develop a methodology for a class of spatio-temporal stochastic processes. We investigate how structural identifiability depends on the type of available data, distinguishing between single-particle trajectories and total particle density measurements. For trajectory data, we use a particle-based description that explicitly represents single-particle dynamics. For population-level data, we derive a partial differential equation representation, that describes the evolution of total particle density, and apply a differential algebra approach, common to ordinary differential equation analysis. We further introduce Taylor-series-expansion and Fourier-transform approaches to study the initial condition. We apply our methodology to an example model with a specified class of initial conditions. We show that the model is globally structurally identifiable given infinitely many, infinitely long single-particle trajectories, but only locally structurally identifiable from total particle density data, demonstrating that parameter identifiability depends on the type of data available.

items.title: Open Biomedical Knowledge Graphs at Scale: Construction, Federation, and AI Agent Access with Samyama Graph Database
items.summary: Biomedical knowledge is fragmented across siloed databases---Reactome, STRING, Gene Ontology, ClinicalTrials.gov, DrugBank, DGIdb, SIDER, PubMed, ClinVar, ChEMBL, OpenTargets, and more. We present an open, reproducible biomedical knowledge graph ecosystem built on Samyama, a Rust-native graph database: three foundational graphs detailed end-to-end---Pathways KG (118,686 nodes, 834,785 edges), Clinical Trials KG (7,774,446 nodes, 26,973,997 edges), and Drug Interactions KG (32,726 nodes, 191,970 edges)---and their expansion into a 22-graph, 2-cohort merged biomedical store (328,130,739 nodes and 1,441,425,733 imported edges, including 295,000 synthetic OMOP CDM patients from Synthea). First, we describe a reproducible ETL and portable .sgsnap snapshot pattern where graphs load alone or compose into one store. Second, we analyze single-store cross-KG integration via query-time property joins and load-time identifier deduplication (--dedup-keys): across all 24 snapshots (Samyama-Graph v1.13.0), 328.1M nodes and 1.44B edges load in 2,269.1 s (37m 49s) within 366.5 GB peak RSS (254 B/edge), merging 132,511 cross-source entities across five audited keys (mondo_id,uniprot_id,go_id,drugbank_id,symbol)---87.8% of the 150,965 Bound A sound-identifier ceiling, with zero conflicting-ID refusals. On a frozen 81-query suite, 62 queries return results (17 data-gap empties, 2 timeouts); on an expanded 200-query oracle suite, 195 of 200 pass (97.5%). Third, we introduce schema-driven Model Context Protocol (MCP) server generation: on the 40-question BiomedQA benchmark over the 3-KG subset, domain-specific MCP tools achieve 98% accuracy vs. 85% for schema-aware text-to-Cypher and 75% for standalone GPT-4o, with zero schema errors.

items.title: Explainable AI-Driven Neural Activity Analysis in Parkinsonian Rats under Electrical Stimulation
items.summary: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by motor dysfunction and abnormal neural oscillations. This study combined graphene-based cortical stimulation with an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) framework to investigate spatial and frequency-related features contributing to pre- and post-stimulation classification in Parkinsonian rats. Electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals were recorded before and after stimulation and classified using EEGNet and DeepConvNet. Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) and DeepLIFT were applied to identify frequency bands and recording channels contributing to the classification. The anatomical locations of these channels were mapped onto a cortical map. XAI analyses were performed separately for each animal to examine individual attribution patterns. Our XAI analysis revealed frequency-band- and region-specific contributions to pre- and post-stimulation classification in Parkinsonian rats. Our approach provided complementary insights into the features contributing to pre- and post-stimulation ECoG classification alongside PSD-based analyses. These findings highlight the potential of combining graphene-based cortical stimulation with explainable deep learning to identify classification-relevant features across frequency bands and cortical areas in pre- and post-stimulation recordings.

items.title: Les Houches Lectures on Community Ecology: From Niche Theory to Statistical Mechanics
items.summary: Ecosystems are among the most interesting and well-studied examples of self-organized complex systems. Community ecology, the study of how species interact with each other and the environment, has a rich tradition. Over the last few years, there has been a growing theoretical and experimental interest in these problems from the physics and quantitative biology communities. Here, we give an overview of community ecology, highlighting the deep connections between ecology and statistical physics. We start by introducing the two classes of mathematical models that have served as the workhorses of community ecology: Consumer Resource Models (CRM) and the generalized Lotka-Volterra models (GLV). We place a special emphasis on graphical methods and general principles. We then review recent works showing a deep and surprising connection between ecological dynamics and constrained optimization. We then shift our focus by analyzing these same models in "high-dimensions" (i.e. in the limit where the number of species and resources in the ecosystem becomes large) and discuss how such complex ecosystems can be analyzed using methods from the statistical physics of disordered systems such as the cavity method and Random Matrix Theory.

items.title: Transmission and filtering of stochastic rhythms in bursty gene expression
items.summary: How stochastic rhythms in upstream regulatory signals are transmitted to downstream gene expression is a fundamental question in systems biology. Although experiments have shown that molecular degradation strongly influences downstream rhythmic responses, a general quantitative theory explaining how degradation, stochastic bursting, and upstream timing variability jointly govern rhythm transmission remains lacking. Here we develop a general analytical framework based on a martingale-based orthogonal decomposition, applicable to arbitrarily complex upstream dynamics, including memory effects. We derive exact autocorrelation and power-spectrum transmission laws, establish an oscillation-efficiency contraction principle, and identify a critical degradation rate that provides a necessary and sufficient condition for stochastic rhythm transmission. An explicit rhythm-transmission relation reveals that increasing burst frequency and modulation depth promotes rhythm transmission, whereas greater variability in upstream cycle duration suppresses it. In particular, increasing burst size leaves oscillation efficiency unchanged. The predicted degradation threshold correctly separates all ten pulsing and nonpulsing p53 target proteins reported in previous experiments. These results provide a theoretical foundation for understanding how cells selectively preserve or integrate rhythmic regulatory signals.

items.title: D2ML: Models for Direct-to-Biology Small Molecule Screening
items.summary: Direct-to-biology (D2B) screening enables rapid testing of newly synthesized molecules without purification. However, uncertain concentrations in crude mixtures and limited purified-compound measurements complicate the use of these data in machine learning. Here we show that models tailored to the structure of D2B data can improve prediction and guide the discovery of more potent and selective compounds. Our assay-aware models predict activity from single-point screens, relative potency across targets from crude dose-response assays, and absolute potency from purified-compound measurements. For crude assays, potency ratios between targets tested from the same well can retain selectivity information despite uncertain concentrations. A joint model that shares information across stages and balances their contributions to training improved predictions over separate neural networks. The largest gain was in crude dose-response selectivity prediction, where rank correlation increased from 0.27 to 0.40. In a separate experiment, independently trained models guided the selection of 84 new compounds to improve ROS1 potency while limiting activity against the anti-target TRKB. Synthesis and testing identified compounds that extended the measured Pareto front, achieving better combinations of potency and selectivity than those in the training data. The most selective new compound achieved a ROS1 IC50 of 14.7 nM and 233-fold selectivity over TRKB. By comparison, the most selective training compound had a ROS1 IC50 of 20.3 nM and 79-fold selectivity. ATLAS provides the experimental setting for this approach, supporting synthesis and screening of 1,000-10,000 model-selected compounds in two- to three-week cycles. Together, these results show how assay-aware learning can use the full D2B assay sequence to guide multi-objective molecular optimization.

items.title: Morpheus.AI: agents autonomously generate, execute and refine virtual tissue models
items.summary: Virtual tissue models link observations to mechanistic hypotheses, but building them demands expertise in biology, mathematics and programming. Here, large language model (LLM) agents paired with the simulator Morpheus (Morpheus.AI) autonomously built such models from fifteen benchmark studies, five without a published model. With a frontier LLM, agents that ran their simulations met 83-86% of study-specific criteria in under two hours and for under US\$4 per model. Such agents could make in silico modeling routine.

items.title: Localizing predictive concepts encoded in neural representations via hierarchical testing
items.summary: Understanding which regulatory sequence motifs a genomic deep learning model has learned, with statistical error guarantees, is essential for trusting its use in downstream tasks such as variant effect prediction. Existing approaches to identifying which units in a trained network encode human- understandable concepts fall into two groups. Exploratory methods rank and visualize units but offer no statistical guarantee that the selected units are associated with the prediction target across the population of inputs. Testing-based methods test only single units or one pre-defined set of them, and do not control the error across the many sets of units. We introduce CUTTIE (Cluster-tree Unit Top-down Testing of Independence with Error control), which clusters the units of each layer into a tree and tests the clusters top-down with conditional independence tests, localizing information about the target while controlling the family-wise error rate. Thereby, we identify clusters that carry information about the target beyond the rest of the layer. For the units in the identified clusters, conditional attribution maps then reveal what motifs they encode. In a controlled simulation, the procedure identifies the clusters whose concepts affect the target. We apply the procedure to a convolutional model predicting cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility from DNA sequence, where the concepts encoded in the identified clusters map onto known regulatory motifs.

items.title: Contribution of chromosome-naïve transposon-seeded network of DNA templates to intracellular pools of protein dimers of liquid-liquid phase-separated condensate-forming proteins
items.summary: Molecular mechanisms governing protein-protein interactions (PPI) contributing to the biogenesis of membraneless condensates remain poorly understood. Observations reported in this contribution demonstrate that liquid-liquid phase-separated (LLPS) condensate-forming proteins and their variants harboring condensate-disrupting human pathogenic mutations are significantly enriched among PPI cascade constituents of the Hybrid Assembly Pathway (HAP) of endogenous multiprotein complexes (EMC). In contrast, no structured or disordered proteins defined as condensate-negative molecules were detected among PPI cascade constituents. Cumulative evidence derived from different lines of analytical inquiries support the concept of the significant contributions of PPI cascade constituents of HAP to the biogenesis of intracellular pools of cell type-specific protein heterodimers assembled with the engagement of at least one protein monomer selected from condensate-forming protein molecules. Analytical evidence documented in this study support the concept that genome-wide chromosome-naïve networks of transposon-seeded DNA-templates nucleate the initiation of PPI cascade chain reactions with the capacity to facilitate the concurrent iterative assembly in human cells of both the membraneless biomolecular condensates and the structured multiprotein complexes. AlphaFold 3D modelling of mutation patterns and analysis of partner-bound experimental structures identified variants located at a measured protein dimerization interface. This contribution nominates numerous protein heterodimers of potential relevance to human pathophysiology for follow-up mechanistic studies of potential fundamental and translational impacts.

items.title: A Closed-loop Framework to Discriminate Models Using Optimal Control
items.summary: Predicting the response of an observed system to a known input is a fruitful first step to accurately control the system's dynamics. Despite the recent advances in fully data-driven algorithms, the most interpretable way to reach this goal is through mechanistic mathematical modeling. Here, we leverage optimal control and propose a closed-loop iterative method to choose among a set of candidate models the one that most accurately predicts an observed system. We assume that one has control over an input of the observed system and access to measurements of its response. Our approach is to identify the input control that maximally discriminates the response of the candidate models, allowing us to determine which model is best by comparing such responses with the observed data. We demonstrate our proposed framework in numerical simulations before applying it during an electrophysiology experiment, successfully discriminating between different models for photocurrents produced via opsin dynamics.

items.title: A Framework for Evaluating Forward Contamination Risk for Bio-ISRU Microorganisms
items.summary: NASA planetary protection policy seeks to avoid inadvertent forward contamination of celestial bodies and backward contamination of Earth during space exploration. For Mars missions, it has historically focused on sterilization of landers and rovers. Current policy provides no framework for assessing the forward contamination risk of missions that deliberately include living organisms and must not be sterilized, such as a human crew, agriculture, or biotechnology for manufacturing and life support. We propose the PRIM (Propagation Restricted, Inert on Mars) framework to evaluate the forward-contamination risk posed by known organisms. Building on the biocontainment literature and probability-of-contamination model, PRIM bounds the ability of an organism released from a worst-case off-nominal event to sustain growth on the Martian surface at a probability under P_c <= 10^-4 using independent single-stressor propagation assays. We apply the PRIM framework to two engineered Mars biological in situ resource utilization chassis organisms, using low water activity and carbon starvation to qualify them for low forward contamination risk even at high bioburden, and outline how to extend the assays to phototrophs and anaerobes. PRIM offers a path to flight-qualify living organisms for Mars based on laboratory assays rather than bioburden alone. This enables biological life support infrastructure for a sustained presence on Mars while keeping forward contamination risk demonstrably low.

items.title: When Does Context Help? A Systematic Study of Target-Conditional Molecular Property Prediction
items.summary: We present the first systematic study of when target context helps molecular property prediction, evaluating context conditioning across 10 diverse protein families, 4 fusion architectures, data regimes spanning 67-9,409 training compounds, and both temporal and random evaluation splits. Using NestDrug, a FiLM-based architecture that conditions molecular representations on target identity, we characterize both success and failure modes with three principal findings. First, fusion architecture dominates: FiLM outperforms concatenation by 24.2 percentage points and additive conditioning by 8.6 pp; how you incorporate context matters more than whether you include it. Second, context enables otherwise impossible predictions: on data-scarce CYP3A4 (67 training compounds), multi-task transfer achieves 0.686 AUC where per-target Random Forest collapses to 0.238. Third, context can systematically hurt: distribution mismatch causes 10.2 pp degradation on BACE1; few-shot adaptation consistently underperforms zero-shot. Beyond methodology, we expose fundamental flaws in standard benchmarking: 1-nearest-neighbor Tanimoto achieves 0.991 AUC on DUD-E without any learning, and 50% of actives leak from training data, rendering absolute performance metrics meaningless. Our temporal split evaluation (train up to 2020, test 2021-2024) achieves stable 0.843 AUC with no degradation, providing the first rigorous evidence that context-conditional molecular representations generalize to future chemical space.

items.title: Temporal and spatial couplings in the dynamics of human walking and running
items.summary: Rhythmic behaviours such as walking and running are commonly modelled as dynamical systems around a stable limit cycle. To keep such models tractable, it is usually assumed that each step depends only on the previous one, that the limit cycle is fixed, and that the sagittal and frontal planes can be studied separately. Here, we test these assumptions in seven public datasets of human gait (71 participants), including 16 people who both walked and ran. We fit linear step-to-step maps and validate them by cross-validation, holding out more data where more data exist. At first sight, gait has memory: the state two steps back lowers the prediction error by up to 29\%. Yet most of this temporal coupling vanishes once the operating point may drift slowly and measurement noise is modelled; gait remains limit-cycle-like, around an operating point that moves. Running keeps more memory than walking in the same people. Spatial coupling between the planes is present in most participants, mainly from sagittal to frontal, but weak. This supports planar models of healthy gait, while a repeatable, task-dependent coupling index may serve as a measure of gait quality. The simple models are wrong, but useful enough.

items.title: Immersed Boundary Electrodiffusion in the Wasserstein Gradient Flow Formalism: Global Well-Posedness, Non-Equilibrium Thermodynamics, and Singular Asymptotics
items.summary: We introduce a unified optimal transport framework for the Immersed Boundary (IB) electrodiffusion active pump model. By representing membrane chemical potential barriers and active pump potentials via smoothed Eulerian kernels ($Ψ_w, \mathcal{H}_w$), we formulate the passive dynamics as an $L^2$-Wasserstein ($W_2$) gradient flow coupled to non-conservative active pushing fields representing ATP-driven $3:2$ $\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+$ exchangers. We establish global weak existence of solutions to the continuous Poisson--Nernst--Planck--IB system via a split-step Jordan--Kinderlehrer--Otto (JKO) variational scheme, backed by Calderón--Zygmund bounds for non-local Poisson drift and $H^3(\mathbb{S}^1)$ interface regularity under Stokes flow. We prove the continuous Rayleighian energy balance and establish exponential $W_2$-stability of Non-Equilibrium Steady States (NESS) under a quantitative Bakry--Émery curvature threshold. Furthermore, we analyze the dual singular limits of kernel smoothing width $w \to 0$ and dimensionless Debye length $g = λ_D / L \to 0$. We establish the precise asymptotic regime connecting regularized and sharp models, prove the $Γ$-convergence of regularized energy functionals, derive distributional interface flux jump conditions, and resolve $O(λ_D)$ Debye space-charge boundary layers to confirm bulk electroneutrality.

items.title: Basis statistics for phylogenetic tree shape: tree balance formulas beyond expectations
items.summary: Summary statistics that measure the shapes of phylogenetic trees contributed to quantitatively understanding evolutionary processes. Among phylogenetic summary statistics, the tree balance indices have been designed to capture intuitive notions of balance or imbalance in trees. Here, we characterize the tree balance indices in terms of basis statistics, mapping the exponentially large space of rooted, binary, unlabeled trees to lower-dimensional spaces. We observe that many tree balance indices can be represented in terms of linear functions of these low-dimensional spaces, enabling us to compute exact formulas for the means, variances, and covariances of many balance indices under the Yule--Harding model. The new framework recapitulates existing formulas for the expectations of 8 indices: Sackin index, average leaf depth, total cophenetic index, $\hat{s}$-shape statistic, Colless index, corrected Colless index, quadratic Colless index, and rooted quartet index for binary trees. It produces new formulas for the expectations of 9 additional indices: equal weights Colless index, total $I$ index, total $I'$ index, Rogers $J$ index, total internal path length, total path length, average vertex depth, stairs1 index, and stairs2 index. Moreover, the framework also allows us to calculate the exact variance of all 17 indices that are represented by the bases as well as the covariance and correlation for all $\binom{17}{2} = 136$ pairs among the 17 indices.

items.title: Predicting Dose-Response Success from Primary Screening Data
items.summary: High-throughput drug screening uses inexpensive primary screens to select compounds for more costly follow-up dose-response experiments, which estimate compound potency (pXC50) by determining the concentration required to produce a specified biological effect. However, many promoted compounds fail to yield a reportable potency, even when activity is subsequently confirmed. We investigated whether inexpensive three-point primary-screening data could predict whether a more costly 11-point dose-response experiment would yield a reportable pXC50. Using a dataset of 32,971 compound-assay pairs with three-point primary-screening and 11-point dose-response measurements, we trained random-forest models to predict successful potency quantification. Our model achieved an AUROC of 0.939 +/- 0.002 and generalized to previously unseen chemical scaffolds and assay-mechanism families. We found that primary-screen response features were more predictive of dose-response quantifiability than molecular structure-based features. Successful potency quantification was also strongly associated with primary-screen response amplitude. Across eight chronological test releases, the model retrospectively retained 90% of reportable potencies while selecting only 55.7% of historically promoted compound-assay pairs for follow-up profiling. These findings suggest that predicting potency quantifiability from primary-screening data could improve the efficiency of compound prioritization and reduce unnecessary dose-response experiments.

items.title: GraphTFactor: A graph-based approach for proteins transcription factor prediction
items.summary: Transcription factors (TFs) play an important role in regulating gene expression, making their identification a fundamental task in computational biology. In this work, we propose GraphTFactor, a novel end-to-end framework that models protein sequences as graphs and directly classifies transcription factors. By encoding sequences into graph structures, the proposed approach naturally handles variable-length inputs while preserving relevant relational information, without imposing length constraints. Experimental results show that GraphTFactor outperforms state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of graph-based representations for TF prediction while providing interpretable insights into the sequence regions contributing to the model's predictions. To support reproducibility and practical adoption, we release an open-source software package and an interactive web application that let users easily perform TF prediction on custom sequences.

items.title: Hydrodynamic flow in the gut hinders the fixation of beneficial mutants but accelerates their invasion
items.summary: Gut bacteria experience a spatially structured environment with hydrodynamic flow. Using a branching-process approach, we show that beneficial mutants arising randomly upon division have a reduced fixation probability compared to the well-mixed case. The suppression factor is set by the spatial heterogeneity of mutant fate across the gut. In contrast, the invasion of mutant lineages that avoid early stochastic extinction is accelerated in the gut compared to a matched well-mixed case. Stronger advective flow decreases fixation probabilities while accelerating mutant invasion.

items.title: Expression of White and Gray Matter Autism Functional Network Connectivity Signatures in Infancy
items.summary: Functional connectivity studies have provided valuable insights into altered brain organization in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, most functional connectivity studies focus exclusively on either gray matter (GM) regions or white matter (WM) tracts and examine specific age groups, rather than investigating their functional interactions across brain development. This limits our understanding of how GM-WM functional interactions evolve developmentally and may obscure important aspects of brain network organization in ASD. We combined integrated WM+GM functional network connectivity (FNC) with brain-wide risk scores (BRSs) to quantify ASD-associated pattern expression in ABIDE I/II and an independent infant cohort. We employed a NeuroMark framework with predefined WM and GM intrinsic connectivity networks templates, to estimate subject-level FNC. First, we identified two distinct patterns of altered WM+GM FNC in ASD: GM-related hypoconnectivity centered on the paralimbic network and WM-GM hyperconnectivity centered on the frontal network. These findings highlight the involvement of higher-order cognitive networks and the importance of WM-GM functional interactions in characterizing ASD-related connectivity alterations. Second, infants with a higher familial likelihood of autism exhibited greater mean expression of ASD-associated FNC patterns than those with a lower familial likelihood, as quantified by BRS. These group-level findings do not establish developmental persistence or predict diagnostic outcomes at the individual level.

items.title: Taxonomic Classification with Tag Arrays
items.summary: Taxonomic classifiers based on exact matches differ in which matches they use and in how each match splits its credit among the taxa containing it: Kraken~2 gives a $k$-mer's credit to the lowest common ancestor of those taxa, SPUMONI~2 labels each position of the read, Tagger gives each maximal exact match (MEM) one label, and Cliffy splits a match's credit evenly over a roughly logarithmic sample of the taxa. We compare these schemes on the same long MEMs, mainly on short 16S rRNA reads classified to genera with SILVA, where credit proportional to the number of occurrences of the MEM in each taxon is the most accurate, by 1.0 to 6.8 percentage points. We compute long MEMs with Boyer--Moore--Li on a run-length compressed suffix array, and count their occurrences in each taxon with a complete, run-length compressed tag array, in time proportional to the number of tag runs in the MEM's BWT interval, without locating any occurrence. We bound the number of tag runs in terms of the BWT runs and of how often suffixes with long common prefixes have different tags, and show that tags constant on $d$ blocks of the text have a macro scheme with at most $r + 2d$ phrases. On SILVA our index takes 1.44\,GB and classifies a read in 66\,$μ$s with one thread at 93.8\% accuracy; on the same reads and server, it is 14 times smaller than Cliffy's undigested index, and 4.4 times faster and 8 percentage points more accurate than Cliffy's LCA query on it. Over minimizer digests it takes 0.49\,GB and reaches 92.5\%; on the server, 92.1\% against 84.2\% for Cliffy's LCA query on its digested index. On nanopore reads from whole genomes, where almost every long MEM occurs in one species, we instead use each read's longest MEMs, found in one pass of a variant of Boyer--Moore--Li with a $k$-mer filter, which assigns 99.6\% of the reads to their species with no length threshold.

items.title: How many mutations does it take to evolve a new function?
items.summary: Biochemical and genetic networks in cells evolve to produce new functions. Evolution is guided by the genotype to phenotype map which describes how mutations at the molecular scale lead to changes in network function at the cellular scale. The number of genotypes is astronomically large which makes these maps very high dimensional. In this context, the simple question: How many mutations does it take to evolve a new function?, is usually hard to answer. Here we consider this question in the context of a simple Boolean-network model of a genotype-phenotype map. The nodes and edges of the Boolean network represent the genotype while the Boolean function the network computes is the phenotype. The network evolves by rewiring of its edges, while keeping the number of nodes fixed. We compute the number of mutations needed to achieve a new Boolean function as a function of the number of nodes in the network. We show that the number of mutations scales with the number of nodes of the network as a power-law with an exponent determined by local geometrical features of the genotype-phenotype map. Our theoretical study emphasizes the role of the genotype-phenotype map in determining the time to evolve a new function.

items.title: Hyaluronic acid over-expression drives tissue architecture in both healthy and diseased states
items.summary: Tissue architecture is shaped by a variety of biomechanical and biochemical mechanisms, including morphogen patterning, differential growth, and spatial variations in cellular contractility. These mechanisms typically emphasize forces generated within cells. Here, we explore a complementary mechanism in which intercellular space itself exerts forces that shape tissue architecture. More specifically, we focus on hyaluronic acid (HA), a glycosaminoglycan of the extracellular matrix, that draws fluid into the spaces between cells through osmotic pressure, allowing these spaces to expand and mechanically deform the surrounding tissue. We propose that spatial patterning of HA-mediated extracellular forces, acting together with tissue geometry and junctional mechanics, provides a common physical framework capable of generating distinct tissue architectures. We test this hypothesis using a computational framework coupling a cell-based extended vertex model for biological tissues to a flow network representing HA and extracellular fluid in the extracellular space. This coupled model demonstrates a range of architectural responses spanning changes in tissue topology and morphology: global HA overexpression drives fluid accumulation and cell-cell junction rupture to produce multiple lumens in nontrivial patterns; a localized HA-rich region generates pressure gradients that drive budding; {\it multiple localized HA-rich regions generate branching;} and {\it extended HA-rich patterns can drive tubular structures.} Our results have direct experimental implications and establish the spatial patterning of HA-mediated intercellular forces as a mechanical morphogen helping shape tissue architecture.

items.title: Advancing Clinical Genomic Analysis with a Skill-Centred Agent
items.summary: Clinical genomic analysis requires experts to integrate evolving guidelines, databases, and computational evidence. As sequencing has become increasingly accessible, this complex and labor-intensive process has become a major bottleneck to the timely use of genomic information in clinical decision-making. To fill this gap, we developed ClinGeX, a large-language-model agent that composes 105 curated executable skills through task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration. On 223 temporally held-out benchmark cases, ClinGeX achieved 71.7\% macro-averaged task-level concordance with expert reference classifications, compared with 45.7\% for the strongest comparator. In a three-condition, counterbalanced human-AI collaboration study, 45 clinical genomic professionals assessed 135 clinically derived cases under routine (no AI assistance), DeepSeek-assisted and ClinGeX-assisted conditions. ClinGeX assistance increased raw case-level concordance across criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making (51.1\%, 57.8\%, 64.4\% versus 15.6\%, 31.1\%, 20.0\% in comparator conditions) and reduced reported interpretation time in all scenarios. During an exploratory one-month real-world non-interventional assessment, 11 experienced professionals submitted feedback on 96 self-selected analysis episodes and reported frequent conclusion adoption and time savings. These findings support executable domain skills as a promising approach to augment specialist genomic interpretation.

items.title: A heterogenetic theory of living systems
items.summary: The problem of the dynamics of living systems and their mathematical representation essentially unfolds on two levels. Firstly, the principles of autopoiesis and operational closure describe how a living system produces and maintains itself. Secondly, living phenomena are recognised as historical, involving the evolution of dynamics and spaces of possibility that change over time. Currently, no differential model can incorporate both of these aspects. We propose adopting the differential heterogenesis framework, which enables us to define differential operators that change in space and time, producing event-based and historical dynamics. In this construction, heterogeneous operator assemblages will be constrained by the principles of autopoiesis and operational closure, providing a theoretical framework for event-based and historical living systems. Finally, we provide a specific example of assembly with Gray-Scott kinetic equations, along with numerical simulations and results.

items.title: A Low-Rank Space Captures Linear Alignment Between LLM and Human Neural Activity During Naturalistic Language Listening
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human language processing, yet it remains unclear which components of their representations drive alignment with neural activity. Here, we use ridge reduced-rank regression to identify the brain-predictive subspace of LLM representations: the representational directions that support linear prediction of neural responses. Across three naturalistic language-listening datasets spanning intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI, and six model conditions spanning autoregressive, bidirectional masked, and randomly initialized language models, we find that full linear encoding performance can be recovered using only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality. These low-dimensional subspaces generalize across held-out participants and, to a lesser extent, across datasets, suggesting that neural predictivity is concentrated in a compact and partially shared representational space. We next compare these brain-predictive directions with the principal axes of variation in the embeddings. Principal component analysis requires substantially more dimensions to recover neural prediction, demonstrating that the directions most useful for predicting neural activity are distinct from those capturing the most overall variance within LLM representations themselves. Finally, characterizing the learned subspaces allows us to surface interpretable features that are overrepresented in neural activity above and beyond the LLM representations. Together, these results show that LLM-brain alignment is supported by a small, structured subset of model representations and provides a framework for better understanding exactly why these representations align. Code can be found at: https://github.com/thefinnlab/low-rank-alignment

items.title: Learning developmental dynamics from lineage context
items.summary: A central goal of biology is to predict the dynamics of multicellular systems. Lineage context (the states of a cell's sisters, cousins, etc.) could inform these predictions, but how best to leverage it remains unclear. Here we introduce lineage inpainting, a generative modeling approach that uses lineage context with tree-structured transformers and stochastic interpolants to model cell state dynamics across lineage trees. Applied to a lineage-traced transcriptional atlas of mouse embryogenesis, it recovers dynamics not resolved by gene expression alone, including multiple transcriptional convergence events where distinct lineages are drawn to a common state. Despite being fit on unperturbed development, lineage inpainting can generate hypotheses about perturbation responses by simulating counterfactuals. These simulations agree in many cases with observed developmental phenotypes, including a single-cell measurement of the Tbx5 knockout response. Our results show that lineage information provides a rich source of context for learning multicellular dynamics.

items.title: Yoga biomechanics through energy optimization: diverse kinematics and low-dimensional kinetics
items.summary: Yoga is widely practiced for improving physical and mental health, yet the biomechanical demands of individual yoga poses remain poorly characterized. Existing experimental studies typically examine only a small number of poses or muscles, limiting their ability to guide pose selection for rehabilitation or exercise prescription. Here we present a computational framework for predicting whole-body joint torques and contact forces from two-dimensional images of yoga poses. The framework combines manual pose digitization, a sagittal-plane MuJoCo human model, and constrained metabolic energy minimization subject to static equilibrium. We applied the framework to 55 sagittally symmetric yoga poses from Light on Yoga, generating a dataset of joint kinematics, contact locations, and predicted joint torques and contact forces. These poses collectively span nearly the full physiological range of motion of the major joints while exhibiting a wide range of predicted joint torques, with the greatest average demands on the lower extremities and lumbar region. Principal component analysis revealed a striking contrast between kinematics and kinetics: nearly all ten dimensions were required to represent the joint-angle data, whereas the first three principal components captured over 90% of the variance in joint torques. Thus, yoga poses exhibit substantial diversity in body configurations but comparatively low-dimensional patterns of predicted joint loading. Predicted joint torque rankings were also largely insensitive to uncertainty in the relative weighting of joint metabolic costs. This framework enables systematic biomechanical analysis of yoga poses and provides a foundation for quantitatively evaluating their mechanical demands and informing future rehabilitation strategies.

items.title: Agentic LLM reasoning in pediatric diabetes outcome prediction from multimodal medical records
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are proposed for clinical prediction but are untested in pediatrics, where cohorts are small and outcomes are uncommon. Using records from 2,489 youth with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and 4,018 with type 1 diabetes (T1D), spanning structured data, note-derived social determinants and, in T1D, continuous glucose monitoring data, we predicted seven T2D outcomes, four also in T1D, at 24 months from 18 months of follow-up. CEDAR (Clinical Evidence-Driven Agent for Risk-prediction), an evidence-citing, self-auditing LLM pipeline, outperformed trained machine learning in both cohorts (pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.815 versus 0.656 to 0.700 in T2D and 0.756 versus 0.603 to 0.631 in T1D), most on the sparsely screened outcomes. Only 4 of 70,246 values it cited did not match the chart. Reading only the evidence and reasoning cited by CEDAR, two pediatric endocrinologists reached the same prediction as CEDAR in about nine of ten cases, agreeing with each other on 90.5%.

items.title: Morphological Features of Murine Pulmonary Arterial Networks for Diagnosing Vascular Disease
items.summary: Hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension results from prolonged time spent in a low-oxygen environment. The induced pulmonary hypertension leads to vascular remodeling, including vessel dilation and decreased compliance. This study aims to identify changes in vascular morphology in mice with pulmonary hypertension induced by hypoxia. To do so, we examine the pulmonary arterial network morphology using methods from geometry, topological data analysis, and statistical shape analysis. Tools from these fields are applied to arterial networks excised from micro-CT images of thirteen mice at four pressures. Networks from the hypertensive mice were normalized via a radius pruning algorithm, and analysis was conducted on the entire arterial network, as well as on a per-lobe basis. The main objective of this study was to present an adaptable pipeline for extracting features from micro-CT images to study how vascular disease affects arterial network morphology. Using this pipeline, we showed that the hypertensive mice have increased radius ratios and decreased length-to-radius ratios. Persistent homology analysis revealed that hypertension leads to lower branch-to-branch proximity and lower directional complexity in both the posterior and anterior directions. Persistence curves, particularly Betti curves, revealed lobe-specific differences in the left and inferior lobes. The first two shape principal component scores were also able to discriminate between control and hypertension at lower pressures. Importance metrics for each feature are computed using a boosted decision tree, and then an SVM classification model is fit with the most informative predictors for hypertensive classification.

items.title: gpuGEM: GPU-based linear optimisation of genome-scale metabolic models
items.summary: Summary: Genome-scale metabolic models increasingly challenge CPU linear-programming solvers in repeated optimisation. We present gpuGEM, an open-source Python library for GPU-based optimisation using NVIDIA cuOpt, with size-adaptive settings validated against HiGHS and Gurobi. Across ten models spanning four orders of magnitude, gpuGEM achieved 1.1x to 94x speed-ups over the faster HiGHS method (dual simplex or interior point), and outperformed Gurobi on three models (1.6x to 2.5x). In candidate-gene prioritisation, gpuGEM reduced end-to-end query time from 41 s to 21 s. Availability and Implementation: gpuGEM is released under the MIT licence at https://github.com/Digital-Metabolic-Twin-Centre/gpuGEM and on PyPI (pip install gpugem); release v0.1.3 is archived at https://zenodo.org/records/23422813. It requires an NVIDIA GPU of compute capability 7.0 or newer (Volta onward), Python 3.11 or later, CUDA 12 and cuOpt 26.6 or later. Contact: ronan.mt.fleming@gmail.com Supplementary information: Supplementary data are available as an ancillary file on arXiv.

items.title: pyAvalanches: A Python Package for Analyzing Spatiotemporal Propagation in Neuronal Avalanches
items.summary: The analysis of neuronal avalanches offers insights into brain dynamics utilizing the framework of criticality, but the reproducibility and comparability of studies are limited by the use of fragmented, lab-specific scripts. To address this issue, we introduce pyAvalanches, an open-source Python package providing a standardized, end-to-end pipeline for avalanche analysis from electrophysiological recordings (e.g., electroencephalography-EEG). Starting from the detection of neuronal avalanches the package provides their core statistical characterization, including size and duration distributions. Beyond this, the main aim of pyAvalanches is to characterize the spatiotemporal organization of activity propagation during avalanches. To this end, the core innovation of pyAvalanches is the compuation of Avalanche Transition Matrices (ATMs) to map spatiotemporal propagation patterns. Building on this, the package derives network-based metrics from the ATMs, bridging the study of the topology and organization of the underlying dynamical interactions with network neuroscience adopting the framework of neuronal avalanches. The entire workflow is encapsulated in a modular and scikit-learn compatible architecture. We demonstrate the utility of pyAvalanches through an illustrative group-level analysis on a public resting-state EEG dataset, comparing propagation patterns across different clinical populations. By providing a user-friendly, tested, and extensible tool, pyAvalanches facilitates reproducible research, enables the development of novel avalanche-based biomarkers, and makes complex avalanche analysis accessible to a broader scientific community. The package is fully documented and distributed via the Python Package Index (PyPI).

items.title: Latent Prediction Yields Cross-Subject Alignable Representations in Sensory-Evoked fMRI
items.summary: Decoding sensory-evoked functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data is a central analytical tool in cognitive neuroscience. Here we ask whether self-supervised learning (SSL), which has been scarcely explored in this domain, can yield representations that support strong downstream performance. To do so, we adapt a joint embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) to train participant-specific encoders on brain data alone. The encoders never see the stimulus images or any representation derived from them. Applied to the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we evaluate our learned brain embeddings on the downstream tasks of brain captioning and image reconstruction, as well as cross-participant generalization. Our self-supervised approach achieves competitive performance with parameter-rich supervised pipelines that are trained end-to-end with access to image and language data. We further find that encoders trained independently for different participants can be aligned fully unsupervised, using neither images nor stimuli shared between them. After alignment, a neural decoding head trained on one participant can be applied to another without fine-tuning and retains most of its within-subject performance on image reconstruction and brain captioning. By removing the need for images and shared stimuli, our approach is a step towards pooling fMRI data across participants and, eventually, across datasets.

items.title: PCR-ALERA: A PCR-ELISA analogue but antibody-free DNA detection system
items.summary: PCR-ALERA is a new concept for DNA detection that combines DNA amplification by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with an activator-linked enzyme reactivation assay (ALERA). PCR-ALERA resembles the commercial, semi-quantitative PCR-ELISA assay that offers high sensitivity and high-throughput screening in microplates. PCR-ALERA overcomes a major drawback of PCR-ELISA since it does not require the time-consuming handling of expensive antibodies. In the first step of the assay, commercially available modified nucleotides were incorporated during PCR amplification of the target DNA. A selenocysteine containing peptide (the activator) was linked to the amplified DNA by click chemistry. This peptide has been optimized for the highly efficient activation of the latent protease papain by selenolate-triggered disulfide cleavage. The DNA-peptide hybrid was then immoblized in microplate wells and incubated with latent papain. The latter was readily activated and converted a fluorogenic substrate to a fluorescent product with high catalytic turnover. Overall assay time is about 4 hours including PCR.

items.title: Beyond $χ^2$: Ensemble null tests for reliable scientific discovery
items.summary: Unrecognized systematic errors can survive standard checks and undermine scientific discoveries. Null tests and experimental controls can expose these failures, but averaging measurements or reducing them to scalar statistics can hide important structure. We propose ensemble null tests that compare multivariate distributions with references from observations or simulations. We demonstrate their benefits across science. In cosmic microwave background simulations, they detect systematic effects missed by conventional $χ^2$ tests. In Gaia data, they detect velocity asymmetry as sensitively as an informed search. In a CRISPR screen, they expose a control mismatch in DNA damage and reveal which cellular profiles drive it. As scientific datasets grow, ensemble testing turns repeated measurements into a broader search for unknown unknowns, strengthening the empirical foundation for scientific discovery.

items.title: Core physical principles of allostery
items.summary: Allostery is a basic property of proteins that represents the functional coupling of distantly positioned amino acids. In different manifestations, this property underlies signal transmission, cooperative binding, regulation, catalysis, and evolvability---the elementary features of molecular processes in living cells. While thermodynamic models have provided excellent abstract phenomenological descriptions and classifications of allostery, comparable descriptions and classifications at a more microscopic level, where the nature of physical interactions is specified, are lacking. Starting from minimal assumptions, we derive the essential physical principles of allostery and show that previously described forms of allostery can be viewed as specific implementations of a combination of two core principles: actuation of a soft mode and switching between two states. Organizing allostery by these principles may provide a simpler and more universal language to describe the physics of allostery in proteins.

items.title: Counting approximate breakpoint medians of random genomes
items.summary: Unsigned linear unichromosomal genomes with genes labeled 1, . . . , n are represented by permutations of these labels, whose adjacencies are the unordered pairs of genes occurring consecutively. The breakpoint distance counts the adjacencies of one genome that are absent from the other, and a breakpoint median minimizes the total breakpoint distance to a given set of genomes. Deciding whether a permutation is a median often requires a minimization over the whole symmetric group, which makes the median set resistant to exact counting. We replace this global condition by a local one: a c-approximate median is a genome having at most c adjacencies absent from all the input genomes. For a fixed genome we introduce its approximate median inverse, the set of ordered k-tuples of genomes ad- mitting it as a c-approximate median, and we construct and count this set explicitly. For k genomes chosen uniformly and independently at random, this gives the probability that a given genome is a c-approximate median and the expected number of such approximate medians. The relaxation is not only technical: approximate medians and near-optimal genomes co- incide up to a shift of the tolerance that remains bounded in probability as the number of genes grows. Finally, we derive an explicit upper bound on the probability that a given genome is an exact median, and on the expected number of exact breakpoint medians.

items.title: The Verification Wall in Microbial Metabolomics
items.summary: Computational methods now propose structures for gut microbial metabolites faster than any laboratory can confirm them. We argue that verification, not generation, is the binding constraint, and that better models will not relieve it. Confirming a structure to the field's own standard means having the molecule in hand. Automation can lower what that costs per compound, but the cost stays proportional to the number of structures and never amortizes across them. Two substitutes are on offer and neither removes that requirement. In-silico spectral prediction ranks candidates instead of confirming one, and the strongest current model puts the right structure first 33.5% of the time on a scaffold-split benchmark. Any assignment resting on spectral similarity is, by the field's own definition, made without a reference standard. Microcrystal diffraction does return a structure, but it needs the compound to crystallize out of a trace mixture, which is a different problem rather than an easier one. We sorted 10,645 computationally inferred metabolite structures by what verifying each would take. Between 5% and 37% have no verification route identified under our analysis. That spread reflects where the thresholds are set rather than a measured count of unverifiable compounds, and the inaccessible ones cluster among the most speculative entries. Those figures understate the problem, because the gut makes far more compounds than any database records. HMDB holds only what someone has already thought worth cataloguing, and structure generators are bounded by nothing at all. The claim is easy to disprove. Show a route that confirms structures as fast as they are proposed. Until someone does, two problems stay unsolved. Nobody knows how to spend a verification budget that will always be too small, or what a biologist may conclude from a structure that was never confirmed.

items.title: Emergent topological structure in spontaneous brain-organoid activity
items.summary: Neural activity is widely held to organize on low-dimensional structure embedded in a high-dimensional state space. Persistent homology reads such structure directly from the pattern of pairwise correlations, without assuming in advance which variables are relevant. We apply persistent homology to microelectrode-array (MEA) recordings of spontaneous activity from human (Lancaster) and mouse (Pasca) cortical organoids, spanning 25-197 sorted units, and ask whether topological data analysis resolves structure at the node counts that neural recordings actually deliver. Building weighted networks in correlation space and characterizing them by Vietoris-Rips filtration, we find that the first homology (H1, loops) rises significantly above a rate- and population-preserving null in 14 of 18 datasets, all of which remain significant after correction for testing 18 datasets. Random removal of neural units leaves the loops largely intact. Removing the units that form the loops disrupts them more than removing equally connected units does. Topological richness grows with network size, and second homology (H2) exceeds the null only in the larger networks. These results show that persistent homology resolves structured topology in neural recordings at the scale experiments actually deliver.

items.title: Confidence Filtering in Video-Based Gait Assessment: Measurement Error versus Selection Shift
items.summary: Video-based gait assessment often keeps only high-confidence pose observations, which can lower measurement error but change the movement assessed. We compared confidence selection with budget-matched random selection in a Parkinson-related cohort (n = 96) and an NF2-related replication cohort (n = 18). In the Parkinson-related cohort, confidence selection produced a small but consistent shift in the observed movement summary (+0.05 SD, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.07), while held-out Mini-BESTest error stayed flat (-0.04 points, -0.13 to 0.05); a policy preserving motion-group proportions reduced the shift, while NF2 showed no shift and its predictor did not beat a constant baseline. Because this shift mixes measurement error with selection shift, we decompose and simulate both on the cohort's window structure. Filtering lowers local error when error depends on confidence, but biases the endpoint once confidence tracks movement more than error. In the Parkinson-related data, confidence was only weakly tied to movement (rho = 0.14). There, filtering is harmless if well-tracked windows are unbiased. If instead systematic error only redistributes within participants, filtering can add up to 0.58 degrees. Unchanged clinical error from such small-cohort predictors therefore cannot show that quality filtering preserves the assessed movement.

items.title: AI-driven structural informatics reveals diverse glycosylation machinery across double-stranded DNA viruses
items.summary: Glycosylation is widespread in biology and shapes molecular recognition, yet the diversity and biosynthetic organization of viral glycosyltransferases (GTs) remain poorly understood. Here we integrate structural-alphabet-guided searches and structure similarity networks with genomic-neighbourhood and biosynthetic gene cluster embedding analyses to examine viral GT-A proteins. This approach reveals extensive structural diversity overlooked by sequence-based annotation, including previously uncharacterized viral GT lineages. Most strikingly, we identified a jumbo-phage locus encoding five tandem glycosyltransferases alongside hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine biosynthetic and sulfation-associated enzymes, suggesting a previously unrecognized form of viral DNA modification involving a sulfated pentasaccharide. Beyond these examples, predicted saccharide-associated loci span divergent double-stranded DNA viruses, from giant viruses to tailed phages, and occupy multiple regions of the reference biosynthetic landscape. Together, our findings uncover an underappreciated repertoire of virus-encoded glycosylation machinery and suggest that viral glycan biosynthesis encompasses diverse molecular contexts and potential biological functions.

items.title: Comparison of anomaly detection and supervised learning for acute myeloid leukemia blast identification: A proof-of-concept study
items.summary: Background. Flow cytometry is the established standard for identifying leukemic blast populations in AML, but relies predominantly on subjective, time-consuming manual gating. Machine learning approaches are being explored to support automated blast detection, yet the relative performance of anomaly detection versus supervised classification remains incompletely characterized. Methods. We compared six computational approaches for blast identification: four anomaly detection algorithms (Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, Local Outlier Factor, Half-Space Trees), a supervised Random Forest classifier, and an unsupervised UMAP-HDBSCAN clustering approach. The models were developed on the BLAST110 cohort (110 samples) using nested cross-validation with patient-level grouping, and externally validated on two independent LAIP29 samples spanning high (about 41%) and low (about 1%) blast prevalence. Results. Random Forest achieved the strongest external validation performance (F1 = 0.965 diagnostic sample; F1 = 0.587 follow-up sample). Anomaly detection methods showed weaker, more variable performance, with substantial further decline at low blast prevalence (F1 as low as 0.0006); One-Class SVM performed best among anomaly detectors (F1 = 0.731, diagnostic sample). Several models showed a marked drop in performance between cross-validation and external validation. UMAP-HDBSCAN clustering failed to separate blast and non-blast populations into distinct clusters. Conclusions. Supervised classification substantially outperformed the anomaly detection and unsupervised clustering approaches evaluated here, contrasting with prior work favoring anomaly detection for AML blast identification. This divergence may reflect differences in anomaly detection design; label-efficient approaches may still hold practical value where labeled data collection is limited.

items.title: CMADiff: Cross-Modal Aligned Diffusion for Controllable Protein Generation
items.summary: AI-assisted protein design has emerged as a critical tool for advancing biotechnology, as deep generative models have demonstrated their reliability in this domain. However, most existing models primarily utilize protein sequence or structural data for training, neglecting the physicochemical properties of proteins.Moreover, they are deficient to control the generation of proteins in intuitive conditions. To address these limitations,we propose CMADiff here, a novel framework that enables controllable protein generation by aligning the physicochemical properties of protein sequences with text-based descriptions through a latent diffusion process. Specifically, CMADiff employs a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) to integrate physicochemical features as conditional input, forming a robust latent space that captures biological traits. In this latent space, we apply a conditional diffusion process, which is guided by BioAligner, a contrastive learning-based module that aligns text descriptions with protein features, enabling text-driven control over protein sequence generation. Validated by a series of evaluations including AlphaFold3, the experimental results indicate that CMADiff outperforms protein sequence generation benchmarks and holds strong potential for future applications. The implementation and code are available at https://github.com/HPC-NEAU/PhysChemDiff.

items.title: GenoBERT: A Language Model for Accurate Genotype Imputation
items.summary: Genotype imputation enables dense variant coverage for genome-wide association and risk-prediction studies, yet conventional reference-panel methods remain limited by ancestry bias and reduced rare-variant accuracy. We present Genotype Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (GenoBERT), a transformer-based, reference-free framework that tokenizes phased genotypes and uses a self-attention mechanism to capture both short- and long-range linkage disequilibrium (LD) dependencies. Benchmarking on two independent datasets including the Louisiana Osteoporosis Study (LOS) and the 1000 Genomes Project (1KGP) across ancestry groups and multiple genotype missingness levels (5-50%) shows that GenoBERT achieves the highest overall accuracy compared to four baseline methods (Beagle5.4, SCDA, BiU-Net, and STICI). At practical sparsity levels (up to 25% missing), GenoBERT attains high overall imputation accuracy ($r^2 approx 0.98$) across datasets, and maintains robust performance ($r^2 > 0.90$) even at 50% missingness. Experimental results across different ancestries confirm consistent gains across datasets, with resilience to small sample sizes and weak LD. A 128-SNP (single-nucleotide polymorphism) context window (approximately 100 Kb) is validated through LD-decay analyses as sufficient to capture local correlation structures. By eliminating reference-panel dependence while preserving high accuracy, GenoBERT provides a scalable and robust solution for genotype imputation and a foundation for downstream genomic modeling.

items.title: Frequency-induced Tipping: Resonance-Driven Tipping in a Threshold Predator-Prey System
items.summary: Tipping points refer to abrupt, substantial, and often irreversible transitions in dynamic systems that can be triggered by minor perturbations. Existing tipping mechanisms are usually classified by the nature of the trigger: bifurcation-induced tipping occurs when a parameter crosses a critical threshold, noise-induced tipping is caused by random perturbations, rate-induced tipping occurs when a system fails to track a moving attractor, and phase-induced tipping is triggered by timed perturbations relative to an oscillatory state. In this paper, we identify a new mechanism for tipping: frequency-induced tipping, in which periodic forcing drives a transition through resonant amplification. This occurs by destabilization of an equilibrium via subthreshold perturbations of the appropriate frequency. Filippov analysis of a piecewise-smooth model identifies admissible crossings that lead either to predator loss or to extinction of predator and prey, and numerical simulations show that tipping persists after smoothing of the thresholds. These results extend the current tipping framework to include critical transitions under recurrent environmental forcing.

items.title: How complex behavioural contagion can prevent infectious diseases from becoming endemic
items.summary: Infectious disease transmission in human populations has a complex two-way interaction with changes in host behaviour. It is increasingly recognised that incorporating adaptive behavioural change into epidemic models is important for improving understanding of infectious disease dynamics and developing policy-relevant modelling tools. An important aspect of behavioural dynamics is social contagion, where people tend to adopt behaviours exhibited by others around them. In a simple behavioural contagion model, the behaviour uptake rate increases linearly with the number of contacts who have adopted a given behaviour. Here, we explore an epidemic model with complex behavioural contagion, where the behaviour uptake rate is a nonlinear function of the number of behaving contacts. We identify key bifurcation parameters of the model, which include the basic reproduction number $R_0$, the strength of the behavioural effect on disease transmission, and the speed of behaviour uptake relative to behaviour abandonment. We show that, in some regions of parameter space, the model has multiple disease-free equilibria. In this situation, the occurrence of an epidemic in a population with an initially low level of behaviour practice can trigger a self-sustaining increase in behaviour, which then causes the disease to be eliminated. In some cases, while moderate values of $R_0$ lead to the disease becoming endemic, higher values of $R_0$ may lead to behaviour-driven disease elimination. We demonstrate that this mechanism of epidemic-triggered uptake of behaviour leading to disease elimination can occur in the presence and absence of temporary post-infection immunity.

items.title: Bridging the Simulation-to-Experiment Gap with Generative Models using Adversarial Distribution Alignment
items.summary: A fundamental challenge in science and engineering is the simulation-to-experiment gap. While we often possess prior knowledge of physical laws, these physical laws can be too difficult to solve exactly for complex systems. Such systems are commonly modeled using simulators, which impose computational approximations. Meanwhile, experimental measurements more faithfully represent the real world, but experimental data typically consists of observations that only partially reflect the system's full underlying state. We propose a data-driven distribution alignment framework that bridges this simulation-to-experiment gap by pre-training a generative model on fully observed (but imperfect) simulation data, then aligning it with partial (but real) observations of experimental data. While our method is domain-agnostic, we ground our approach in the physical sciences by introducing Adversarial Distribution Alignment (ADA). This method aligns a generative model of atomic positions -- initially trained on a simulated Boltzmann distribution -- with the distribution of experimental observations. We prove that our method recovers the target observable distribution, even with multiple, potentially correlated observables. We also empirically validate our framework on synthetic, molecular, and experimental protein data, demonstrating that it can align generative models with diverse observables. Our code is available at https://kaityrusnelson.com/ada/.

items.title: Active morphodynamics of intracellular organelles in the trafficking pathway
items.summary: From the Golgi apparatus to endosomes, organelles in the endomembrane system exhibit complex and varied morphologies that are often related to their function. These membrane-bound organelles operate far from equilibrium due to directed fluxes of trafficking vesicles, yet the physical principles governing the emergence and maintenance of these morphologies remain elusive. By coarse-graining the active mechanochemical cycles associated with individual fission and fusion events, we show how vesicular trafficking manifests at the hydrodynamic scale, generating not only fluxes of membrane area and encapsulated volume but also active stresses that mediate momentum transfer between an organelle and its cytosolic environment. The fluid and deformable nature of the bounding membrane gives rise to novel physics by coupling these nonequilibrium forces to organelle composition, morphology, and hydrodynamic flows. We demonstrate how both stable compartment drift and ramified sac-like morphologies, reminiscent of Golgi cisternal motion and shape, emerge from the same nonequilibrium dynamics of fission and fusion.

items.title: What to randomize matters: a controlled study of volume, axis and representation in low-data molecular generation
items.summary: Chemical language models can struggle to generate new molecules when trained on small datasets, where a model may reproduce training examples rather than learn a useful generative distribution. Randomized SMILES augmentation varies atom traversal, whereas Sequential Attachment-based Fragment Embedding (SAFE) also allows the order of fragment blocks to vary. How these distinct sources of representational variation affect low-data molecular generation has not been clearly studied. Here, using 1,000 seed molecules to train an autoregressive sequence model, we compare canonical SAFE with randomized SAFE at increasing corpus sizes, isolate atom-order and fragment-order axes of SAFE randomization, and compare fully randomized SAFE with randomized SMILES at molecule-by-molecule matched training corpora. Three findings emerge. First, randomization of SAFE alone raises the genuine yield of novel molecules more than 450-fold, turning a model that merely reproduces its training set into a practical molecular generator. Second, the two axes of randomization act jointly rather than additively: atom order alone reaches a tenth, and fragment order alone a seventh, of the genuine yield obtained when both vary, which is four times their combined contribution. Third, at matched corpus size and compute, randomized SAFE delivers 2.8 times the genuine yield of randomized SMILES. Welch tests with Games-Howell post-hoc comparisons resolve every difference on the primary outcomes. In the low-data regime, thus, what one randomizes rather than only how much determines whether augmentation produces new molecules or merely new spellings of the training set.

items.title: Kinetic Proofreading Activation Times Beyond the Weibull Limit
items.summary: T cells can detect a few foreign peptide-major histocompatibility complexes (pMHCs) among a far larger number of self pMHCs. Kinetic proofreading explains this discrimination: a receptor that has bound its ligand must complete nKP signaling steps, each at rate kp, before it activates, and dissociation at any step resets its progress. When many receptors are engaged at once, the time to the first activation has been approximated by a Weibull law taken from the short-time limit of this process. The Weibull law is convenient, but it does not contain the dissociation rate koff, even though koff is what proofreading uses to tell ligands apart. Using the exact first-passage law of the underlying continuous-time Markov chain together with stochastic simulations, we show that the relative error of the Weibull law is set by a single dimensionless number $Λ$, the Weibull-predicted activation time measured in units of nKP + 1 bound-state lifetimes. For $Λ$ < 1 the first receptor to activate does so before its ligand has ever dissociated, and the Weibull law holds. As $Λ$ grows, activation relies increasingly on repeated unbinding and rebinding. The true activation time then exceeds the Weibull prediction by up to 2900-fold on our parameter grid, and the effective Weibull shape falls to one, so activation becomes memoryless instead of timer-like. We derive a closed form that keeps koff by treating the successful pass through the proofreading chain separately from the time lost to failed attempts. It matches exact medians to within 2% in 19 of 25 parameter sets, with a worst case of about 6%, and reproduces the loss of timer-like behavior. Because $Λ$ is computed from the Weibull prediction itself, it shows in advance how far that formula can be trusted; where it cannot, the new expression requires only a one-dimensional root find.

items.title: Automatic Construction of Strong Simple Baselines
items.summary: To rigorously establish the value of a novel deep learning method, it must be compared against appropriate baselines. As deep learning has become increasingly common in the physical and life sciences, there have been numerous cases in which apparent progress has turned out to be an artifact of omitted or missing baselines. In this work, we investigate whether this problem can be mitigated by using large language models to automate the construction of baselines. We assemble 36 supervised classification and regression tasks from peer-reviewed studies in Nature, Science, and Cell-family journals that investigate novel deep learning methods for scientific applications. We then use a language model to construct simple baselines for each task. These automatically constructed baselines are strong, recovering a median of 95.5% (mean 85.7%) of the gap between a trivial predictor and the score of the deep learning model. The median simple baseline matches or exceeds the performance of the deep learning model in 12 studies. We further examine the variation across scientific domains and publication venues and we characterize the effects of test-time compute and access to different levels of study context. As human peer review has struggled to keep up with the rapidly increasing volume of research articles in recent years, our results suggest that automated baseline construction is a practical and scalable check on deep learning contributions in the physical and life sciences.

items.title: Prospective Coding and Path Integration Emerge as Equilibrium Solutions of Self-Organizing Neural Networks with Firing-Rate Adaptation
items.summary: Continuous Attractor Neural Networks (CANNs) traditionally rely on pre-wired recurrent connectivity to model spatial representations, path integration, and anticipatory dynamics. However, the biological mechanisms through which this structured connectivity emerges via learning remain relatively unexplored. This work presents a theoretical framework revealing how continuous attractor connectivity and its computational properties self-organize through Hebbian plasticity, firing-rate adaptation, and global inhibition. We show that translationally invariant inputs naturally drive the emergence of stable, Gaussian-profiled feedforward weights.
