In addition, PMC requires no density evaluation, making it applicable to simulation-based inference, as we demonstrate in an application with protein images.

items.title: Efficient Gaussian Process Modeling for Large Replicated and Censored Data in Industrial Research
items.summary: Gaussian process regression is widely used for modeling responses in both physical and computer experiments. In practice, data from physical experiments may include replications and be subject to censoring due to equipment limitations or contextual constraints, and such datasets can be large, posing a scalability challenge for standard Gaussian process inference. Motivated by a real-world industrial research study, we develop a Gaussian process modeling framework that efficiently analyzes large replicated and censored data. Our approach integrates a Vecchia approximation for computational scalability with a likelihood-based formulation that fully exploits replication and rigorously incorporates information from censored observations, analogous to exact simulation from truncated distributions. Through experiments on synthetic data and a real case study from industrial research, we demonstrate that the proposed method yields improved predictive accuracy and reliable uncertainty quantification compared to existing approaches, making it well suited for large-scale applications with structured replication and incomplete data.

items.title: High-dimensional Four-Level Structured Functional Principal Component Analysis for Unbalanced Level Data with Application to Concussion Data
items.summary: We implement the Structured Functional Principal Component Analysis (SFPCA) framework of Shou et al. (2015) in a four-level nested setting with arbitrarily unbalanced group sizes at every level of the hierarchy. While the SFPCA framework can in principle accommodate deeper hierarchical structures, practical implementations remain challenging when the number of curves is large and the hierarchy is highly unbalanced. Our contributions are twofold. First, we operationalize SFPCA for four hierarchical levels with arbitrary unbalancedness across units. Second, we propose a memory-efficient computational strategy that makes the analysis of large collections of curves feasible on conventional hardware. In particular, we construct the four design-specific matrices required for the Method of Moments (MoM) estimators of the level-specific covariance operators while controlling their memory footprint, which would otherwise grow prohibitively with the number of curves. We illustrate the approach using three subsets of the NCAA-DoD Grand Alliance Concussion Assessment, Research, and Education (CARE) Consortium dataset (2014-2017).

items.title: Generalized and Scalable Deep Gaussian Process Emulation
items.summary: Gaussian process (GP) emulators have become essential tools for approximating complex simulators, significantly reducing computational demands in optimization, sensitivity analysis, and model calibration. While traditional GP emulators effectively model continuous and Gaussian-distributed simulator outputs with homogeneous variability, they typically struggle with discrete, heteroskedastic Gaussian, or non-Gaussian data, limiting their applicability to increasingly common stochastic simulators. A scalable Generalized Deep Gaussian Process (GDGP) emulation framework is introduced to accommodate simulators with heteroskedastic Gaussian outputs and a wide range of non-Gaussian response distributions, including Poisson, negative binomial, and categorical distributions. The GDGP framework leverages the expressiveness of DGPs and extends them to latent GP structures, enabling it to capture the complex, non-stationary behavior inherent in many simulators while also modeling non-Gaussian simulator outputs. GDGP is made scalable by incorporating the Vecchia approximation for settings with a large number of input locations, while also developing efficient inference procedures for handling large numbers of replicates. In particular, methodological developments are presented that further enhance the computation of the approach for heteroskedastic Gaussian responses. A series of synthetic and empirical examples demonstrates that these extensions deliver the practical application of GDGP emulators and a unified methodology capable of addressing diverse modeling challenges. The proposed GDGP framework is implemented in the open-source R package dgpsi.

items.title: Decoupling Distance and Networks: Hybrid Graph Attention-Geostatistical Methods for Spatio-temporal Risk Mapping
items.summary: Accurate spatial prediction and rigorous uncertainty quantification are central to modern spatial epidemiology and environmental risk analysis. We introduce a statistically principled hybrid modelling framework that integrates the nonlinear, attention-based representation learning capabilities of a dynamic Graph Attention Network (GATv2) with a latent Gaussian spatial process from model-based geostatistics (MBG). This framework jointly captures relational dependence encoded in graph structures and continuous spatial dependence governed by physical proximity. We evaluate the proposed model via a controlled simulation study and an applied analysis of malaria prevalence data, comparing its predictive accuracy, calibration, and uncertainty quantification against classical geostatistical models and standalone GATv2 architectures. Our analyses show that GATv2 captures complex nonlinear interactions but fails to account for residual spatial autocorrelation, resulting in miscalibrated predictive distributions. Conversely, geostatistical models provide coherent uncertainty quantification through structured covariance functions yet are constrained by linear predictor assumptions and by their reliance on Euclidean distance to encode spatial structure. By integrating attention mechanisms and nonlinear features with an explicit probabilistic spatial random field, the hybrid model captured the relational dependence, consistently improved predictive accuracy, and provided more realistic uncertainty quantification in both simulation and applied settings. Overall, the findings demonstrate that the hybrid model constitutes a statistically coherent and empirically robust framework for modelling complex spatial and spatio-temporal processes in settings where both distance-based and structure-based dependencies operate.

items.title: Bayesian Superpopulation Models for Population-Based Diabetes Surveillance Using Multi-Site Electronic Health Record Data
items.summary: Electronic health records (EHRs) are increasingly used for disease surveillance. However, data collected in EHRs may not be a representative sample of the target population for inference. Methods for EHR-based surveillance remain in their nascence. In addition to simple weighting approaches, researchers have used multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP), a popular technique for finite population quantity estimation that remains understudied in EHRs. We are motivated by a US-based collaborative to modernize diabetes surveillance using EHR data from different health system centers across the country. To estimate type 1 diabetes (T1D) prevalence in children and adolescents, we propose and evaluate three Bayesian superpopulation models that are distinguished by how they account for two important features of EHR data: unobserved heterogeneity and data sparsity. The three models include an analysis of variance-inspired approach; a model with geographic effects varying by demographic subgroup; and MRP, which we consider as the reference model. We apply the models to estimate prevalence overall and in demographic- and geographic-based subgroups. Using plasmode simulations, we evaluate model estimation performance while preserving the complexity of the EHR data. Our results show that the superpopulation-based prevalence estimates were higher than those observed in the EHR sample alone, with the magnitude of the differences varying by health system center. The bias and coverage probabilities of MRP markedly worsened when the EHR sample size was smaller or the selection mechanism was more complex. Overall, the superpopulation model based on analysis of variance demonstrated the best estimation performance.

items.title: Predictability over Volatility: When simple strategies help households save on fuel
items.summary: What reasonable strategies can households use to save on gasoline or diesel purchases under different pricing functions? We assess basic strategies households might employ under a simplified model of a 10-gallon tank, fixed fuel consumption between refill opportunities, and price changes at each opportunity to refill. Purchases always fill the tank, and if the tank is empty, it must be refilled regardless of price. We explore three strategy types: price-independent (filling once the tank is below a specific level), price-dependent (filling when the price is below the last $n$ days or their average), and mixed (filling only below a set level, and then only when the price is below the last $n$ days or their average). We construct price functions from the nearest-in-time US weekly averages of regular gasoline and diesel, filling in higher-frequency values with a smoothing spline, linear interpolation, and random draws from normal and uniform distributions based on national averages. Additional simulations are built using Brownian motion. Together, these pricing models span a wide range of volatilities. We find that price-independent strategies are effective for the spline and linear functions, which have low volatility, while price-dependent strategies are effective for the normal and uniform distributions, which are highly volatile. Brownian motion, despite its mid-range volatility, admits no effective strategy. Our findings suggest that the predictability of price movements, whether prices trend or revert toward a stable level, matters more for household strategies than overall volatility: the random walk is volatile in the middle of our range yet offers households no usable signal. Policymakers can therefore assist households by addressing how prices move from day to day, not only the retail prices they face.

items.title: Exact signal recovery from generative priors with sigmoid output activation
items.summary: We show exact signal recovery in generative compressed sensing for feedforward neural networks with piecewise-linear activations and a final sigmoid activation, with no assumption of expansivity. Consider a ReLU network of depth $d$ with a sigmoid final activation, whose input layer, of dimension $k$, is the narrowest, and let $K$ be the geometric mean of the widths of its layers. We show that, with high probability, all signals of the range whose entries lie in $[δ, 1 - δ]$ are uniformly recovered from $m \gtrsim k(d \log(K/k) + \log(1+\log(1/δ)))$ measurements.

items.title: Recovery Theory for Projected Power Iterations in Permutation Synchronization
items.summary: We study the projected power method for permutation synchronization: recovering $n$ unknown permutations of $m$ objects from pairwise relative permutations, observed independently with probability $p$ and independently corrupted by uniform permutations with probability $1-π_0$. Our main theorem establishes uniform one-step contraction for all estimates with optimally aligned block-error fraction at most $1/2-ε$, for fixed $ε>0$, including measurement-dependent estimates. When $np\ge C_0\log(n)$ and $m=o(npπ_0^2)$, one update contracts the error by a factor $O(m/(npπ_0^2))$, up to a floor of $O(e^{-c\min\{m\,npπ_0^2,\,npπ_0\}} + \log(n) / n)$. Thus, every initialization in this majority basin achieves $o(1)$ error after one update and maintains it uniformly over subsequent iterations. A reference-block spectral initializer enters the basin with probability $1-o(1)$, yielding end-to-end almost-exact recovery. If additionally $\min\{m\,npπ_0^2,\,npπ_0\} \ge C\log(n)$ for sufficiently large $C$, the method achieves exact recovery in finitely many iterations. We also establish prescribed-block recovery under weaker conditions for measurement-independent estimates and extend the guarantees to independent permutation-valued corruptions with uniform mean and to partial permutations with common visible support.

items.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Global-local Clustering of High-dimensional Functions
items.summary: There is a rich literature on clustering functional data with applications to time-series modeling, trajectory data, and even spatiotemporal applications. Existing methods are classified into two categories of global clustering that assigns an identical membership over the whole domain, and local clustering that allows multiple memberships based on the sub-domains. Classical literature has typically focused on global clustering that may struggle with degenerate clustering or produce numerous spurious clusters for high-dimensional functions. In contrast, a limited number of local clustering approaches have been proposed that are not scalable to high-dimensional functions and have limited theoretical guarantees. Focusing on basis expansions for high-dimensional functions, we propose a novel global-local framework that partitions coefficients into exclusive subsets and imposes independent Dirichlet process priors on each subset. The proposed framework reduces the total number of possible clustering configurations compared to local clustering and therefore provides greater scalability, while simultaneously providing enhanced flexibility compared to global clustering by relaxing the assumption of identical clustering for all elements in the high-dimensional function. Moreover, the proposed method incorporates spatially correlated errors to provide better model fitting and shows posterior consistency properties that asymptotically recover the true density of random functions. An efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm is developed for implementation. Extensive simulations involving images illustrate the improved scalability, clustering, and function estimation under the proposed method compared to classical approaches. We apply the proposed approach to a spatial transcriptomics application where the goal is to infer clusters of genes with distinct spatial patterns of expressions.

items.title: Transport along Local Annealing Paths: Wasserstein Geometry and Multimodal Sampling
items.summary: Variational approaches to learning transport maps for multimodal sampling can suffer from mode collapse. One way to mitigate this problem is to learn transport along a prescribed path of intermediate distributions defined by geometric annealing. We show that annealing can take a substantial detour in Wasserstein space: when mass moves between modes, the path can be much longer than the distance between its endpoints. We further link path geometry to transport learning, showing that long annealing paths can slow population optimization, while sufficiently regular paths permit rapid convergence. Motivated by these findings, we propose componentwise annealed transport (CAT) to reduce the need for mass transfer between modes. Starting from a mode-informed mixture reference, CAT constructs an exact mixture decomposition of the target and learns separate transport maps along componentwise annealing paths. We estimate the component weights separately and show that these estimates remain consistent even when the learned flows are inexact. We also develop adaptive annealing schedules guided by transport effort. Experiments on multimodal synthetic distributions and Bayesian inference problems demonstrate improvements in transport learning and sampling efficiency.

items.title: Geometric ergodicity of the block Gibbs sampler for Bayesian linear mixed models with scale mixtures of normal random effects
items.summary: We study a Bayesian linear mixed model whose random effects follow a scale mixture of normal distributions with an arbitrary mixing distribution, a class that contains the Student-t, slash, contaminated normal, normal-generalized inverse Gaussian and Laplace laws. Conditionally conjugate priors lead to a three-block Gibbs sampler that alternates between the variance components, the latent precision weights, and the regression coefficients together with the random effects. Using a drift function built from fractional powers, we give sufficient conditions for geometric ergodicity of this chain, which involve a moment of the mixing distribution of some order larger than 1/2 and its behaviour near the origin. An equivariance of the sampler under rescaling of the design then shows that the conditions hold for all the families above, including Student-t random effects with any degrees of freedom, for every random-effects design matrix, full rank or not, with the rank entering only the conditions on the priors of the variance components. Together with posterior moment bounds, geometric ergodicity justifies Monte Carlo standard errors and effective-sample-size stopping rules for the regression coefficients and the log-variance components. Simulations examine these procedures at practical run lengths: joint confidence regions need a correction for the number of batches, and under sequential stopping their observed coverage remains slightly below the nominal level. We illustrate the methods with longitudinal beta-HCG measurements from early pregnancies, in which the latent weights reveal larger between-subject variability among abnormal pregnancies.

items.title: Post-Progression Treatment Regimes and the Limits of Cross-Trial Survival Transport
items.summary: Models transporting overall survival (OS) effects across clinical trials fail when they ignore the "post-progression treatment regime"---the subsequent therapy rates across biomarker strata and randomized arms. Because this trial-level regime is systematically omitted from published reports, standard correction families are structurally inadequate: crossover adjustments target an unrealistic counterfactual with zero subsequent therapy, erasing critical environmental differences; population adjustments (including MAIC, STC, AIPW, and density ratios) match baseline individual covariates, leaving trial-level regimes mismatched. We show that these correction approaches carry near-identical bias, proving the failure is informational rather than methodological. Simulations demonstrate that ignoring the target setting's landscape can leave the directional sign of the transported effect completely undetermined, even when mechanisms are fully known. Conversely, providing the target regime to a regime-aware estimator successfully recovers the true treatment effect. Code is available at https://github.com/felizzi/post-progression-transport-WMHS-NeurIPS-2026.

items.title: A covariance density for a point process and a random field
items.summary: The spatial point process literature offers a well-developed theory for characterizing covariances within a point process or between different point processes using joint intensity functions or cross joint intensity functions. However, similar summary statistics are missing for characterizing the covariance between a point process and a random field. We introduce a normalized mixed covariance density that fills this gap for covariances between variables of a random field and linear functionals of a point process. We construct a non-parametric kernel estimator of the covariance density and a data-driven method for bandwidth selection. We further use our estimate of the covariance density to test the dependence between a point process and a random field. Several existing tests require observations of the random field at the events of the point process. These are often not available when the random field is sampled on a grid unrelated to the point process. Then interpolation is needed to impute random field values at point process events. Our covariance density estimate in contrast does not require interpolation. We investigate the performance of our non-parametric estimator and the method for bandwidth selection in applications to simulated and real data.

items.title: Near-Minimax Sample Complexity for Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning under Generative Models
items.summary: In multi-objective reinforcement learning, preferences may be specified only after data collection, requiring one dataset to support a continuum of reward trade-offs. We study finite discounted Markov decision processes with unknown transitions, $S$ states, $A$ actions, and $m$ known reward functions taking values in $[0,1]$, given access to a generative model. The learner must provide an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy for every convex combination of these rewards without further sampling, with a guarantee that holds simultaneously over all preferences and initial states. Writing $H=(1-γ)^{-1}$, we establish the constant-confidence minimax sample complexity $\widetildeΘ\!\left( \frac{SAH^3}{\varepsilon^2}\min\{S,\log(em)\} \right)$, where the suppressed factors are logarithmic in $S,A,H,\varepsilon^{-1}$ and the dependence on $m$ is explicit. Thus, up to these logarithmic factors, the worst-case statistical cost of supporting all preferences grows logarithmically with the number of objectives and saturates at the number of states. The upper bound uses uniform state--action sampling and empirical planning, with reward rounding in the logarithmic-objective regime. Its analysis chains optimal-value increments over covers of the reward hull. A one-sided Bellman variance bound controls signed value differences under a second transition kernel, preserving the $H^3\varepsilon^{-2}$ dependence. A complementary uniform guarantee for all bounded rewards yields the state-dimension saturation. We establish lower bounds matching up to logarithmic factors through a rare-exit construction with subset rewards and action encoding. These bounds apply to adaptive simulator queries and arbitrary randomized history-dependent output policies, while the upper bounds are attained by deterministic stationary policies.

items.title: Support Vector Machines Directly Minimise KL Divergence
items.summary: Support vector machines (SVMs) are fundamentally grounded in geometric margin maximisation and currently lack a mainstream probabilistic interpretation. This keeps them theoretically isolated from probabilistic machine learning models that are naturally comparable and combinable. In this paper, we bridge this gap by proving that the dual objectives of both support vector classification and support vector regression are exact, constrained Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence minimisation tasks between two Gaussian measures. We further show that this same divergence formulation recovers the exact objective function for kernel ridge regression when domain constraints are removed and $L^2$ regularisation is applied. By demonstrating that SVM duals directly minimise relative entropy, our results provide a unified information-theoretic model for standard kernel machines and lay the foundation for unifying broader kernel-based algorithms under probability theory.

items.title: A Unified Framework for Training-Dataset Aggregation and Exact Machine Unlearning via Gibbs Probability Measures
items.summary: In this paper, three operations on Gibbs probability measures are studied: renormalization, normalized log-linear combination, and nesting. The resulting measures are shown to be Gibbs probability measures with explicit expressions for their objective functions, reference measures, and regularization factors. These measures are further characterized as unique solutions to optimization problems involving linear combinations of the original objective functions, subject to either relative entropy regularization or relative entropy constraints. When the reference measures are probability measures, geometric interpretations of these three operations are established involving Pythagorean identities and exponential geodesics.A central result is the equivalence between nesting and normalized log-linear combinations of Gibbs probability measures. These results are then applied to supervised machine learning with Gibbs algorithms, which are represented by Gibbs probability measures. In this context, either through nesting or log-linear combinations, Gibbs algorithms trained on local datasets are used to form new Gibbs algorithms trained upon the aggregation of all local training datasets. Interestingly, the parameters of such operations, determine the weights of each training data point on the aggregated dataset. %Operations on local Gibbs probability measures are shown to control the contributions of training data. This observation is leveraged for achieving: (a) exact machine unlearning in centralized, decentralized, and federated learning systems; and (b) centralized-equivalent performance, in the sense of producing algorithms trained on the aggregation of all local datasets in decentralized and federated learning .

items.title: Generalized Hyperrectangular Prediction Sets in Multivariate Conformal Prediction
items.summary: In multivariate conformal prediction, many nonconformity scores yield prediction sets with complex geometry (e.g., ellipsoids or density level sets) that are difficult to interpret and visualize. Hyperrectangles offer a practical alternative by providing one interval per output. We extend this notion to Cartesian products of arbitrary one-dimensional sets, which we call generalized hyperrectangles. We introduce a rectangularization framework that turns any continuous multivariate nonconformity score, or conditional density, into one yielding generalized hyperrectangular prediction sets with finite-sample coverage. We establish key geometric properties of our rectangularization framework and provide useful intuitions on generalized hyperrectangles. We further establish a representation theorem showing that a broad class of hyperrectangular conformal methods based on max-aggregated coordinate-wise scores can be interpreted as rectangularizations of implicit conditional densities. Through synthetic and real-world experiments, we quantify the efficiency cost of rectangularization, while highlighting its benefits, especially for practical applications of uncertainty quantification.

items.title: Towards Efficient Whole Page Ranking with One-Pass Inference
items.summary: Whole-page ranking jointly optimizes advertisements and organic content to balance business outcomes and user engagement under complex layout and business constraints. Existing non-autoregressive (NAR) approaches enable efficient page generation but typically score candidate items independently of previously selected items, limiting their ability to capture order-dependent interactions. Autoregressive (AR) methods address this limitation through sequential conditioning, but incur substantial inference overhead that challenges large-scale deployment. Bridging this quality-efficiency gap remains a challenge in industrial whole-page ranking. We propose Multi-Item Scoring (MIS), a prefix-aware NAR-style framework that incorporates sequential context into efficient multi-item scoring. MIS integrates global candidate interactions, localized prefix conditioning, and position-aware scoring within a shared representation architecture. By computing reusable representations once per request and performing lightweight prefix-conditioned scoring during constrained beam search, MIS captures important sequential dependencies without repeated full-model inference. Experiments on KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS demonstrate that MIS approaches the generation quality of an autoregressive CGA baseline while achieving 4.07x and 3.54x faster CPU decoding, respectively. In a randomized evaluation on a large-scale social-video platform, MIS improves the realization metric by 0.104% and watch time by 0.058%, while reducing ranking-service CPU consumption by 9.73%. These results demonstrate that prefix-aware multi-item scoring can narrow the quality gap between NAR and AR generation while retaining the efficiency required for industrial scalability.

items.title: Tight Lower Bounds under Matched High-Order Hölder Smoothness and Uniform Convexity
items.summary: In this paper, we provide tight lower bounds for minimizing high-order Hölder-smooth and uniformly convex functions when their orders match. Specifically, we consider functions whose $p^{th}$-order derivatives are Hölder continuous with degree $ν$ and parameter $H$, and that are uniformly convex with degree $q$ and parameter $σ$. When these orders match, namely, $q = p + ν$, we show that any deterministic algorithm with access to derivatives up to order $p$ requires $Ω\left(\left(\frac{H}σ\right)^{\frac{2}{3(p+ν)-2}}\log\frac{Δ_0}ε\right)$ oracle calls to reduce an initial optimality gap of $Δ_0$ to $ε$. This matches the corresponding upper bound and establishes a higher-order uniformly convex counterpart to Nesterov's classical first-order lower bound for strongly convex functions. Rather than directly generalizing Nesterov's classical quadratic-chain construction, we develop a multiscale phase-wise construction that preserves previous oracle responses while maintaining global Hölder smoothness and uniform convexity. Our result resolves the matched case left open by existing lower bounds for the two asymmetric regimes.

items.title: TOPPO: Rethinking PPO for Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Critic Balancing
items.summary: Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and its variants dominate Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) due to their off-policy sample efficiency, while on-policy methods such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remain underexplored. We diagnose that PPO in MTRL suffers from a previously overlooked issue: critic-side gradient ill-conditioning, which may cause tail tasks to stall while easy tasks dominate the value function's updates. To address this, we propose TOPPO (Tail-Optimized PPO), a reformulation of PPO via Critic Balancing -- a set of modules that improve gradient conditioning and balance learning dynamics across tasks. Unlike prior approaches that rely on modular architectures or large models, TOPPO targets the optimization bottleneck within PPO itself. Empirically, on the Meta-World+ MT50 benchmark, TOPPO achieves stronger mean and tail-task performance than prior SAC-family and ARS-family methods while using substantially fewer parameters and reaching their final performance in fewer environment steps. Notably, TOPPO matches or surpasses strong SAC baselines early in training and maintains superior performance at full budget. Ablations confirm the effectiveness of each module in TOPPO and provide insights into their interactions. Our results demonstrate that, with proper optimization, on-policy methods can rival or exceed off-policy approaches in MTRL, challenging the prevailing reliance on SAC and highlighting critic-side gradient conditioning as the central bottleneck.

items.title: Inference on the Reliability Function with Type-I Censored Weibull Data
items.summary: Reliability inference based on parametric distributions is an important problem in electrical and mechanical engineering. Most existing methods rely on approximations or bootstrap procedures, which may not perform satisfactorily when data are censored or sample sizes are small. Hence, there is an urgent need to develop exact inference approaches for these situations. This article introduces a new approach for deriving exact parametric tests and confidence intervals for distributions such as the lognormal, loglogistic, and Weibull. We revisit several issues in classical reliability analysis based on the survival function. Because lifetime data are often censored in practice, the proposed approach is designed for such settings. We illustrate the method using the Weibull distribution and expect it to be applicable to other widely used lifetime distributions such as the loglogistic distribution. Our Simulation study show that the new approach provides better performance than existing methods when handling complete data and type-I censored data. Two numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the application of the proposed method. The proposed method is expected to be widely applicable in reliability engineering and survival analysis, offering a robust alternative to existing methods, particularly in scenarios involving censored data and small sample sizes.

items.title: A simple adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method for unconstrained convex optimization in $p$-norm geometry
items.summary: Efficient preconditioning plays an important role in large-scale first-order optimization. In this paper, we propose an adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging ($\text{A}^2$ODA) method for unconstrained convex optimization that adopts low-cost preconditioning based on $p$-norm geometry for $p\in[2,\infty]$. The method is line-search-free and employs a new stepsize selection technique based on an aggregated affine lower model. Its update structure is simple and unified across $p\in[2,\infty]$, with the case $p>2$ requiring no more elaborate updates than the Euclidean case $p=2$. Under a generalized local smoothness condition, we derive a convergence bound that separates the effects of constant and gap-dependent curvature, with the latter potentially yielding faster-decaying terms. In the special case of local smoothness, this bound recovers a nearly optimal convergence rate.

items.title: Quantification of Tail-trimming Effects for Interval CVaR Based Nonlinear Regression
items.summary: The tail trimming strategy is widely adopted for robustness against outlier contamination in statistical learning and operations research. However, it generally lacks the thorough understanding that to what extent the tail-trimming technique is effective for nonlinear regression. In this paper, we address the robust nonlinear regression based on the so-called interval conditional value-at-risk (In-CVaR), which is introduced to guard against outliers by trimming extreme losses. We first analyze the trimming effect of the In-CVaR based estimator under distributional perturbation. Our first finding is that the In-CVaR based estimator is qualitatively robust under distributional perturbation in terms of the Prokhorov metric if and only if the largest portion of losses is trimmed. Furthermore, under sample contamination, we derive a probably approximately correct (PAC) bound for the In-CVaR based estimator, showing that the preliminary covariate filtering that is customary in the literature is not needed for In-CVaR based regression. The nonconvexity of the In-CVaR objective, together with unboundedness of covariates, responses and parameter space create the technical challenges for our developed theory, and thus necessitate the new treatment of the qualitative robustness and PAC analysis. Overall, this study rigorously analyzes robustness properties of In-CVaR based nonlinear regression models, which illustrates to what extent the right tail-trimming of the loss by In-CVaR risk measure is essential and effective for robust nonlinear regression. These theoretical findings are further supported by numerical experiments.

items.title: Interpretable Social Network Churn Prediction via Ergodic Markov Chains
items.summary: Predicting social network churn before it becomes visible in aggregate metrics remains an open challenge, particularly in enterprise settings where heterogeneous usage patterns, sparse data, and deployment constraints preclude standard supervised approaches. We formalize this problem as finite-step engagement projection over contributor-role Markov chains, with a stationary-distribution interpretation for ergodic chains in the long-run limit. For each engagement feature type within a network (e.g., Q&A, communities, articles, etc.), users are classified monthly into four behavioral states and a transition matrix is estimated from six months of history. Six-step propagation yields a label-free projection of the contributor mix; for ergodic chains, the Perron-Frobenius theorem establishes convergence under repeated propagation. Comparing projected future engagement to current engagement produces the Health Ratio, a single score requiring no trained model, no labels, and no infrastructure beyond SQL. Validated across seven rolling prediction windows on 11,500+ tenant-level networks, the Health Ratio achieves mean AUC 0.917 with a 156 times churn-rate gradient across risk tiers, outperforming all single-signal baselines and the growth-adjusted variant previously deployed in production. An ablation study shows that six-step propagation achieves similar churn discrimination to the eigenvector-based score. Deployed on Microsoft Engage since October 2025, the framework powers customer health monitoring and has enabled proactive intervention on at-risk networks before decline becomes visible in traditional metrics.

items.title: Logarithmic Regret for Alternating Mirror Descent
items.summary: Alternating online mirror descent (AltOMD) is a simple learning rule for zero-sum games, which improves upon simultaneous OMD numerically and theoretically. Previous work obtained $O(T^{1/3})$ and $O(T^{1/5})$ regret bounds for AltOMD, by leveraging modified-energy-function-based analyses. However, settling whether AltOMD achieves near-constant regret has remained an open question. In this paper we resolve the question of whether AltOMD achieves near-constant regret in the affirmative. In particular, we show an $O(log(T))$ regret bound on the sum of the players' external regrets for any two-player zero-sum bilinear game with compact convex strategy sets, under mild regularity assumptions on the regularizers. We verify that our assumptions hold for the negative entropy regularizer, thereby obtaining logarithmic regret for the alternating multiplicative weights updates algorithm. The regret bound also yields an $O(log(T)/T)$ duality gap bound for the averaged strategies.

items.title: Shrinkage prior for implicit generative models
items.summary: Implicit generative models based on deep neural networks have revolutionized many scientific fields, from weather research to language generation. They successfully model complex random objects arising in real-world problems. In this work, we propose a sample-efficient training mechanism for these models. Our approach leverages regularized inference with shrinkage priors and generalized Bayes. In the large $p$ (parameter dimension) and small $n$ (sample size) setting, sparsity-inducing priors have been successfully used for linear regression when $p \gg n$. However, their application to implicit generative models remains challenging due to the intractability of the likelihood function. To address this, we adapt a scoring rule posterior based on a strictly proper scoring rule, following the generalized Bayes framework. We then propose a block SGMCMC within Gibbs sampling mechanism. This enables efficient exploration of high-dimensional parameter spaces by identifying a sparse representation of neural implicit generative models. We demonstrate the performance of our proposed method through experiments on $p \gg n$ linear regression and an application of neural generative models.

items.title: Post-stratified importance sampling
items.summary: Importance sampling is a building block of modern statistical computing, but the weighted estimate is prone to high or infinite variance. Moreover, its empirical standard error is often unreliable, leaving importance sampling without practical uncertainty quantification. Motivated by multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP) in survey sampling, we propose post-stratified importance sampling (PIS) for estimating target expectations from proposal draws. PIS reformulates arbitrarily high-dimensional weighting into two one-dimensional probabilistic modeling problems: regression for the conditional mean given the importance ratio and marginal density estimation for the importance ratio. Different modeling choices yield a family of PIS estimators, encompassing ordinary importance sampling as a special case. We develop a model-based implementation that combines one-dimensional Gaussian process regression for the conditional mean and score-informed heavy-tailed density estimation for the marginal law, using both the observed weights and the available density evaluations. We study the oracle gains of PIS and establish consistency under general and model-specific conditions. Simulations and applications to cross-validation demonstrate improvements in estimation accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

items.title: Scalable Bayesian inference for time-discretised Markov jump processes via exchangeable particle Gibbs
items.summary: Inference in stochastic reaction-network models, such as the susceptible-exposed-infectious-recovered (SEIR) epidemic model, is crucial for understanding the dynamics of interacting systems in epidemiology, ecology, and systems biology. These models are typically represented as Markov jump processes (MJPs), with discrete, noisy observations and intractable likelihoods. Particle Markov chain Monte Carlo (PMCMC) offers a natural mechanism for inference on these hidden Markov models, but, even in moderate dimensional state spaces, particle degeneracy typically leads to poor mixing of the PMCMC algorithm. This paper focuses on improving the efficiency of particle Gibbs for inference on reaction networks by addressing the degeneracy problem. Building on recent work on the exchangeable particle Gibbs (xPG) sampler for diffusions, this paper develops a novel version of xPG tailored to discrete-state-space reaction networks, where randomness is driven by Poisson processes rather than Brownian motion. We focus on the $τ$-leap discretisation of the MJPs. The proposed method retains the exchangeability framework of xPG while adapting it to the structural and computational challenges specific to reaction networks. The new method is applied to several examples, including four coupled SEIR models, where it substantially improves mixing efficiency compared with standard particle Gibbs. In this example, xPG improves sample efficiency by more than an order of magnitude relative to standard particle Gibbs, making inference feasible in hours rather than weeks. As part of our tuning strategy, we provide a mechanism for tuning the number of particles that is applicable more generally, to any particle Gibbs algorithm.

items.title: Post-Inference Model Chaining: A Problem Statement and a Model-based Bootstrap for Training End-to-End Digital Twins
items.summary: End-to-end digital twins can be constructed by fitting separate stage models and connecting them after inference. We investigate the Frequentist prediction properties of a commonly used Monte Carlo simulation scheme that forwards complete predictive draws through such a chain when measured stage outputs contain independent normal errors, but the latent stage means are deterministic. Analytical two-stage examples show persistent asymptotic interval and coverage inflation and, with quadratic propagation, mean bias dependent on the parameters to be estimated. Simulations of four- and eight-stage linear-quadratic univariate chains with 7, 15 or 30 training runs demonstrate pronounced input-dependent distortions. A diagnostic using error-free latent training predictors shows that the effect is mainly not attributable to errors in variables, but to the MCSim approach even showing underestimation of coverage. We propose a model-based bootstrap: an initial chain forwards fitted means, bootstrap chains are refitted on fixed-center bootstrap data while forwarding their mean prediction, and a target-stage future error enters a studentized prediction root. Across the investigated scenarios, relative mean bias is substantially reduced, and coverage is closer to the nominal 90%. At sample size 30, the eight-stage bootstrap has mean width ratios of 1.16-1.42 relative to the known-parameter normal reference, compared with 4.11-4.97 for observed-to-observed MCSim. These results support improved endpoint prediction in the tested setting. Further investigations of the bootstrap scheme in the supplement for a bivariate 6-stage process show similar satisfactory results.

items.title: The Hidden Markov Ising Model with Exogenous Covariates
items.summary: The Ising model, a type of Markov Random Field, from statistical physics has a long history of modeling spatial and network data as well as particle interactions. In this work, we consider inserting the Ising model into the framework of a Hidden Markov Model, a type of Bayesian Network, to model temporal state changes in a sequence of Ising observations. While this is entirely a discrete probability model, a main challenge is the fitting of such a probabilistic graphical model due to the exponential intractability of normalizing constants within the Ising model. To circumvent this problem, we consider the usage of maximum pseudolikelihood estimators that have a long history in Markov Random Fields. Validity of the pseudolikelihood Baum-Welch algorithm, model identifiability under likelihood, and consistency for large networks is also proved. The proposed Hidden Markov Ising Model is further extended to incorporate exogenous variables resulting in a hybrid hidden Markov autologistic model with graphical dependencies integrated into the model. This model is applied to a five year sequence of weekly gun violence events across the 3109 counties of the continental United States to identify state changes in gun violence activity from 2021 to 2025.

items.title: Privacy for Free in Efficient Agnostic Halfspace Learning
items.summary: We provide the first computationally efficient, differentially private algorithms for agnostically learning halfspaces. In particular, we study three different settings of agnostic learning: improper learning under Gaussian and log-concave marginals; proper learning under Gaussian marginals; and semi-agnostic learning under Gaussian marginals. In all three aforementioned settings, the added cost in the sample complexity due to privacy matches the respective non-private sample complexity, implying that we get privacy for free.

items.title: Exact association-test distributions for prior-informed stepwise SNP prioritization
items.summary: Prioritizing causal variants in Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) is challenging due to linkage disequilibrium and high dimensionality. We propose an iterative algorithm for the selection of genetic variables that allows the integration of biological priors. The proposed algorithm requires the specification of the power function of a test statistic and incorporates a priori information on each SNP. We derive the approximate and exact distributions of several commonly used test statistics. At each step of the proposed algorithm, we select the SNP with the largest a posteriori probability of being causal. We consider several stopping criteria for the algorithm. We conduct comprehensive simulation studies to assess the performance of several versions of the proposed algorithm and to make a comparison to some existing competitors. The use of the proposed prioritization algorithm is illustrated with a cis-eQTL application to a human gene-expression data, using European discovery and Yoruba cross-population replication.

items.title: Statistical Theory in the Age of Machine-Assisted Mathematics
items.summary: The computational revolution is advancing at an unprecedented pace. The combination of proof-assistant technologies and generative AI tools has recently enabled the solution of complex problems in pure mathematics at a scale that seemed unattainable only a few years ago, but they have not yet become standard tools in the development of statistical theory. In this paper we do not present new theoretical results; instead, we discuss five case studies involving classical problems in statistics and describe how a machine proof checker changes the thought process behind their proofs, in order to stimulate reflection on how these technologies may transform theoretical research and advanced statistical education. Statistical theory compresses mathematical content into expressions such as ``under the usual regularity conditions''; once AI writes the proofs and machines check them, the human reader is left with the statement and its hypotheses, which is exactly what such expressions compress. Against the fear that automation erodes skills, our experience was the opposite: what changes is the job of the theorist, which moves from the steps of a proof to its statement. The new paradigm can have positive effect also on methodologists and applied statisticians, because these tools allow for quick and precise check of formal guarantees necessary to justify the application of a specific model and/or methodology. We draw consequences for refereeing, doctoral teaching, and we encourage a collective effort toward shared formal libraries for statistics. Just as high-level programming languages revolutionized empirical research, machine-assisted formalization may introduce a new paradigm for the development, verification, and communication of statistical theory.

items.title: Macrocanonical Generator Networks: Data-Efficient Neural Surrogates for Amortized Physics Simulation
items.summary: Many scientific simulations are computationally expensive, limiting their use in simulation-based inference, uncertainty quantification, and decision making. We introduce macrocanonical generator networks, a framework for learning fast, data-efficient neural surrogates for amortized simulation of stationary physical processes by matching multiscale statistics of a target process. Inspired by microcanonical maximum-entropy synthesis, which matches feature statistics per sample by inner-loop optimization, our approach instead trains a neural generator to satisfy the same constraints in expectation, preserving physically realistic sample-to-sample fluctuations. We prove that gradient-descent training induces preconditioned gradient-descent dynamics in sample space that inherit the symmetry-preservation properties of the microcanonical gradient descent of Bruna and Mallat, amortizing its per-sample inner-loop optimization into a single training run after which every sample is generated in one forward pass. We further show that residual generator parameterizations initialized near the identity, trained with a small learning rate, preserve entropy locally during early optimization and mitigate mode collapse. Experiments on cosmology and fluid simulations show that macrocanonical generators recover realistic samples from extremely small training sets, in some cases a single training example, while generating new realizations more than $10^6$ times faster per sample than the reference simulator and more than $10^3$ times faster than microcanonical gradient descent. The trained generators can be reused for downstream pretraining, including simulation-based inference, providing a data-efficient route to multi-fidelity scientific machine learning workflows.

items.title: A Random Matrix Analysis of Symmetric Tensor Unfolding
items.summary: We study a fundamental problem in machine learning: partial recovery of a planted signal $\boldsymbol{v} \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ from a spiked tensor $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{X}} = λ\, \boldsymbol{v}^{\otimes p} + \boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$, where $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$ has symmetric Gaussian entries of variance $\asymp n^{-1}$. While previous works replace $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$ by an i.i.d. standard Gaussian tensor to circumvent technical difficulties caused by dependencies, this paper directly analyzes the symmetric model via random matrix theory. We show that the square unfolding algorithm is subject to a sharp phase transition for partial recovery at $λ\asymp n^{(p-2) / 4}$, validating an open conjecture from Montanari and Richard (2014). We get precise expressions for the limiting spectral distribution, deterministic equivalent, phase transition threshold and overlap. The main message is that unfolded symmetric tensors spectrally behave like standard Wigner matrices, up to simple transformations accounting for high-order symmetries. We consider extensions to multiple orthogonal spikes, recursive unfolding and non-square unfolding via disproportionate random matrix theory, leading to an interesting conjectured statistical-computational tradeoff regarding the choice of unfolding: square versus long.

items.title: Beyond Multi-Index Models: Learning Intersections of Degree-2 PTFs
items.summary: We give an algorithm for PAC learning intersections of $k$ degree-2 polynomial threshold functions over $R^d$ under a Gaussian distribution. Our algorithm achieves classification error $ε$ using $d^{O(k)}2^{O_k(\log^3(1/ε))}$ time and samples, improving over the $d^{O(k^2/ε^2)}$ running time of the polynomial regression approach. To our knowledge, our result is the first to obtain a dimension exponent independent of the accuracy parameter, even for $k=2$. We complement our algorithmic result with an SQ lower bound showing that the complexity dependence of $d^{Ω(k)}$ is unavoidable. Lifting the input to polynomial features turns the target into an intersection of $k$ halfspaces. This suggests using the first two labeled moments for subspace recovery. In the lifted space, however, these moments can reveal nothing. Our starting point is a Gaussian comparison theorem showing that, for sufficiently regular defining quadratics, the labeled moments needed for subspace recovery are approximately preserved. To handle arbitrary defining quadratics, we establish a new structural result showing that every direction with significant resampling influence can be detected through degree-$O(k)$ moments. These results yield an initial $d^{O(k)}2^{\mathrm{poly}_k(1/ε)}$-time learner using adaptive restrictions. To improve the exponential dependence on $1/ε$, we develop a two-stage dimension-reduction approach that avoids the costly adaptive partitioning. After identifying a subspace containing all directions with large influence, we use generalized regularity and Gaussian comparison to recover the remaining relevant quadratic features through a new derivative-based moment operator. The recovered features support an intersection close to the target. Combining them with robust hinge-loss minimization gives our quasipolynomial-time learner.

items.title: The Pivotal Information Criterion
items.summary: The Bayesian and Akaike information criteria aim at finding a good balance between under- and over-fitting. They are extensively used every day by practitioners. Yet we contend they suffer from at least two afflictions: their penalty parameters $λ=\log n$ and $λ=2$ are too small, leading to many false discoveries, and their inherent (best subset) discrete optimization is infeasible in high dimension. We alleviate these issues with the pivotal information criterion: PIC is defined as a continuous optimization problem, and the PIC penalty parameter $λ$ is selected at the detection boundary (under pure noise). PIC's choice of $λ$ is an upper quantile of a statistic that we prove to be (asymptotically) pivotal, provided the loss function is appropriately transformed. As a result, simulations show a phase transition in the probability of exact support recovery with PIC, a phenomenon studied with no noise in compressed sensing. Applied to real data, for similar predictive performances, PIC selects the least complex model among state-of-the-art learners.

items.title: Conformal prediction regions for dependent censored lifetimes
items.summary: Joint-life insurance and annuity benefits depend on two or more dependent lifetimes, which portfolio data observe only up to a valuation date. Given the covariates of a new contract, such as the entry ages of a couple, we construct one lower bound per remaining lifetime such that, with at least a prespecified probability, every life survives beyond its bound. The first step is to characterize the functions which allow for a useful projection from a multivariate to a univariate setting. The construction then relies on univariate conformal prediction, which calibrates any fitted model on held-out data, so that this statement does not rely on a correct mortality or dependence model. Censoring is handled by calibrating on the contracts observed for at least a fixed horizon, weighted by the inverse of their probability of being observed that long. We show that, when the lives can be censored at different times, this is possible precisely for joint statements that every life survives beyond its own bound, and that a common censoring time also permits bounds on the second-death time. If censoring is independent of the lifetimes given the covariates, coverage holds for every sample size when these probabilities are known, and approximately in large samples when they or the conditional lifetime quantiles are estimated consistently. As an application, we analyze a Canadian joint-life annuity portfolio.

items.title: Enabling risk and reliability analysis in next-generation computational tools via multifidelity methods
items.summary: Risk and reliability analysis are fundamental to the design, assessment, and operation of safety-critical complex systems; however, their integration into next-generation computational tools is constrained by the cost of uncertainty quantification with expensive computational models. The computational challenge is particularly prohibitive for tail-sensitive quantities, such as probabilities of failure, conditional values-at-risk, and buffered probabilities of failure, where accurate estimation can require a large number of model evaluations. Multifidelity methods provide a framework for addressing this computational bottleneck by combining information from models of varying accuracy and cost while retaining the predictive accuracy of the high-fidelity model. This review summarizes the state of the art in methods that enable scalable risk and reliability analysis using multifidelity control variates, multifidelity importance sampling, and multifidelity active learning.

items.title: Score-Based Modeling of Effective Langevin Dynamics with State-Dependent Mobility
items.summary: In a previous work [L. T. Giorgini, Phys. Rev. E 114, L012102 (2026)], we introduced stochastic reduced-order models that reproduce by construction the stationary density and short-time correlations of the observed variables, using a constant mobility matrix and the score, the gradient of the logarithm of this density. Here we generalize the framework to state-dependent mobilities, calibrated so that the model also reproduces the finite-lag correlation functions of chosen target observables. The calibration uses exact finite-lag forms of the generalized fluctuation-dissipation theorem, which express time derivatives of lagged correlations as averages over observed pairs of states and are linear in the mobility. When the mobility is expanded on a basis of known fields, its coefficients follow from a least-squares problem involving only the stationary score, and the observables and basis are selected by data-driven diagnostics. Otherwise, a neural-network mobility is calibrated through the conditional score of the finite-time transition density. We validate the approach analytically on a Cox-Ingersoll-Ross process and numerically on a two-dimensional nonequilibrium diffusion with multiplicative noise and a 36-dimensional soft-spin Landau-Lifshitz chain. Both methods reproduce the stationary statistics and the target correlations accurately. Because the identities can be integrated between consecutive lags, so that no time derivatives need to be estimated, the recovered drift and diffusion are much less sensitive to coarse sampling than Kramers-Moyal estimates, which require short sampling intervals. Calibration requires no simulation of the model and applies to high-dimensional systems.

items.title: Surprisal-Rényi Free Energy
items.summary: The forward and reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergences arise as limiting objectives in learning and inference, yet they induce markedly different inductive biases that cannot be explained by expectation terms alone. We introduce the Surprisal-Rényi Free Energy (SRFE), a normalized Rényi-Chernoff log-moment functional of the likelihood ratio. Although SRFE is algebraically related to Rényi divergence for fixed values of the order parameter, its endpoint-symmetric normalization yields a distinct free-energy viewpoint for analyzing how forward- and reverse KL behavior emerges near singular limits. We show that SRFE recovers the forward and reverse KL divergences as endpoint limits and derive local expansions around both regimes in which the variance of the log-likelihood ratio appears as a first-order correction away from the KL objective. These expansions reveal an explicit mean-variance tradeoff governing departures from KL-dominated behavior. We further establish a Gibbs-type variational characterization in terms of weighted KL projections and prove that SRFE controls large deviations of excess code length through Chernoff-type bounds, giving a Minimum Description Length interpretation of the functional. We evaluate SRFE on two synthetic settings (two-dimensional Gaussian-mixture variational inference and multi-class classification) and the long-tailed CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (CIFAR-LT) datasets. On CIFAR-LT, retraining the best configuration of each loss over five seeds, SRFE matches cross-entropy accuracy on CIFAR-10-LT and gives mixed results on CIFAR-100-LT, improving few-shot accuracy at one of three imbalance factors. Together, these results position SRFE as a variance- and tail-sensitive, normalized Rényi-Chernoff free energy that clarifies the geometric, statistical, and large-deviation structure underlying the transition between forward- and reverse-KL limits.

items.title: On Global Joint Lower Bounds in Zeroth-Order Nonconvex Optimization
items.summary: Must the dimension and accuracy costs of zeroth-order optimization multiply? Global upper bounds for smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization scale as $O(dε^{-4})$, with both factors separately necessary. We show that their product is unavoidable. We establish an $Ω(dε^{-4})$ lower bound for smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization, yielding an $Ω(dδ^{-1}ε^{-3})$ bound for nonsmooth Goldstein stationarity. Both match the best-known full-space upper bounds, establishing joint minimax optimality in dimension and accuracy. These bounds hold against fully adaptive randomized algorithms with unrestricted queries and outputs, even under arbitrary sample reuse. As a byproduct, we establish noiseless exact-value lower bounds for both smooth and Goldstein stationarity, even against randomized algorithms.

items.title: The Price of Scale in Proactive Memory Recall
items.summary: A long-lived assistant that brings up memories without being asked must decide at every turn whether anything in its store is worth an interruption. We show that this decision is a multiple-testing problem whose difficulty grows with the store size N. On replays of LongMemEval, a similarity threshold tuned to 5% false alarms at N=8 reaches 84-100% at N=2048 across embedding models and cue types; LoCoMo and LLM judges show it too. We prove that a gate which thresholds the best of N independent irrelevant scores at false-alarm rate alpha operates at a per-item false-positive rate of about -ln(1-alpha)/N, which pins its hit rate to the far left of the ROC and makes it regularly varying in N under regular variation. Replayed hit rates stay within its bounds for mixed cues up to 0.3 points, and hit rates carry over to held-out questions to within 6.0 points. At matched false alarms the deployed score recalls 14-26 points more than raw cosine. A cue-swap conformal gate, which ranks the current cue among other cues on the same store, has a finite-sample false-alarm guarantee under exchangeability. With a background from the user's unfiltered history it keeps false alarms at 3-6% on LongMemEval at the hit rate of a label-tuned threshold; on LoCoMo it overshoots or turns conservative depending on the source of its reference cues. In a chronological replay with the user's own earlier messages as references, it fires on 5-8% of questions on stores without their answer and on 6-8% of session-opening turns, against 57% for the deployed gate at N=2048, at a median 0.4 s CPU per decision. A cross-encoder pays the same price of scale, and on a prospective-memory benchmark, similarity gates recall at most 9% of constraints at controlled false alarms. One human and two LLM annotators judge most false alarms unhelpful for a response. Code and data: https://github.com/RiverChenStillCompiling/price-of-scale

items.title: Modified treatment policies that depend on the sequence of natural treatment values
items.summary: Longitudinal modified treatment policies (LMTPs) are a class of interventions that allow the definition, identification, and estimation of causal effects in general settings, including continuous or multivariate exposures and treatment regimens that require grace periods. Targeted machine learning estimators (i.e., double/debiased) have been formulated for LMTPs that assign exposure at time $t$ as a function of the natural treatment value at time $t$. However, applications such as delaying treatment initiation or withholding a potentially harmful treatment require LMTPs that also depend on the sequence of prior natural treatment values. This paper develops identification and targeted learning methods for estimating mean counterfactual outcomes under prespecified LMTPs that may depend on this sequence. We define the effects and propose estimators that use an augmented-data version of the sequential regression form of the longitudinal g-computation formula. Our estimators are based on the efficient influence function and provide $\sqrt{n}$ inference under standard doubly robust rate assumptions on the convergence of the outcome and treatment regressions. We apply the estimators to higher-risk pain treatment to assess the effect of withholding treatment during the first month it would naturally be indicated on the 12-month incidence of opioid use disorder.

items.title: On the non-uniformity of the 2026 FIFA World Cup draw
items.summary: The group stage of a sports tournament is often made more appealing by introducing additional constraints in the group draw that promote an attractive and balanced group composition. For example, the number of intra-regional group matches is minimised in several world championships. Under such constraints, the traditional draw procedure may become non-uniform, meaning that the feasible allocations of the teams into groups are not equally likely to occur. Our paper quantifies this non-uniformity of the 2026 FIFA World Cup draw for the official draw procedure, as well as for 47 reasonable alternatives implied by all permutations of the four pots and two group labelling policies. We show why simulating with a recursive backtracking algorithm is intractable, and propose a workable implementation using integer programming. The official draw mechanism is found to be optimal based on two of five non-uniformity measures, including the average distortion of the 771 non-zero assignment probabilities. Nonetheless, non-uniformity can be more than halved if the organiser aims to treat the best teams drawn from the first pot equally.

items.title: Missing data and cluster graphs: cluster-level missingness vs variable-level missingness
items.summary: Missing data is pervasive in many scientific domains such as public health, environmental science, and the social sciences. Recoverability from missing data is typically studied using fully specified variable-level missingness models despite that, in many applications, only coarse structural information is available, for instance when variables are grouped into clusters due to limited knowledge or interpretability reasons. In this paper, we investigate recoverability from such abstract representations. We introduce two classes of cluster-based missingness graphs: the m-C-DMG, which retains variable-specific missingness indicators, and the cm-C-DMG, which aggregates missingness mechanisms at the cluster level. We formalize the notion of compatibility between these abstract graphs and underlying variable-level missingness models, and study how this abstraction affects the recoverability of probabilistic and causal queries. In particular, we give graphical conditions of recovering the joint distribution as well as graphical conditions of recovering a macro causal effect.

items.title: Estimating Treatment Effects with a Single Arm Clinical Trial and Data Summaries from an External Control Group: is it Possible?
items.summary: Randomized controlled trials are crucial for assessing new treatments, but they are often infeasible due to ethical or practical constraints. In these cases, single-arm trials combined with external control data constitute an alternative approach for estimating treatment effects. However, individual patient-level data on external controls are frequently inaccessible due to privacy and economic concerns. Therefore, investigators rely on data summaries published by previous studies of the control therapy. We propose a method for inference on the treatment effect of an experimental therapy using patient-level data from a single-arm trial and a few published data summaries from an external control group. We introduce and study the Interval of Potential Effects (IPE), described as the range of plausible levels of the treatment effect that are compatible with the patient-level data from the experimental treatment and the available summaries on the control group. The width of the IPE quantifies the uncertainty on the treatment effect attributable to the lack of individual patient data from the control group. We demonstrate, through simulations and a case study, how the IPE indicates whether the available summaries are sufficient for accurate estimation of the treatment effect. We also illustrate that IPEs can support decision-making in the early phases of development of new treatments.

items.title: Exact Selective Inference for Spectral Clustering via Piecewise-Constant Graph Perturbation
items.summary: Cluster labels are often used twice: first to discover groups, and then to test whether the discovered groups differ. This double use of the data makes ordinary two-sample $p$-values anti-conservative. Selective inference fixes this by conditioning on the clustering event, but for spectral clustering the event appears difficult because the algorithm combines an affinity map, an eigendecomposition, and a rounding step. We show that, for spectral clustering based on unweighted $\varepsilon$- or $k$-nearest-neighbor graphs, the obstruction is the affinity construction rather than the eigendecomposition. Along the one-dimensional perturbation used by the truncated-$χ$ selective test, graph changes occur only at finitely many real roots of data-dependent quadratic distance comparisons. Between these breakpoints, the graph, Laplacian spectrum, embedding, rounding, and reported cluster pair are deterministic functions of a finite graph state. Consequently, in real arithmetic and under a known-scale spherical Gaussian model, the selection set is an exact finite union of intervals, yielding finite-sample selective $p$-values for selected spectral-cluster pairs. The same argument gives feature-wise truncated-normal tests. We also record direct extensions to known feature covariance, eigengap-selected $K$, and auxiliary-coordinate graphs. We validate null and partial-null calibration, operational power, numerical sensitivity, and model-scope diagnostics, and give a working-model PBMC algorithmic illustration. Smooth kernels such as RBF affinities fall outside the finite-state guarantee.

items.title: Vector incremental treatment effects
items.summary: Causal questions involving multiple binary treatments are poorly served by standard causal approaches. Potential outcomes grow exponentially with the number of treatments, many treatment combinations are rarely or never observed, and fixing everyone to one combination can require implausible positivity assumptions. We extend incremental propensity score interventions to vector-valued binary treatments, defining causal effects through counterfactual distributions that scale the odds of each treatment by a user-specified factor. Because marginal odds constraints do not uniquely determine the joint distribution, we define it as the minimum-divergence projection of the observed law onto the constrained set, for a user-specified separable divergence, preserving the observed conditional support. The resulting counterfactual mean outcome is identified under consistency and conditional mean exchangeability, without requiring every treatment combination to have positive conditional probability. For a class of smooth divergences, we derive the efficient influence function and construct cross-fitted one-step estimators that are consistent at the parametric rate and asymptotically normal when marginal treatment probabilities are exactly 0, exactly 1, or bounded away from those values. We relax this requirement by specifying a different estimand and deriving a corresponding estimator, which is asymptotically normal under a convergence-rate condition on the estimated active set. We also extend sensitivity analysis to address unmeasured confounding. Applying the framework to 159,466 New York Medicaid beneficiaries with serious mental illness, we estimate how healthcare costs would change under uniform improvements in the odds of six recommended quality-of-care processes. Increasing recommended care is associated with lower total, inpatient, and mental-health cost and higher outpatient cost.

items.title: Deep Learning of Compositional Targets with Hierarchical Spectral Methods
items.summary: Why depth yields a computational advantage over shallow methods remains a central open question in learning theory. We study this question in a controlled high-dimensional Gaussian setting, focusing on compositional target functions. We analyze their learnability using an explicit three-layer fitting model trained via layer-wise spectral estimators. The target combines polynomial latent features with a scalar readout, and its compositional structure allows learning to proceed in stages. Recovering an intermediate representation reduces the problem to lower-degree spectral estimation tasks, as in multi-index models. Our analysis establishes Gaussian comparison bounds for projected moments when $0<\varepsilon<1/3$, and motivates separations in sample complexity between two- and three-layer learning strategies, conditional on a conjectured spectral recovery step.

items.title: How Deep Are Deep GPs, Really? A Sharp Threshold and a Non-Gaussian Limit for Compositional GPs
items.summary: Compositional priors describe the generic properties of layered functions in deep Bayesian models, where deep neural networks with random weights are a canonical example. In the wide-network limit, the prior is a Gaussian process (GP) with a depth-dependent kernel, and its behaviour as depth grows has been extensively studied through this kernel. Here, we study another case, where each layer itself is a vector valued Gaussian process, and our aim is similarly to understand the limiting behaviour of the prior as depth grows. Previous GP work has established that for the radial basis function (RBF) kernel and a certain range of bandwidths $r$, the prior degenerates in the limit, converging to the set of constant functions, which is not useful as a probabilistic model. In this paper we establish several new results. First, we identify a sharp bandwidth threshold $r_c(d) = Θ(\sqrt{d})$ above which the limit is degenerate, strengthening the earlier bounds. Second, and more importantly, we show that for $r$ below the threshold $r_c(d)$ the prior converges to a limit distribution $π_{\bar{Z}}$. We also prove that these distributions are non-degenerate and non-Gaussian, with non-vanishing dependence between coordinates. In contrast to the previously known degenerate regime, deep Gaussian process priors can therefore admit non-trivial limits. Empirically, we verify the threshold across a range of dimensions $d$, and demonstrate a complex multimodal behaviour of the limit distributions $π_{\bar{Z}}$, a regime that becomes increasingly narrow with $d$ and would be hard to identify without knowing the threshold.

items.title: One-step Outcome Imputation: An Alternative to Multiple Imputation
items.summary: Missing outcomes in randomized controlled trials are often handled by multiple imputation (MI). Rubin's rules are routinely used to estimate standard errors but can fail to provide valid standard error estimates for some commonly used procedures, such as reference-based imputation. We propose a one-step alternative by explicitly targeting the treatment effect implied by a given imputation model and constructing an efficient one-step estimator for that treatment effect via its influence function. Unlike Rubin's rules, this approach yields asymptotically valid inference. Moreover, the proposed method circumvents the stochastic component and computational burden of MI. We illustrate the approach with examples spanning a range of imputation models, including reference-based imputation, intercurrent-event-dependent imputation, and repeated measures imputation. The one-step imputation estimation procedure is implemented in the `targeted` R package.

items.title: Amortized Nonlinear Variable Selection with Prior-Data Fitted Networks
items.summary: Variable selection is an important task for interpreting potentially complex systems in fields such as biology, business, and sociology. The importance of variable selection has attracted considerable attention in statistics and machine learning. In this paper, we are mainly interested in model-agnostic variable selection for identifying variables that have general nonlinear dependence on the response. We propose MambaPFN, short for Model-Agnostic Markov BlAnket selection with Prior-data Fitted Networks, which is built upon the Transformer, a building block of many popular large language models. Specifically, we consider a functional-mapping perspective on variable-selection learning, in which the Transformer is treated as a learnable mapping from a dataset to its relevant variables. To learn this mapping, MambaPFN introduces three new components: (i) a faithful, rich, and scalable scheme for generating pretraining data, (ii) an objective that targets each variable's posterior inclusion probability, and (iii) a modified Transformer architecture tailored to variable selection. Once pretrained, MambaPFN is applied to new datasets without parameter updates. Empirically, MambaPFN achieves desirable variable-selection performance in simulation studies and exhibits a scaling law---more pretraining datasets and larger models can continuously improve its performance. Applied to a Facebook comments dataset, MambaPFN selects the fewest variables and achieves the highest computational efficiency and predictive performance, improving upon the best baselines by about 20%.

items.title: Random mixtures in Bayes Hilbert spaces
