items.summary: Sector rotation is a common decision in benchmark-relative portfolio management, where portfolio managers rank sectors for overweight and underweight positions. We formulate this task as ranking sector actions by expected future risk-adjusted active performance, measured with forward sector-benchmark Sharpe ratios. Such rankings should preserve temporal information, express model outputs through economically familiar signal characteristics, account for changes in signal relevance across macroeconomic environments, and capture dependencies among sectors. We propose RegimeRank, an interpretable sector-ranking model that represents fundamental and technical signals through expert-defined temporal characteristics, conditions them on learned macro factors via cross-attention, and models cross-sector dependencies through self-attention. Expected-gradient attributions identify the contributions of individual signal-transformation pairs, while macroeconomic and cross-sector attention maps provide diagnostics of the learned conditioning and relational structure. We evaluate RegimeRank on weekly S&P 500 data from 2002 to 2024 under combinatorial purged cross-validation, where it outperforms representative ranking and machine-learning baselines across multiple ranking metrics. Ablation studies support the contributions of latent macro states, regime conditioning, and cross-sector modelling, while attribution and attention analyses illustrate the temporal characteristics, macro states, and sector relationships underlying its rankings.

items.title: SHADE: Shrinkage via Halted Alpha-stable Denoising for Heavy-Tailed Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
items.summary: Time-series observations are particularly susceptible to noise, and many real-world series have low signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) together with heavy-tailed and time-varying disturbances. When Gaussian diffusion models are used for forecasting, reversing all the way to the zero-noise endpoint may yield an overly narrow and overconfident predictive distribution. We propose SHADE, an alpha-stable Lévy diffusion forecaster that reads out at a nonzero depth so that the residual stable kernel acts as distribution-level shrinkage. By decomposing halting risk into smoothing bias and estimation error, we develop a scale-calibrated halt for estimating the optimal shrinkage $τ^*$ and a context-amortized halt that requires no explicit noise labels. Gains concentrate in the extreme heavy-tailed regime $α\leq1.3$: Across synthetic noise settings, median CRPS improves by 21.7\%, while the NLL falls significantly; Cryptocurrency and foreign-exchange data provide further evidence of improved tail calibration in real-data implement. On near-light-tailed or high-SNR data, the model reverts to Gaussian diffusion or full denoising. SHADE maintains overall forecast error comparable to strong baselines while providing more honest tail uncertainty for heavy-tailed series.

items.title: Trading Frictions in Dynamic Cap-and-Trade Markets
items.summary: Using 2.8 million EU ETS transactions and compliance records, 2005-2022, we document three facts about the world's largest carbon market: each year, 37% of regulated operators do not trade, and non-trading is persistent. Purchases concentrate in the April surrender month, when returns are systematically high. Operator order flow predicts returns, concentrated among frequent traders. A model with costly market access, limited intermediation, and heterogeneous information rationalizes all three. Because access is endogenous, the frictions interact non-additively, shaping how efficiently the market corrects the externality. Staggering deadlines across four groups lowers the surrender-month premium by 58% without changing the cap.

items.title: When Values-Based Screens Disagree: Continuous Shariah Compliance and Classification Dynamics
items.summary: Does the design of a values-based screening rule generate eligibility changes when reported accounting inputs remain unchanged but market valuations move? We apply seven Shariah financial-screening rulebooks to 1.34 million U.S. security-months from 1999 to 2024 on a common, threshold-anchored scale. Applied retrospectively, the full emulations disagree on 35.9% of complete permissible-sector observations (38.8% from 2015, when all were in force), and the financial-ratio screens alone on 47.3%. Under AAOIFI's spot market-capitalisation denominator, market-capitalisation movement alone is sufficient for 65.6% of breaches, and half of denominator-driven breaches reverse within three months; numerator movement dominates under asset-based rules. Holding the threshold and sample fixed, a 24-month average denominator cuts debt-screen transitions from 2.51% to 1.03% a month, whereas raising the threshold barely matters. Among breaches of similar severity the reversal gap narrows but persists. Portfolio and fund-holdings evidence qualifies these findings: benefits are modest under a binding single-rule mandate.

items.title: Market Efficiency in a Changing Asset Population: Mobility, Entry, and Survival over Cryptocurrency's Full History
items.summary: Weak-form efficiency implies symmetry restrictions on the Markov chain governing movement across the cryptocurrency capitalisation distribution. We test them on the full listed population: 8,970 assets, 690 weekly cross-sections, 2013 to 2026, with entry, exit and survival observed rather than inferred. Symmetry is rejected in every era, but the asymmetry falls by seventy percent, and what converged is entry-driven compositional churn rather than coins' own valuations. The bottom decile earns 27.5% per week on paper and nothing among assets that trade, on capacity of $293,000. Compensation for neglect exists precisely where trading does not.

items.title: AuDQ: Auditable Data Quality through Agentic Rule Discovery
items.summary: High-stakes tabular pipelines rely on scattered, static quality checks that are hard to evolve and audit against policy intent. Regulated domains particularly suffer as the LLM-era automation raises expectations for traceability and accountability. We propose a vision for an ontology-grounded, repository-native data quality layer in which rules are first-class artifacts: versioned, provenance-linked to governance texts, and re-playable through immutable execution traces. As a first step toward validating this vision, we present a concrete implementation of its agentic rule-discovery core with two rule acquisition modes (Full-Agentic and Guided) and a human-in-the-loop (HITL) review interface. We define an evaluation framework and run experiments addressing whether our fully autonomous, divide-and-conquer agentic rule discovery produces rules of the same quality and diversity as those specified by a human expert, reporting preliminary results on two real world industry datasets in the finance and retail domains.

items.title: PALM: Point-in-Time Adaptation for Financial Language Models
items.summary: Language models used in financial backtests suffer from look-ahead bias, as a model trained on text published after the study period has already observed the outcomes it is asked to predict. To handle this issue, point-in-time (PIT) language models are pretrained on chronologically filtered corpora and released as one checkpoint per calendar year, each with a documented cutoff. However, each additional year costs another pretraining run, and whether that run is necessary has never been tested. In this paper, we show that a newer checkpoint is not detectably better on the decision it informs, as its information coefficient on a fixed evaluation window shows no decay with age that we can detect. Motivated by this observation, we propose PALM (Point-in-time Adaptation for financial Language Models), a simple yet effective alternative to annual pretraining that fits a low-rank adapter on financial text the checkpoint is allowed to read, without modifying any pretrained weight. We further find that the gain comes from the financial domain rather than from recency, which leaves the point-in-time constraint without a detectable cost. We validate PALM on a decade of financial news and on three families of PIT models, whose cutoffs span two decades. The pooled gain keeps its sign across experimental settings and comes at a small fraction of the cost of pretraining. Code is available at: https://github.com/seunghan96/palm.

items.title: Conflicting History in Foundation Model Return Forecasts
items.summary: Older observations can help a forecaster learn a predictive relationship while becoming misleading when that relationship changes. We study this tension using paired return histories that differ in older observations but share recent returns and the conditional distribution of the next return. Across five foundation-model forecasting procedures and three simulated processes, each evaluated on 1,024 independent replications, conflicting history reduces the probability of improving on zero in all 30 higher-signal comparisons. This loss of usefulness occurs despite successful signal recovery under stable conditions. A separate exploratory comparison on 56 assets finds that shortening inputs from 256 to 64 returns increases mean absolute error for every model by 1.77-4.58 basis points; neither length improves observed overall error over zero. The evidence distinguishes the ability to extract a signal from the ability to withstand conflicting history, while showing why context sensitivity alone does not justify discarding older data.

items.title: Topological Compression of Prediction Market Belief States for Event Forecasting
items.summary: Topological Data Analysis (TDA) and Persistent Homology (PH) have been utilized in numerous fields$-$from protein modeling to financial analysis$-$to understand the underlying structure of data. In this paper, we incorporate TDA and PH into forecasting models over a prediction market universe to determine whether the belief state of such markets forms an underlying structure whose shape can provide predictive insight. We conclude that single-parameter PH is able to improve predictive ability and calibrated accuracy of linear forecasting models, while two-parameter multipersistence produces similar benefits for nonlinear models.

items.title: Arbitrage-Free Implied Volatility Surface Reconstruction via Additive Martingales
items.summary: This work focuses on reconstructing a continuous implied volatility (IV) surface from a small number of option quotes, a fundamental task for option pricing and risk management. We propose Additive Martingale (AddMart), a few-shot IV surface reconstruction framework that satisfies static no-arbitrage conditions by construction. Rather than predicting IVs directly, AddMart maps sparse quotes to non-negative increment densities of an exponential additive martingale, from which valid risk-neutral marginals and IVs are recovered. By incorporating the no-arbitrage structure directly into its architecture, rather than enforcing it through regularization in the learning objective, AddMart produces IV surfaces that satisfy static no-arbitrage conditions throughout the domain. Extensive experiments on ten real-option datasets demonstrate that AddMart achieves competitive reconstruction accuracy with no material static arbitrage violations, while directly enabling the estimation of VaR, CVaR, and crash probabilities.

items.title: Probabilistic Limit Order Book Forecasting with Conditional Diffusion Models
items.summary: Modeling limit order book (LOB) dynamics is central to market forecasting and execution-strategy evaluation. While diffusion models achieve strong empirical performance, existing LOB snapshot models typically lack a learned recurrent encoder and formal statistical guarantees. We introduce LOBGrad, a conditional DDPM framework for probabilistic LOB forecasting that combines an autoregressive RNN encoder with a diffusion-based generator. In particular, we establish an excess-risk oracle inequality for the one-step DDPM noise-prediction objective under exponential mixing and regularity assumptions. We further show that, under contractive dynamics, the dependence on the conditioning-window length can be reduced to a dependence on the latent-state dimension. Experiments on BTC/USDT, GOOGL, and META show that LOBGrad improves on its encoder-free diffusion ablation across all reported queue metrics and obtains competitive results against other baselines. It also reproduces the key stylized facts of LOB microstructure, and yields reasonably calibrated queue-based predictive intervals. A stylized downstream task illustrates the potential value of the generated forecasts.

items.title: More Mentions, Less Information? Diagnosing Identity and Alignment in Reddit Embeddings for Volatility Forecasting
items.summary: Since the 2021 GameStop short squeeze, r/WallStreetBets (WSB) has been associated with episodes of extreme volatility, and its text is increasingly used to forecast volatility. A model using only large language model (LLM) embeddings of WSB posts attains an out-of-sample $R^2$ of 0.13 for log realized variance. That number shows predictive power, but it does not reveal where the information comes from or how much the text adds beyond a firm's own volatility history. We answer these questions with a diagnostic protocol that nests embeddings on a heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) benchmark, compares them with text-free firm-identity controls, shuffles the day-to-text pairing within firm-years to test day-specific alignment, and checks whether gains persist across periods and coverage groups. We apply the protocol to frozen LLM embeddings in a panel of 202,145 mentioned stock-days, using retrospective rolling out-of-sample tests over 2015-2022. The results indicate that most of the standalone fit reflects firm or firm-year information: on firms seen in training, a text-free firm baseline reaches $R^2 = 0.32$, shuffling preserves 89-92% of the standalone fit, and masking ticker strings reduces standalone $R^2$ to -0.005. Adding embeddings to HAR reduces equal-date MSE by 1.22% (95% CI [0.94, 1.49]). This small but statistically significant gain survives firm controls and ticker masking, but is largely eliminated by alignment shuffling. The gain is concentrated in 2015-2019 and is not distinguishable from zero in 2020-2022. Expanding coverage by 48% through off-hours and weekend posts adds stock-days with no reliable positive increment. More mentions therefore do not imply more incremental forecasting information.

items.title: Bias correcting transaction cost models for characteristic function based estimators
items.summary: Effective transaction cost is a necessary step for devising any competing financial trading strategy in the absence of quote data. Classically, Roll's model estimated the transaction cost using the first order autocovariance of the difference between daily transaction prices, while Hasbrouck's Bayesian approach used iterative posterior simulation. However, Roll's model fails when the first order autocovariance becomes positive, while Hasbrouck's estimator is computationally intensive, especially when many securities are involved. We develop empirical characteristic function methods with a first order bias correcting for spread estimation, and establish the asymptotic distribution of the corrected estimator under suitable conditions. Our numerical experiments illustrate the bias-variance tradeoff of characteristic-function methods compared to Roll's model, and their computational advantage over Hasbrouck's model.

items.title: Conformal Kelly: When Marginal Coverage Transfers and the Economics Do Not
items.summary: We size portfolio positions from conformal prediction intervals, reading the interval half-width as the scale in a capped fractional-Kelly rule (Conformal Kelly), and evaluate the rule under a pre-registered protocol. The development record is an autonomous LLM-agent search over roughly 200 configurations on a single six-year window (2016-2021) of eight US-listed ETFs. All later data was sealed before the search, and two final configurations, nine comparison books and the mapping from outcomes to conclusions were registered before unsealing. On the sealed 2022-2024 window, realized coverage was 0.745 against a 0.750 target, but the two configurations' annualised net log growth was 8.5% and 7.0% (28.5% and 25.8% in development), below an unlevered equal-weight book (9.5%), the leveraged passive books (15.6-16.8%) and a registered hindsight four-equity book (10.8%, at a 46% drawdown); both ranked last of eleven entries on Sharpe and Calmar. A post-hoc split, outside the registered protocol, shows the passing coverage averaging 0.592 in 2022 and 0.842 afterwards, with the entire loss in the under-covered year. The split does not show that under-coverage caused the loss: the leverage cap bound on every 2022 trading day, so narrow intervals could not enlarge the book, and a long-equity book in an equity bear market is the simpler account. But the registered acceptance test passed a sixteen-point conditional failure, which motivates, without establishing, conditional coverage as an endpoint for rules that read interval width as a scale. On the development window, a slow per-asset conformal quantile out-grew every locally adaptive alternative tested, but only under a binding leverage cap, and block-bootstrap intervals include zero for 11 of the 13 contrasts we could re-derive.

items.title: Buy the Rumor, Sell the News: When Is News Priced In?
items.summary: Two old market sayings hold that news is already priced in by the time it is published, and that the rumor is bought while the news is sold. Both are empirical claims about event time: they place the price move associated with a piece of news before and at publication rather than after it. Whether the claims hold, for which kinds of news, and by how much are basic questions about how fast markets absorb public information. We test them on 4.57 million financial news articles covering roughly 3,000 US stocks (2023-2026). A large language model teacher, distilled into a compact classifier through active learning, assigns each article one of 17 event tags and five attributes; articles are clustered into stories to separate first reports from follow-up coverage; and beta-adjusted abnormal returns are measured around the resulting 1.68 million stock-day events, with 364{,}405 neutral-sentiment events as a placebo group. Three results follow. First, the price move associated with news concentrates before and at publication: pooled across all signed events, the cumulative move in the news direction by the close of publication day is 2.8 times its value twenty days later, and for rumor-flagged events the directional return is concentrated around the rumor event, with little incremental return at the subsequent linked non-rumor event. Second, measured against the placebo of comparable stocks, markets underreact to numbers and overreact to stories: quantified fundamental news (earnings, dividends, guidance, analyst actions) keeps drifting in the direction of the news for weeks, while soft story-driven news (launches, macro commentary, leadership) gives back its move. Third, news carries width as well as direction: neutral news raises publication-day volatility. The study also produces a table of measured drift for each event tag, usable as a prior in news-conditioned forecasting models.

items.title: On the utility problem in a market where price impact is transient
items.summary: We consider a discrete-time model of a financial market where a risky asset is bought and sold with transactions having a transient price impact. It is shown that the corresponding utility maximization problem admits a solution. We manage to remove some unnatural restrictions on the market depth and resilience processes that were present in earlier work. A non-standard feature of the problem is that the set of attainable portfolio values may fail the convexity property.

items.title: Conditionally Identifiable Latent Representation for Multivariate Time Series with Structural Dynamics
items.summary: We propose the Identifiable Variational Dynamic Factor Model (iVDFM) for multivariate time series. The model combines variational inference with partial identifiability guarantees up to a known ambiguity class. Innovations follow a conditional exponential-family prior over observed auxiliary context and regime embeddings. Linear diagonal dynamics map innovations to factors and preserve that class, so factors are partially identifiable up to permutation and component-wise affine maps. We train by maximizing the ELBO and estimate uncertainty in both latent trajectories and forecasts. Under explicit assumptions, we prove partial identifiability up to the stated class and provide the full proof in the appendix. We evaluate factor recovery on synthetic DGPs, intervention behavior on synthetic SCMs, and forecasting on real benchmarks with CRPS and MSE.

items.title: Coherent risk from finite models
items.summary: Coherent estimators at different sample sizes need not describe the same population risk. We prove that dyadic estimators do so exactly when duplicating every scenario leaves the estimate unchanged, and recover the population dual set from the finite models. The risk of a Bernoulli loss determines the exact Wasserstein, Kolmogorov and total-variation moduli on a common bounded support. It also characterises uniform estimability, with an impossibility bound for arbitrary randomised estimators. An intrinsic floor on tail levels gives an explicit optimal Lipschitz constant and a uniform approximation defect; every deterministic vanishing floor preserves pointwise strong consistency. A nonstandard construction supplies compatible estimators at all finite sample sizes, explicit block-sum weights, and a formula for the worst-case mass created by infinitesimal tail levels. Finally, we derive uniform regret bounds for data-driven risk-averse optimisation and specialise them to stop-loss retention. Exact binomial calculations compare regularised and original estimators against the same population target.

items.title: Same Book, Different Fills: Partial Identification of FIFO Execution from Aggregate Order Books
items.summary: Price-level limit order book (L2) data reveal aggregate liquidity but not the ordered queue required by price--time priority. Passive-execution backtests can therefore depend on an unobserved cancellation-allocation rule even when observed prices, quantities, and trades are held fixed. We frame recovery of market-by-order histories from aggregate snapshots as a conditional partial identification problem: multiple histories can reproduce the same aggregate path. Holding that path, reconciled market removals, latent order partitions, and additions fixed, our path-preserving compiler varies only cancellation allocation among front, quantity-weighted-random, and back rules. Within this compiler class, we establish front--back fill ordering for a virtual tagged order during one touch-price spell. We study seven months of synchronized 2025 Tokyo Stock Exchange data for two instruments with different trading activity: RIC 1301.T and RIC 7911.T. Ten-level L2 snapshots provide book states, while L1 trades permit inference of market removals and resting side through reconciliation. Each instrument contributes 1,080 matched five-minute episodes over the same 18 held-out trading days. The aggressive benchmark is invariant across FIFO realizations, but passive execution is sensitive to the cancellation rule. For 1301.T, front rather than back cancellation raises preterminal completion by 8.01 percentage points and reduces implementation shortfall by 1.010 bps. For 7911.T, the corresponding differences are 7.39 percentage points and 0.384 bps. Thus, observationally equivalent aggregate-book paths can imply economically different passive-execution outcomes. Execution policies evaluated from aggregate data should be accompanied by FIFO sensitivity analysis rather than reported as single-point estimates based on an unobservable queue assumption.

items.title: Optimal Control of the Ethena Yield-Bearing Stablecoin
items.summary: We formulate and solve stochastic control problems that model the core yield-generating strategy of the Ethena protocol, a decentralized finance (DeFi) stablecoin that earns yield by combining a long position in staked Ethereum (stETH) with an equal-sized short position in ETH perpetual futures. The combined position is delta-neutral with respect to the ETH spot price, yet earns carry from two sources: staking rewards on the stETH leg, and funding-rate payments received from long perpetual holders when the perpetual trades at a premium to spot. A key feature of our model is that the control -- the rate of simultaneously buying stETH and shorting the perpetual -- exerts two distinct types of price impact. \textit{Permanent} impact shifts the mid-market prices of both legs, compressing the basis and permanently eroding future funding income. \textit{Temporary} impact reflects execution slippage on each leg. We study both an infinite-horizon discounted problem and a finite-horizon problem in which the protocol maximizes total wealth up to a fixed date $T$, subject to a terminal cost for liquidating any remaining position. In both cases the optimal control is obtained explicitly.

items.title: Conditional Weight of Evidence for Gradient-Boosted Credit Models: Estimation, Additivity and Its Relation to Adverse Action Reasons
items.summary: Traditional weight of evidence assigns a credit characteristic a value based on its association with default across a population. Credit analysis also requires an assessment of that characteristic in the context of an individual applicant's record. We study conditional weight of evidence for this purpose. It measures the change in default log odds from observing a characteristic after the remaining credit information is known. Its sign identifies whether the characteristic adds adverse or favorable information for that applicant, and its magnitude measures the strength of that information. The same characteristic value can therefore receive different assessments for applicants with different payment histories or other credit attributes. We develop estimators using gradient-boosted trees and evaluate their accuracy in a bureau-style simulation. Regressions of the full model's predicted probabilities recover conditional evidence more accurately than separate models fitted to default outcomes, provided the full model is accurate. They also recover a deliberately constructed file-age effect whose direction varies with utilization and is often missed by marginal weight of evidence. Local class-frequency estimates improve on marginal weight of evidence but remain inaccurate for some weak effects. An application to FICO HELOC data illustrates estimation when the population evidence is unknown. Conditional weight of evidence provides an applicant-specific interpretation of the information in a credit characteristic; its population summary, a conditional information value, splits the joint information in the record across blocks when averaged over orderings. Neither is an adverse action reason, which explains the fitted score difference between the applicant and chosen passing records.

items.title: Optimal Trading Filters and the Value of Predictive Signals
items.summary: The value of a forecast depends on its accuracy, but also on its actionability. In trading, an investor must translate return forecasts into positions while accounting for trading costs and the lingering impact of earlier trades. We solve the stationary quadratic trading problem with transient price impact using tools from prediction theory: Wiener-Hopf factorization gives the optimal policy as the composition of a conditional forecast and an explicit causal linear filter. We recover the Gârleanu-Pedersen aim-portfolio under exponential resilience and derive fractional trading filters under power-law impact decay, requiring memory beyond finite-dimensional LQR control. At fixed positive risk penalty, signals of equal instantaneous predictive strength have equal frictionless Markowitz value. With trading costs, net attainable value is determined by the mean square of the friction-weighted conditional forecast. Under power-law impact with exposure bleeding, we find an intermediate optimal mean-reversion rate for Ornstein-Uhlenbeck signals.

items.title: Rachev-Ratio Portfolio Optimization with TimeGAN Scenarios: Replacement versus Supplementation
items.summary: This study evaluates the reliability and investment consequences of scenarios from a specified time-series generative adversarial network (TimeGAN) in Rachev-ratio portfolio allocation. Using 12 exchange-traded funds, we compare historical, replacement and hybrid policies across five training seeds with delayed execution and transaction costs. Synthetic probability mass varies independently of draw count under a fixed training protocol; optimal generator fidelity is not assumed. Generated scenarios understate volatility and tail losses and distort dependence. Limited longer-training diagnostics improve reconstruction loss without improving cross-asset correlation accuracy. Higher-mass hybrids earn larger average net returns in some configurations, but all conditional generated-versus-historical return intervals include zero at the reference block length. Full-period TimeGAN means exceed resampling controls, while direct paired return, Sharpe and realized-tail-ratio intervals include zero. Replacement raises turnover and is sensitive to the modified objective's denominator floor; changing that floor does not uniformly improve realized downside risk. Exploratory generation-error associations do not identify a causal investment-performance channel. The results illustrate financial model risk from the interaction of imperfect scenarios and a tail-sensitive allocation criterion, supporting joint evaluation of fidelity, numerical behavior and realized outcomes within the tested implementation.

items.title: Dynamic portfolio selection under range value-at-risk with logarithmic returns
items.summary: This paper studies continuous-time portfolio selection under Range Value-at-Risk (RVaR), with both portfolio performance and risk evaluated in terms of logarithmic returns. We formulate a mean--RVaR problem in a continuous-time financial market and reduce the dynamic optimization to a static quantile problem. Using quantile representation, Lagrangian optimization, and convexification, we characterize the optimal terminal wealth through the convex envelope of an RVaR-specific transformed weighting function. The RVaR-specific convex envelope exhibits two distinct geometric configurations. Under Scenario~1, the terminal wealth has a VaR-type structure: the minimum-RVaR payoff is digital-option-like, whereas for $0<λ<1$ it consists of two growth-optimal regions separated by a constant-payoff region. Under Scenario~2, the convex envelope is determined either by a supporting line connecting an interior contact point to the endpoint or by a common supporting line with two interior contact points, leading to a richer multi-region payoff structure. We further show that the RVaR solutions reduce to their VaR and Expected Shortfall (ES) counterparts as $β\downarrowα$ and $α=0$, respectively. Under constant investment opportunities, we also derive closed-form wealth processes and replicating portfolio strategies. Numerical results show that the effects of $(α,β,λ)$ on risky-asset exposure are nonlinear and generally non-monotone. In particular, when $α>0$, pure minimum-RVaR optimization may assign zero terminal wealth in sufficiently bad states because the extreme quantile region $[0,α)$ is excluded from the RVaR criterion. These results clarify how interval-based quantile risk control shapes state-dependent portfolio payoffs and connects RVaR with its VaR and ES limiting cases.

items.title: Latent Flow Matching for Arbitrage-Aware Implied Volatility Surface Generation
items.summary: We propose an arbitrage-aware latent flow-matching framework for unconditional implied volatility surface generation. The method first compresses high-dimensional surfaces into a low-dimensional latent space using a variational autoencoder regularized by differentiable calendar-spread, call-spread and butterfly-arbitrage penalties. A flow-matching model then learns to transport a Gaussian prior toward the empirical latent distribution, and generated latent samples are decoded back into volatility surfaces. We evaluate the approach using marginal and surface-level Wasserstein distances, smile and skew diagnostics, pointwise quantile surfaces, financially interpretable shape metrics, and static no-arbitrage tests. The proposed model closely reproduces the empirical distribution and the main maturity-moneyness structures, achieves the best performance in the extreme Q99 regime, and generates 90.8% of surfaces satisfying all tested static no-arbitrage conditions. Overall, the results show that latent flow matching provides a favorable balance between distributional similarity, tail preservation, and financial consistency without requiring post-sampling reweighting.

items.title: A Pricing and Hedging Framework for Infinite-Dimensional Financial Markets
items.summary: In this paper, we provide a comprehensive study of how the classical Black--Scholes-type market framework behaves in an infinite-dimensional setting. The asset prices are modeled by stochastic evolution equations in a separable Hilbert space. The evolution of the risk-free asset and the corresponding discounting operators are governed by a strongly continuous group of bounded linear operators. Accordingly, we consider contingent claims with Hilbert-space-valued payoffs, whose values are discounted through the corresponding operators. Within this framework, we investigate the pricing and hedging of contingent claims, deriving the corresponding infinite-dimensional Black--Scholes equations and establishing exact replication results for strong solutions and asymptotic replication results for mild solutions through Yosida approximations. We also study the special case where the infinitesimal generator is given by $A=rI$, allowing for real-valued contingent claims. We further investigate no-arbitrage and market completeness, introducing a Hilbert lattice structure to formulate arbitrage and characterizing attainability through operator equations associated with martingale representations. Finite-dimensional noise truncations and Yosida approximations are employed to establish approximate and asymptotic approximate completeness results. We introduce geometric Brownian motions in Hilbert spaces and derive sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of an equivalent risk-neutral measure, together with explicit pricing formulas for some tractable examples. These results extend key aspects of the classical Black--Scholes framework to markets with infinite-dimensional asset-price dynamics. As a concrete application, the model can be interpreted as a segmented market consisting of a sequence of one-dimensional geometric Brownian motions.

items.title: From Alpha to Execution: Trading Horizons, Regimes, and Schedules under Concave Impact and Hurst Scaling
items.summary: Classical execution models assume linear impact, diffusive prices, and an exogenous horizon. We study execution under concave power-law impact and Hurst-scaled price fluctuations, and make two contributions. First, we choose the execution horizon by maximizing the Sharpe ratio of the trade's realized P&L. Price moves during the execution window are part of that P&L, so executing more slowly reduces its variance, and because impact is concave it can also lower cost per share. Urgency comes only from alpha realized while the order is being worked. The problem is governed by the signs of two quantities: (i) the duration elasticity of impact $a$, which under a structural prior equals the impact-persistence gap $β- H$ and can take either sign; and (ii) the net urgency $ν$, the rate of alpha realization net of exposure relief. When $ν$ keeps its sign over the window, an interior optimum exists, to leading order in $T/t_f$, only when both are positive; otherwise the order should be worked at the fastest or slowest admissible pace. In the interior regime the first-order condition involves no impact coefficient, order size or volume, and the objective is flat: for a large-cap example, the window within 1% of maximal Sharpe spans more than an order of magnitude. Second, given the window, we derive the schedule shape by convex programming under an envelope cost. For any increasing per-share cost of delay $w(t)$, the KKT solution is $φ\propto (λ- w(t))_+^{1/β}$. For a Hurst-scaled envelope $w \propto t^H$, the normalized schedule depends only on $(β, H)$, has a closed form via the incomplete beta function, is front-loaded, and tapers smoothly to zero, saving 10-17% of envelope cost relative to a constant-rate (TWAP) schedule of equal duration. Whether it uses the whole window depends on a single dimensionless robustness level, for which we give a calibration.

items.title: Cross-product Modelling in Continuous Intraday Electricity Markets via Hawkes Processes
items.summary: As renewable energy integration accelerates, intraday continuous (IDC) electricity markets have become essential for short-term balancing. However, the simultaneous trading of overlapping contracts with varying granularities creates complex, hidden liquidity dependencies that are critical to market stability but remain poorly understood. This paper proposes a multivariate State-Dependent Hawkes Process (SDHP) to model cross-product liquidity dynamics between Quarter-Hourly and Hourly IDC contracts. To determine how cross-product effects vary under different market conditions, we classify the trading sessions into two distinct regimes: 'Normal' and 'Stressed', based on a composite metric of the bid-ask spread, mid-price volatility and queue imbalance. The model is calibrated on the first month of each quarter of 2024 using level 3 limit order book (LOB) data from the Dutch EPEX SPOT IDC market. We find that order flow is overwhelmingly self-driven, with roughly 95\% of orders arriving in reaction to earlier orders in both regimes. Cross-excitation runs mainly from the Quarter-Hourly to the Hourly contract, but this leadership weakens under stress: the ratio of cumulative cross-excitation falls from 2.8 to 1.5, so the two contracts influence each other almost equally. Stress also makes the Quarter-Hourly to Hourly channel much faster, cutting its mean lag from 6.05 to 0.93 seconds. The strong seasonal variation found in calm periods largely disappears under stress, where all four months converge to the same structure.

items.title: On the skew-curvature power law relationship in a stochastic volatility model with infinite variation Lévy jumps
items.summary: The short-term blow up behaviour of the ATM-IV skew is commonly modelled by either a rough volatility process with small Hurst index or an infinite variation Lévy process in the log-price dynamics. In this paper, we examine which is the effect of mixed dynamics (i.e. rough volatility and infinite variation Lévy processes) on the ATM-IV skew and curvature. The results of the paper show that the analysis of the leading terms of the short-time expansion of both ATM-IV skew and curvature allow us to determine, from a mixed dynamics model, which mechanism originates the power-law behaviour on the skew and on the curvature. Apart from showing that the mixed model also originates a power law, it has also key implications in model design and calibration. Numerical evidences for the rough Heston model with CGMY Lévy jumps are provided.

items.title: Consumption-investment under alternative stochastic-integral conventions
items.summary: We study the Merton consumption-investment problem when risky asset dynamics are written under stochastic-integral conventions indexed by $α$, interpolating between the Itô ($α=0$), Stratonovich ($α=1/2$), and Hänggi-Klimontovich ($α=1$) conventions. Transforming the drift jointly with the convention leaves the optimal policy unchanged; holding the drift coefficient numerically fixed changes the investor's opportunity set. Under logarithmic utility, consumption is unaffected while the optimal portfolio weight shifts by $αV^{-1}d_V$; for a Heston asset, $π_t^\ast=α+(μ-r+α\varrhoξ/2)/V_t$, which can change sign across volatility states. Identifying the convention from return data alone is impossible without additional structural restrictions.

items.title: Algorithmic Collusion Without Deterrence: Auditing the Punishment Mechanism in Q-Learning Pricing Agents
items.summary: Independent tabular Q-learning agents repricing in a simulated Bertrand duopoly converge to supracompetitive prices, and the seminal evidence attributes this to a learned reward-punishment scheme: undercut your rival and it retaliates, so deviation never pays. This mechanistic reading is what turns high prices into a cartel, and into a regulatory target. We replicate the environment of Calvano et al. (2020) and confirm their impulse-response pattern within co-trained pairs. We then audit the pattern on frozen policies, with learning off, and find that on its own it does not identify a mechanism: the return is over-determined rather than selective. In nine of ten converged pairs (914 of 1,024) a single attractor's basin is the entire state space, so every perturbation returns whatever provoked it, and a forced price increase triggers the same retaliatory pattern as an undercut. What co-training produces is a narrow, dyad-specific basin of attraction: re-match frozen agents from independent runs, as Calvano et al. did with learning on, and coordination collapses by 80% with nothing carried across. The deterrence claim is incomplete on its own terms: the one-period undercut of Calvano et al.'s impulse-response test is unprofitable, which we confirm in 92% of pairs, but the optimal deviation, computed by dynamic programming against each partner's frozen strategy, profits by 17.5% on average. The scheme deters only the deviation no optimizer would choose; collusion survives because deviation is never tried, not because it would not pay. Supracompetitive prices are robust; the punishment mechanism read into them does not survive these tests, which changes what the standard test of algorithmic collusion establishes, and what pairing-disruption remedies can be expected to do.

items.title: Basis-Only Funding Is Not Dividend Fair: Settlement Design in Crypto Equity Perpetuals
items.summary: Crypto venues increasingly list perpetual futures on equities and other real-world assets (RWAs), which trade continuously yet reference dividend-paying stocks: a long equity perpetual marked to the ex-dividend cash price bears the ex-dividend drop without receiving the dividend. We ask whether the premium-index funding architecture these venues run -- funding set from the contemporaneous basis $e_t=P_t-S_t$ rather than a carry target -- can replicate shareholder cash flows for traders entering and exiting at arbitrary times. It cannot. Funding serves two roles that coincide for non-dividend crypto assets but split apart for equities: basis control and settlement. We give the fair-funding identity, cast timing fairness as an optimal-stopping condition, and characterize when the basis is a sufficient statistic for the fair target. The decisive obstruction is measure-theoretic: a predictable dividend is an atom, and no absolutely continuous funding path can replicate an atom over holding intervals even in the weak limit, so fairness must match the atom with an atom -- an event credit. Exchange-native data confirm this: at each covered ex-date one venue posts a discrete funding atom equal to $-D/(\mathrm{Mark}-D)$ while a standard premium-index venue posts none, transferring the dividend across venues -- from native funding alone, with no external spot.

items.title: Reading the News Without Hindsight: NoLBERT Topics and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns
items.summary: Language models that read financial news are usually trained on text from the same years used to test them, so a backtest can reward hindsight. We build news topics from NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, adapted into a sentence encoder by contrastive fine-tuning on passages of the same article, with no labels or returns. We compare it with LDA, MiniLM and FinBERT readers on 1.26 million articles from 2012 to 2024, convert each reader's topics into attention shocks and stock exposures, and forecast the returns of the 1,000 largest US stocks with eight models at three rebalancing frequencies. Models are fitted on 2013-2019, choices are made on 2020-2021, and 2022-2024 is held out. The experiment with the best validation score loses money at every frequency. Measuring attention shocks against the past 63 trading days instead of 5 raises the test rank IC of every reader. NoLBERT gives the most stable topics and forecasts about as well as LDA. An equal-weight combination of all readers and models earns a monthly net Sharpe ratio of 1.12, significant against zero before adjusting for the search but not against a price-only benchmark.

items.title: OrderFlowDiT: Transport-Regularized Diffusion Transformer for Probabilistic Limit-Order Supply Forecasting
items.summary: We study the conditional distribution of limit-order volume submitted over the next five minutes, given the current order book and recent order flow. The task requires capturing price placement, total volume, and predictive uncertainty jointly. Coordinate-wise diffusion losses do not explicitly account for price displacement, while normalizing fields to unit mass removes information about total volume. Agreement on selected summary statistics also does not establish fidelity to the joint field distribution. We introduce OrderFlowDiT, a conditional Diffusion Transformer for unnormalized bid and ask volume-at-price fields, trained with an unbalanced optimal-transport (UOT) auxiliary loss. We also develop a full-field evaluation framework that combines a transport cost sensitive to price placement and total volume with proper scoring rules and calibration diagnostics. In the primary comparison on 1950 validation conditions across 30 U.S. equities, adding UOT reduces full-field transport cost by 45.8% and the transport energy score by 26.1% relative to training with mean squared error alone. Both measures improve for every stock. These findings support incorporating price geometry and volume into generative modeling, with field accuracy and predictive uncertainty evaluated together.

items.title: Pricing Generalized Dispersion Swap for Multi-Asset Stochastic Volatility Models
items.summary: This paper develops a generalized variance framework for pricing multi-asset dispersion swap based on the determinant of the instantaneous covariance matrix of asset log-returns. This determinant-based measure captures the joint dispersion of multivariate asset returns while accounting for their dependence structure. We formulate the proposed framework under the Heston and Barndorff-Nielsen-Shephard (BNS) stochastic volatility models, deriving an analytical pricing expression for the three-asset Heston formulation and a tractable approximation for the corresponding BNS formulation. To assess the empirical performance of the proposed approach, we conduct numerical experiments using nine stocks obtained through the quantmod package, randomly partitioned into three groups of three assets. The models are calibrated and evaluated against empirical generalized realized variance across selected time horizons.

items.title: Inverse Learning of Latent Risk-Neutral Densities from Irregular Option Quotes
items.summary: Accurate option prices do not imply accurate recovery of the latent risk-neutral density. We study this distinction with two complementary benchmarks. A controlled benchmark exposes simulator-truth densities for latent evaluation, while a chronological NIFTY benchmark tests only held-out market prices. A two-component lognormal mixture has the lowest aggregate price, $L^1$, Wasserstein, and fixed-tail errors on the synthetic benchmark. Learned operators retain narrower strengths: DeepONet reduces 1% quantile and variance error by 39.0% and 34.6% relative to the mixture, and a quote transformer reduces $L^1$ by 16.4% on the structurally misspecified Merton family. A numerical conditioning analysis explains why these rankings can differ: after enforcing mass and forward constraints, 95 of 126 pricing directions are numerically null, and two densities separated by $L^1 = 0.061$ produce identical prices on the covered strikes. On 524 held-out NIFTY calls, validation-selected test-time adaptation reduces DeepONet RMSE by 28.3%, but per-expiry mixture and SVI fits remain much more accurate. The evidence supports target-dependent inductive bias, not a universal winner.

items.title: Global Multi-Maturity SPX-VIX Calibration Beyond Markovian Stitching
items.summary: We develop a global martingale optimal transport framework for joint S&P 500 (SPX)-VIX smile calibration across multiple maturities, without the conditional independence that Markovian stitching imposes between months. We prove that exact local and global feasibility are equivalent, yet the stitched laws, which carry earlier months only through the current SPX level, can form a strict subset of the global ones, so adjacent smiles cannot identify the dependence across months. We show that relative entropy against the standard Markov reference selects the stitched law, so this dependence must be supplied deliberately. We supply it through a finite-memory reference, in which a latent autoregressive state drives the VIX levels while every VIX marginal stays exact, and calibrate the resulting law on a junction tree whose size grows linearly with the number of maturities. On market data with up to nine SPX maturities, a law with memory and a law without it fit the same quotes but price VIX-conditioned SPX Asian claims differently: on every calendar, memory makes a claim on the maximum VIX cheaper and a claim on the minimum VIX dearer. Varying the memory strength on one calendar moves these differences steadily from zero, so the vanilla quotes, which fix the law of each date, do not determine prices that depend on the joint law across dates.

items.title: Extending the Oracle Approximating Shrinkage to General Distributions
items.summary: The Oracle Approximating Shrinkage (OAS) estimator provides a closed-form, data-driven shrinkage intensity for regularizing sample covariance matrices toward a scaled identity target, but its derivation assumes Gaussian data. In practice, financial returns, neural signals, and many other high-dimensional datasets exhibit heavy tails and non-zero kurtosis, violating this assumption. We extend OAS to any distribution with finite fourth moments by incorporating a correction term $α$ built from the fourth-order joint cumulants of the data. The correction vanishes under Gaussianity, recovering the OAS formula as a special case; it admits a consistent $O(np)$ sample estimator and satisfies $ρ\in [0, 1]$ exactly for both the population cumulant and its sample analogue. Simulations and an equity-returns study confirm that the correction closes the gap between OAS and the Ledoit-Wolf estimator under non-Gaussian data, with OAS-Extended performing comparably across all tested settings. The contribution is a principled correction for OAS practitioners facing heavy-tailed data; structurally, it is distinct from prior work extending Ledoit-Wolf to elliptical distributions, which optimizes against a fixed oracle target and yields a different closed-form formula.

items.title: DYSANOS Generative Dynamic Smooth Arbitrage-free Non-parametric Option Surfaces
items.summary: This article presents with DYSANOS the first generative market model for smooth SANOS option surfaces for all strikes and expiries which are free of static arbitrage. Our model is designed to generate entire paths of daily spot and option prices for years in the future. We present a robust and useful if somewhat simplistic baseline in the form of an AR(1) model. We discuss model setup, data pipeline, and training and investigate market reconstruction, stability, and tail behavior. We illustrate model performance on 891 Option Metrics IvyDB S&P Index surfaces from 2022-01-03 through to 2025-08-29. We also demonstrate how to construct numerically a risk-neutral density. As part of this we develop a new test for zero conditional means under a given measure. We show that for a set of 100,000 simulated paths a trading universe of 48 options and spot is numerically free of dynamic arbitrage.

items.title: Momentum, Commentary Tone, and Earnings Surprise in LLM Financial Forecasts
items.summary: Which inputs drive a language model's financial forecast? We construct synthetic earnings announcements that independently reverse 20-day momentum, non-informational commentary tone, and whether fixed actual EPS beats a manipulated consensus. Six instruction/chat checkpoint conversions from four families (0.49-7.61B base parameters) receive 2,016 prompts each under a direct-answer Q8_0 protocol. The design includes 24 numerical blocks, six commentary pairs, profits and losses, rising and falling annual EPS, and two surprise sizes. Both A/B answer assignments and U/D cover all 384 primary scenarios per conversion. We estimate matched changes in conditional answer-prefix scores, not calibrated market probabilities. Across these checkpoints, the primary EPS contrast ranges from -0.19 to 86.80 percentage points. The magnitude of the primary signed tone contrast exceeds that of EPS in 5 of six models, and momentum exceeds it in 5. Natural-word numerical diagnostic accuracy ranges from 51.0 to 95.8 percent. Answer-encoding, wording, context, and conversion controls qualify these results. The experiment measures observable input reliance and numerical recognition; it establishes neither an internal reasoning mechanism nor realized return predictability. Public benchmark prompts, recorded scores, and an interactive recorded-results explorer accompany the study.

items.title: On the asymptotic shape of quantile surfaces
items.summary: This article is concerned with the asymptotic shape of quantile surfaces, defined as the set of quantiles at a given level $α$ generated by a controlled one-dimensional distribution. Specifically, when the distribution arises as a linear combination of log-normal random variables and the control is a vector of positive coefficients, we prove that quantile surfaces are globally concave in the left tail ($α\to0$) and globally convex in the right tail ($α\to1$). Moreover, these surfaces exhibit asymptotic separation of scale and shape.

items.title: Neural Operators Which Certifiably Simultaneously Solve Infinitely Many Convex Programs using Logarithmic Rank and Linear Complexity
items.summary: Neural operators (NOs) are a class of deep learning models designed to simultaneously solve infinitely many related problems by casting them into an infinite-dimensional space, whereon these NOs operate. Such operator learning problems arise naturally in mathematical finance, for instance, when learning families of optimal portfolios or hedging strategies. Two significant gaps, however, remain between theory and practice: 1) most universal approximation guarantees do not describe practically implementable NOs or are pure existence statements; and 2) worst-case parameter bounds from universal approximation theorems suggest that constructed NOs may require an unrealistically large number of parameters to solve most operator learning problems, which stands in direct opposition to a slew of experimental evidence. This paper closes these gaps by exhibiting a short and simple training algorithm to construct a specific class of NOs, proximal equilibrium operators (PEOs), using (realistic) finite-dimensional deep equilibrium layers to solve families of convex optimization problems over a separable Hilbert space $X$. Here, the inputs are smooth, convex loss functions on $X$, and the outputs are the associated (approximate) solutions to the optimization problems defined by each input loss. Our main result is a certificate showing that, when the input losses lie in a suitable infinite-dimensional set, our PEOs trained with our algorithm do in fact uniformly approximate the corresponding solutions to arbitrary precision, with rank and width growing only logarithmically and the depth growing linearly in the reciprocal of the approximation error. We then validate both our theoretical results and the trainability of PEOs on three applications: non-linear PDEs, stochastic optimal control, and portfolio optimization and hedging problems in mathematical finance.

items.title: Principal component error in high-dimensional factor models
items.summary: In a statistical factor model, principal components (or eigenvectors) of a sample covariance matrix serve as estimates of principal directions, the true drivers of co-movement of a collection of observed variables. We write the often substantial error in these estimates as a sum of two interpretable terms, which we show have almost sure asymptotic limits as the number of variables grows with sample size bounded. This scenario is commonplace in financial economics, genomics, machine learning and signal processing. Out-of-subspace error measures the distance from an estimate to the subspace spanned by population factor exposures. It can be expressed in terms of data, providing an estimable floor for asymptotic error. In-subspace error is driven by a rotation error within that subspace, which arises from the fixed sample size of the latent factor returns and cannot be estimated from data alone. We illustrate our error analysis with a three-factor simulation of the US public equity market, showing the dependence of the magnitude of the error and its components on dimension and sample size. In that simulation, out-of-subspace error dominates. Researchers who rely on principal component analysis to estimate factor models can use our results to quantify errors in model-based predictions and attributions.

items.title: Where Backtests and Live Trading Part Ways: Six Defects from One Intraday System
items.summary: Backtests of intraday strategies can drift away from what the live system actually does; in our case, the drift never showed in summary statistics. We report six defects found while running one intraday US equity system live and comparing its live days with their backtest replay. Three came from data: a default feed that carried a small fraction of real opening volume, historical prices adjusted for dividends that live orders never see, and data the live system downloaded but the backtest never did. Two came from code: a sizing step that exceeded a limit the live account enforces, and UTC timestamps read as New York time. One came from configuration: settings that were switched on but never reached the code that places orders. For each we give the symptom, the size of the error, the cause and the test or control that now guards against it. All six sat where two paths that should agree had drifted apart. We close with a ten-point checklist. We make no claim about whether the system is profitable.

items.title: Feeling the generalised rough SABR boundary
items.summary: We provide an in-depth analysis of a generalised rough version of the SABR volatility model, widely used in the financial industry. We specifically focus on its behaviour at the origin, whether it can reach it and how fast it may do so.

items.title: Real-time identification of the onset of financial rogue waves
items.summary: Extreme events in financial systems, often captured by indicators such as volatility, remain difficult to identify close to their onset. Volatility shares many statistical properties with other natural, complex systems which experience extreme events, which we explore in this manuscript. We extend the analogy between rogue waves in optical and hydrodynamical systems to financial volatility by identifying rogue-wave-like peaks with similar statistical properties. We use a Schrödinger equation where the potential follows the shape of a Kerr nonlinearity to examine the properties of financial volatility indices within a moving time window. We see evidence of Anderson localisation as a rogue peak approaches in the VIX, and show that the numerical gradient of the system's minimum eigenvalue reliably spikes at the onset of an extreme event. We adapt our methodology to simulate the real-time arrival of data, and show that all but one of the VIX's major peaks can be detected given a reasonable amount of history. We then perform two out-of-sample tests, one for the VXO index, and one for the VSTOXX index, and successfully replicate our initial results, identifying all but one major peak (87.5% or 7/8) in both cases. This method of analysis shows considerable promise as a tool for identifying potential financial crises, aiding in their mitigation.

items.title: When Does "Post-Call" Begin? An Availability Contract for Earnings-Call NLP Benchmarks
items.summary: Corporate financial disclosures often unfold over time, with announcements, prepared remarks, and discussion spanning multiple high-frequency return intervals. Financial NLP benchmarks can therefore suffer from a within-event timing mismatch when the prediction target begins before the textual or audio input used by a model could be complete. Chronological train--test splits do not prevent this mismatch, because it occurs inside individual events rather than across samples. We introduce an Availability Contract, which requires a benchmark to state the input boundary, evidence for input availability, the outcome start, and the claims supported by that evidence. We apply this framework to 552 earnings calls from 24 firms. For each call, we hold the return endpoint fixed and compare the previous close, a documentary call-start proxy, and a completion proxy based on reconstructed audio end plus a stipulated processing allowance. At this baseline, moving from the call-start proxy to the completion proxy flips return signs for 9.4% of calls. Holding completion-clock cutpoints fixed, 28.3% change quintile. In an independent release-session analysis of a public earnings-call volatility benchmark, shifting before-market target windows forward by one trading session raises three-day mean squared error by 18.1-21.4% across four frozen prediction streams, while their point rankings remain unchanged. Together, the results show that labels and losses can depend materially on the declared outcome clock even when model rankings appear stable. The Availability Contract makes this assumption explicit and ties post-input claims to the available timing evidence.

items.title: Neural Estimation of Irreversibility in Real and Simulated Limit Order Book Paths
items.summary: A path indistinguishable from its own reverse carries no arrow of time, so time irreversibility is a necessary condition for a directed mechanism to be readable from trajectories alone. In finance it has been measured only on scalar series such as returns and volatility. We define the irreversibility rate of a coarse-grained limit order book path as the forward-to-reverse log-density ratio per event, and estimate it from three weeks of Nasdaq market-by-order data with an order-invariant MLP and a temporal convolutional network that receive identical blocks. For NVDA, the order-invariant and order-sensitive estimates are 0.036 and 0.054 nats per event, respectively. Their difference, the ordering increment, is 0.018. A surrogate preserving the coarse one-step transition table recovers 30 percent less irreversibility than the observed paths. The increment is positive for all twelve symbols on every held-out daytime date, and for NVDA in each session window. It changes more than tenfold with the coarse-graining scale. Neither a linear score nor any single feature group reproduces the full fitted rate. A queue-reactive simulator calibrated on the same days matches the market's ordered rate, 0.052 against 0.054, yet its ordering increment is 0.0006 against 0.018, building temporal asymmetry out of block composition instead of block order. We propose the ordering and scale profile of path irreversibility as a benchmark for order book simulators. Code and audit materials are available at https://github.com/hjyeo30/lob-irreversibility.

items.title: Pricing the Unprovable: Ambiguity, Turnstile Runs, and the Verifiability Discount in Crypto Protocols
items.summary: Privacy-preserving protocols can repair a vulnerability without establishing whether it was exploited beforehand, even when no theft is reported and aggregate supply is protected. We call the potential value reduction from this gap the verifiability discount. A turnstile model shows how early withdrawal can shift a possible shortfall to remaining holders and why credible evidence can become more valuable as exposure grows. We introduce VDISC, a reproducible framework that records reported loss, exposed value, public evidence, returns, and pool flows separately. It combines Orchard's staged disclosures with reconstructed on-chain flows, earlier Zcash cases, and a 40-event security panel. Orchard follows the predicted direction: market responses were muted after repair and supply assurance, while the largest negative return and aggregate shielded-pool net outflow aligned with the acknowledgment that past abuse could not be ruled out. These patterns are directional, not causal. Across events, market-cap-normalized reported loss and unresolved exposure overlap among the 38 events with a public loss figure (Pearson 0.86, Spearman 0.56), partly because exposure is often coded from the loss itself, so returns alone cannot distinguish reported loss from unresolved history. The findings motivate three candidate design priorities: produce privacy-compatible evidence about past states, limit the state exposed by a single flaw, and disclose residual uncertainty explicitly.

items.title: How Much Screening Buys a Second? Speed, Selection, and the Maker's Spread
items.summary: We study the spread a liquidity provider needs to break even against counterparties that can exploit a stale quote, and we place two defenses on a single scale: repricing sooner and screening informed flow. A break-even condition pins down the exact screening rate at which a slower maker matches a faster unscreened venue: the selection that buys back the extra staleness. The result requires only an integrable price innovation and therefore holds under jumps, atoms, and infinite variance. Predictable drift is a centering problem: it widens a spot-centered quote, but its cost vanishes once the quote is recentered on the expected reference. In four USDC-WETH pools benchmarked against Binance ETH-USDT from June to August 2026, the one-second benchmark innovation is sharply non-Gaussian: 73% of seconds show no price change. Cutting cadence from twelve seconds to one sheds 84.5% of the expected shock, so a twelve-second maker must screen at least 84.5% of informed flow to match a one-second venue, far above the 71.1% that a Gaussian model implies. In trending markets, the stale pool is picked off at execution: with-trend fills obtain an effective spread 11.1 bps lower than against-trend fills, with the same sign in all four pools.

items.title: NEST: Stale-Robust Tokenized-Stock Measurement for a Crypto-Treasury LETF Stack
items.summary: Tokenized equities trade while listed markets are closed, so their marks could improve off-hours measurement along layered exposures that link Bitcoin, crypto-treasury stocks, and leveraged ETFs. A token return and the next opening gap, however, share the price move from the previous close to the token mark, so part of their apparent fit is mechanical. We develop NEST, a stale-robust protocol that separates this shared-history fit from conditional measurement value. A shared-history identity and a variance-clock bound show how much fit timing alone can generate. The partial determination index (PDI), the squared partial correlation between token and gap given public controls, measures what remains, and a finite-sample frontier expresses the partial-F decision in PDI units. Product, provenance, timestamp, and execution audits decide whether an informative mark is admissible. For MSTRx, a tracker certificate on MicroStrategy (MSTR), a token-only $R^2$ of 0.916 shrinks to a modest increment once Bitcoin, mark age, and a pre-09:00 MSTR premarket proxy are controlled: the token explains 15.7% of the remaining gap variation (1% frontier 0.031), and 14.0% to 17.0% under stricter clock variants, including one in which every token mark precedes 09:00. A trade-level reconstruction on Gate gives 25.2%; NVDAX and AAPLX clear their frontiers, whereas TSLAX does not. An admitted mark updates, rather than replaces, BTC-unit exposure diagnostics for the BTC-MSTR-LETF chain.

items.title: Long-Horizon Investment with Delayed Information in a Mean-Reverting Market
items.summary: We study long-term investment in an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck diffusion model with exponential utility. We solve the finite-horizon problem explicitly and show that information delay qualitatively alters long-horizon behavior. Under full information, the certainty equivalent generated by mean reversion grows quadratically with the investment horizon. With any fixed positive delay, it grows only linearly, at an asymptotic rate that we compute explicitly. We derive an explicit causal representation of the optimal delayed portfolio and show that projecting the full-information strategy onto delayed information can fail dramatically: the resulting exponential loss becomes infinite for sufficiently long horizons. Numerical examples illustrate the economic impact of information delay.

items.title: Fundamental Theorem of Discrete Asset Pricing
items.summary: Motivated by discrete price quotes in continuous time, we seek a fundamental theorem based on no arbitrage rather than a condition on limiting trading opportunities. We consider a vector of discounted prices taking values in a locally finite subset of $R^d$ in continuous time. For a locally bounded càdlàg price, we prove that no arbitrage, no free lunch with vanishing risk, no free lunch, and the existence of an equivalent local martingale measure are equivalent. An elementary finite-dimensional reduction of portfolios yields a common pathwise bound on admissible wealth. This bound reduces closedness to convex averaging in a weighted Hilbert space, after which the Kreps-Yan theorem applies. Trading gains are finite Stieltjes sums, and the proof uses no Itô integration.

items.title: The end-of-month option in futures contracts and the Gittins index of holding the underlying
items.summary: The end-of-month option allows the short in a futures contract to choose when to deliver during a window in which the delivery price is fixed. We characterize optimal delivery through a universal index obtained from the Bank--El Karoui representation theorem. In the semimartingale setting, this is the Gittins index of holding the underlying and collecting its convenience yield, and the futures price is the retirement reward for which the value of this project equals the spot price. This characterization yields price bounds and a criterion for immediate delivery. Dinkelbach's iteration reduces the price computation to a sequence of standard optimal stopping problems, with an explicit contraction bound. We apply the theory to geometric Brownian motion and the Gibson--Schwartz model with stochastic convenience yield. For geometric Brownian motion, we characterize when the futures price equals spot and derive a square-root boundary asymptotic near expiry. For the Gibson--Schwartz model, we establish monotonicity in the yield and characterize the critical yield below which the price equals spot. Numerical results illustrate the price iteration and delivery regions.

items.title: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery
items.summary: Formulaic alpha mining seeks to discover executable expressions that capture predictive market signals in a vast, noisy search space. Recent LLM-based approaches use prompting, iterative search, or seed-factor evolution, leaving direct factor construction through policy learning less explored. To address this, we introduce AlphaRLM, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors from financial literature without input factor expressions. AlphaRLM incorporates Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO), which conditions factor construction on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, providing semantic priors for exploration. It further aligns the generation policy with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Extensive experiments on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 show that AlphaRLM outperforms strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return. Notably, the 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance, highlighting the promise of literature-conditioned, market-aligned factor generation.

items.title: Pricing American Commodity Options Under the Schwartz Two-Factor Model Using the Alternating Direction Explicit (ADE) Method
items.summary: This project investigates the valuation of American commodity options using the Schwartz two-factor model. We employ the double-sweep Alternating Direction Explicit (ADE) method, an unconditionally stable (for diffusion) finite difference scheme that provides the efficiency of explicit marching with the stability typically reserved for implicit methods, and compare it with the single-sweep alternating variant of Saul'yev. We derive the governing partial differential equation (PDE) and transform the semi-infinite domain into a rectangular computational domain. Furthermore, we apply Fichera theory to determine boundary conditions at the limits of the spot price. Finally, we implement the solver in C++, validating the results first against the closed-form solution of the PDE and Monte Carlo as a European option, then apply the American early exercise constraint and benchmark against Longstaff-Schwartz Monte Carlo to analyze numerical accuracy and convergence. The framework is then extended, following feedback from a commodities trader to exercise on futures prices and use seasonal parameters.

items.title: Loss-versus-rebalancing with external proportional transaction costs
items.summary: We study liquidity provision in automated market makers when trading in the external market incurs proportional transaction costs. We consider both separately collected fees and fees retained in reserves. The benchmark is a self-financing strategy holding the same total risky inventory and trading at the external bid and ask. Under continuous external prices and pure arbitrage, the pool and benchmark have identical liquidation wealth whenever the pool fee or the external spread is positive. Thus loss-versus-rebalancing relative to this transaction-cost benchmark is zero, even without a pool fee if the external spread is positive. We then construct retained-fee utility-indifference pools that implement admissible decreasing inventory schedules, and geometric mean pools that implement feasible constant no-trade boundaries for portfolio weights. These results offer an investment interpretation of liquidity provision: by choosing the pool design, a liquidity provider can specify a trading strategy whose rebalancing is carried out by arbitrageurs.

items.title: Choice of Collateral Currency in Differential Swaps
items.summary: The role of collateral in derivative pricing has evolved beyond credit risk mitigation, particularly following the global financial crisis, when funding costs and basis spreads became central to valuation practices. This development coincided with the transition from the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) to risk-free rates (RFRs) and the increasing standardization of collateralised trading. We study the valuation and hedging of a class of differential swaps referencing backward-looking averages of overnight rates, with Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR) swaps appearing as a particular instance. The focus is on the impact of the collateral currency. Extending the earlier results of Bickersteth et al. [Math. Finance 36 (2026), pp.~180--202], we allow the collateral account to be denominated in a currency different from that of the contractual cash flows and derive explicit pricing and hedging strategies using a futures-based replication approach. We show that the choice of collateral currency can have a non-trivial effect on both valuation and risk management through discounting adjustments and payment-date weights. Numerical experiments validate the closed-form formulas, demonstrate that collateral effects can produce valuation adjustments, and confirm the effectiveness of the futures hedges under discrete rebalancing.

items.title: Requested, Executed and Recoverable Credit: Shared Action Ordering among LLM Borrowers in a Simulated Lending Market
items.summary: We test whether shared action ordering changes executed credit in a simulated collateralized lending market. Three small open-weight language models face a borrowing cap that values collateral at the pool price; only two of the three model families traded. A validation campaign, hash-locked locally before its first model call, pairs 12 common-order markets with 12 balanced-order markets under a revised interface. An exact randomization test rejects the sharp null that common-market net debt is invariant to complete-order assignment (two-sided p = 2/8,100). The pre-specified estimate of the lever-up-first versus delever-first common-market contrast is 1.12 units of initial unused reference borrowing capacity, combining a 0.828 gap between the two groups of common markets with a 0.293 balanced-baseline component. All 24 markets increased debt. An exploratory accounting split shows that lever-up-first common markets borrowed more and repaid less. With requests held fixed, reference-priced collateral narrows the observed common-market order gap from 0.828 to 0.688 capacity units. No market experienced liquidation or realized bad debt. Under the pre-specified fixed-price 30 percent shock benchmark, individual high-LTV loans generate scenario write-offs even though aggregate LTVs remain below the write-off threshold. Most benchmark write-off arises from collateral consumed by the liquidation bonus. The experiment establishes an effect of action order on executed credit; accounting identities and deterministic counterfactuals explain how collateral constraints and borrower-level debt allocation shape conditional creditor recovery.

items.title: $q_x$-Bass Martingales: Optimality, Existence and Convergence
items.summary: We introduce the class of $q_x$-Bass martingales, extending the notion of $q$-Bass martingales.
