Under the CDF linearization, a Riesz-regression criterion estimates the correction automatically; its analysis distinguishes representer estimation from integration against the estimated conditional law. We establish asymptotic oracle equivalence, asymptotic normality, and consistent variance estimation for cross-fitted estimators under continuity and remainder conditions, without requiring functional weak convergence of the first-step estimators. An exact linear representation yields double robustness; for rank-rank regression this property is componentwise. Simulations report reductions in bias and RMSE relative to plug-in estimation, with double cross-fitting improving the finite-sample performance.

items.title: Simultaneous Gradient Learning in First-Price Auctions
items.summary: We study equilibrium learning in discretized Bayesian games, focusing on first-price auctions as a testbed for gradient-based learning dynamics under private information. While the symmetric independent private values model admits a unique Bayesian correlated equilibrium (BCE) in the continuous limit, standard convergence guarantees for gradient-based learners do not apply: classical no-regret theory predicts convergence only to Bayesian coarse correlated equilibria (BCCE), which can remain large and far from the competitive equilibrium even under fine discretizations. To bridge this gap, we introduce the notion of Bayesian semicoarse correlated equilibrium (BSCCE), an equilibrium concept that refines BCCE by restricting deviations to probability-preserving transformations consistent with projected gradient dynamics. We provide a linear programming characterization of BSCCE with polynomially many variables and constraints and establish the inclusion hierarchy $BCE \subseteq BSCCE \subseteq BCCE$. Our main finding is that the BSCCE set contracts in many cases as the discretization of the Bayesian game is refined. Even with priors for which BCCE fails to concentrate, the diameter of the BSCCE polytope shrinks toward zero, indicating convergence to the unique continuous-game Bayes-Nash equilibrium. These results provide a principled explanation for the observed robustness of gradient-based learning in discretized Bayesian games, showing that these dynamics select a smaller equilibrium set than standard no-regret theory predicts.

items.title: Realized Stochastic Volatility Models with Skew-t Distributions for Volatility and Tail Risk Forecasting
items.summary: Volatility forecasts underlie tail risk measures: value-at-risk (VaR) and expected shortfall (ES). This paper compares realized stochastic volatility (RSV) models, which add a realized measure to the stochastic volatility (SV) model, with their SV counterparts under normal, Student's t, two skew-normal, and three skew-t return distributions, and against EGARCH and REGARCH benchmarks. Estimated by Markov chain Monte Carlo on the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the Nikkei 225, the models are compared by their one-day-ahead volatility, VaR, and ES forecasts (the predictive mean for volatility). Adding realized volatility improves volatility forecasts over the main sample for both indices under every proxy and return distribution; the gains are uniformly significant for the Nikkei 225 but, for the Dow Jones, only under the realized variance used in estimation. During the COVID-19 period the gains persist for the Nikkei 225 but vanish for the Dow Jones, where the REGARCH benchmark is best. For VaR and ES the gains are confined to the Nikkei 225 and to the 5% level for the Dow Jones, and few matched-pair differences are significant. Skewed innovations lower the 1% joint loss for the Dow Jones, but no specification dominates across indices, risk levels, and sample periods.

items.title: Pawnshops and Property-Related Crime: Lessons from Interwar Tokyo
items.summary: Using ward-level panel data for 1927 to 1935 and fixed-effects models, this study examines how pawnshops were related to property-related crime in interwar Tokyo. Accordingly, public pawnshops targeting low-income borrowers are compared with profit-oriented private pawnshops. The results reveal that public lending is negatively associated with theft and positively associated with fraud and extortion, whereas private lending is negatively associated with fraud and extortion as well as embezzlement. A simple monetization exercise shows that offense counts and victim losses can yield different assessments. Overall, the relationship between credit and crime depended on both institutional design and crime type.

items.title: When an effort-maximizing team architecture is unstable
items.summary: Organizations choose team structures to intensify competition, yet their members may prefer to reorganize. We ask whether an architecture that maximizes aggregate effort can remain stable when contestants may form a replacement team from incumbent rosters. When a coalition draws from identical teams and reproduces their type, its members and the designer rank the reorganization in opposite directions: the coalition gains precisely when total effort falls. A strict effort optimum can therefore supply its own blocking certificate, while a stable optimum can survive only on a plateau where every reachable reorganization of this kind leaves effort unchanged. In a linear benchmark, we characterize stability against every feasible one-team reorganization and global effort maximization over every feasible partition. Except under pair capacity, the two regions do not overlap; with pair capacity, they meet only at one boundary. The ordering persists in a matched quadratic benchmark with strictly convex effort cost, and broader one-step deviation rights cannot restore overlap. Among standardized full-cap designs, the unique stable-effort optimum uses the largest feasible roster and sets incentive concentration at its blocking boundary.

items.title: A sensitivity analysis for the average derivative effect
items.summary: In observational studies, exposures are often continuous rather than binary or discrete. At the same time, sensitivity analysis is an important tool that can help determine the robustness of a causal conclusion to a certain level of unmeasured confounding, which can never be ruled out in an observational study. Sensitivity analysis approaches for continuous exposures have now been proposed for several causal estimands. In this article, we focus on the average derivative effect (ADE). We obtain closed-form bounds for the ADE under a sensitivity model that constrains the odds ratio (at any two dose levels) between the latent and observed generalized propensity score. We propose flexible, efficient estimators for the bounds that are compatible with machine learning algorithms as well as point-wise and simultaneous (over the sensitivity parameter) confidence intervals. We examine the finite sample performance of the methods through simulations and illustrate the methods on a study assessing the effect of parental income on educational attainment and a study assessing the price elasticity of petrol.

items.title: Optimal Information Disclosure in Classic Auctions Revisited: Endogenous Information Acquisition and Costly Verification
items.summary: We revisit the influential distribution-independent optimal disclosure result of Bergemann, Heumann, Morris, Sorokin, and Winter (2022), whose optimal disclosure policy reveals low bidder values and pools high values at a critical quantile depending only on the number of bidders, and show that this policy is no longer generally revenue-maximizing even for the familiar uniform and binary valuation distributions, once bidders can endogenously acquire private information through costly verification. The underlying reason reflects a fundamental principle of incentive-based mechanism design, rooted in Hurwicz's analysis of structural invariance and echoed in the Lucas critique: economic agents respond strategically to changes in the information and incentives they face. This is the essence of \emph{trust, but verify}. A change in disclosure policy may leave the underlying economic primitives unchanged while altering bidders' verification decisions and the resulting equilibrium information structure. We establish existence and uniqueness of the symmetric Bayesian Nash verification equilibrium, characterize equilibrium-implementable disclosure policies, and derive an exact revenue decomposition and a general characterization of global optimality. We further develop optimality conditions and structural results that provide a systematic foundation for analyzing optimal disclosure with endogenous information acquisition.

items.title: Dynamic Mechanism and Information Design in AI-Agent Environments: A General Analytical Framework
items.summary: TThis paper develops a general framework for dynamic mechanism and information design in AI-agent principal--agent environments, encompassing optimal contracting and integrating evolving hidden information and hidden action with partial verification, technological authorization, and multi-agent interaction. It nests conventional dynamic screening, hidden-action contracting, and conditional dynamic information design, while allowing reporting, action, and information-use decisions to interact through a common continuation mechanism. We establish a dynamic revelation principle and a recursive characterization of implementability in which truthful reporting and post-report obedience are jointly determined through continuation incentives. In quasilinear optimal-contracting environments, dynamic envelope and integral-monotonicity methods yield a verification-adjusted dynamic virtual-surplus representation and identify three distinct margins: dynamic information rents, verification rents, and the implementation cost of hidden action. These margins generate a branched hierarchy separating conventional dynamic screening, hidden-action contracting, and their joint problem. We also study the joint design of monitoring, information use, and incentives: more informative monitoring capacity expands the designer's opportunity set, but full disclosure need not be optimal, and information use can itself alter hidden-action incentives. With multiple agents, correlated information, peer discipline, coupled incentives, joint feasibility, and continuation opportunities create additional strategic interactions. Although motivated by AI-agent environments, the framework applies more broadly to dynamic agency settings with similar economic features.

items.title: Latent community paths in VAR-type models via dynamic directed spectral co-clustering
items.summary: This paper proposes a dynamic network framework for uncovering latent community paths in high-dimensional VAR-type models. By embedding a degree-corrected stochastic co-blockmodel (ScBM) into the transition matrices of VAR-type systems, we separate sending and receiving roles at the node level and summarize complex directional dependence in an interpretable low-dimensional form. Our method integrates directed spectral co-clustering with eigenvector smoothing to track how directional groups split, merge, or persist over time. This framework accommodates both periodic VAR (PVAR) models for cyclical seasonal evolution and generalized VHAR models for structural transitions across ordered dependence horizons. We establish non-asymptotic misclassification bounds for both procedures and provide supporting evidence through Monte Carlo experiments. Applications to U.S. nonfarm payrolls distinguish a recurrent business-centered core from more mobile, seasonally sensitive sectors. In global stock volatilities, the results reveal a compact U.S.-centered long-horizon block, a Europe-heavy developed core, and a more dynamic short-horizon reallocation of peripheral and bridge markets.

items.title: How to Pick a Model if You Must
items.summary: I axiomatize Berk-Nash equilibrium in decision problems with possibly misspecified models. I specify how a rule--which selects a set of action-belief pairs in a problem--ought to compare a correct forecast with an incorrect one, react to the removal of models, and accommodate additional observations that do not distinguish among the models. Together with axioms concerning attitudes toward randomization and payoffs, and a pair of regularity conditions, these axioms characterize Berk-Nash equilibrium.

items.title: Monotone comparative statics under dual submodularity, with an application to aggregate deferred acceptance
items.summary: We develop monotone comparative statics for constrained quantity choices generated by convex costs satisfying dual submodularity, meaning that their Legendre-Fenchel conjugates are submodular. We introduce the Q-order, an exchange order for possibly set-valued quantity choices, and prove a dual counterpart of Topkis's theorem. A closed proper convex function is exchangeable in the Q-order if and only if its conjugate is submodular. Exchangeability implies Q-monotonicity of rejected quantities under price and capacity changes; when the conjugate has a sublattice domain, the comparative-statics property is also a characterization. We apply the result to two-sided matching with divisible masses and welfare-generated, possibly set-valued choices. An aggregate deferred-acceptance algorithm is well defined; the availability sequence and the least waiting-time multiplier sequences converge; and every proposal limit selected by the theorem yields an aggregate equilibrium matching. The construction covers classical stable nontransferable-utility matching and aggregate random-utility specifications.

items.title: Choosing the Dictionary and Penalty for IV-LASSO
items.summary: Estimating an instrumental variables (IV) first stage with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) requires choosing a dictionary and penalty. Existing rules target first-stage objectives, although these choices affect structural estimation. We derive a feasible approximate mean squared error (AMSE) criterion for full-sample IV-LASSO with one endogenous regressor and homoskedastic Gaussian errors. For a prespecified list of dictionary-penalty pairs, the criterion trades off approximation of the optimal instrument against a complexity cost that depends on the first two moments of the LASSO effective dimension and on the degree of endogeneity. The selected pair attains the smallest candidate-specific AMSE component up to vanishing relative error. In simulations calibrated to Paravisini et al. (2015), the criterion improves substantially on the plug-in rule at low endogeneity and on cross-validation at high endogeneity, with nearly identical results under non-Gaussian errors. A supplementary appendix formally extends analysis to a class of non-Gaussian errors.

items.title: Reputation and Delegated Public Spending
items.summary: This paper studies a repeated funding relationship between a grant administrator and an implementing agency. The agency is either committed to implementation or able to divert the advance. The administrator chooses whether to fund and whether to verify, but cannot commit to future decisions. We construct a stationary equilibrium in which agencies with intermediate reputations are audited. An inspection either reveals diversion and ends funding or leads to continued funding with intermittent auditing. In the latter case, audits sustain implementation without further revealing type, while a strategic agency diverts unaudited advances. Cheaper auditing makes funding worthwhile at lower reputations. For initial beliefs audited under both cost levels, it raises the administrator's value but reduces expected long-run implemented spending: a higher reputation is required to retain funding, and fewer strategic agencies meet that requirement. For beliefs audited under both programs, better detection at unchanged cost instead raises implementation without changing the probability of continued funding. These results show why project delivery alone need not measure the value of improved monitoring.

items.title: Tracks to Modernity: Railroads, Growth, and Civic Institutions in Denmark
items.summary: We examine how railroads shaped Denmark's nineteenth-century economic transformation and the diffusion of Grundtvigian institutions. Using a panel of 1589 parishes and a difference-in-differences design for staggered adoption, we find that railroad connection increased local population by 7 percent, partly through internal in-migration, and structural change away from agriculture. Railroad access also brought cultural and institutional change by increasing the local densities of folk high schools and community houses, though these results are less robust than the economic findings.

items.title: Dividing a cake for the irrationally entitled
items.summary: A perfectly divisible cake is to be divided among a group of agents. Each agent is entitled to a share between zero and one, and these entitlements are compatible in that they sum to one. The mediator does not know the preferences of the agents, but can query the agents to make cuts and appraise slices in order to learn. For each entitlement profile, we provide a lower bound on the number of queries that the mediator requires to construct an allocation that respects the entitlements regardless of preferences. If one of the entitlements is irrational, then the mediator requires an arbitrarily large number of queries.

items.title: fastC-GC and fastC-GC*: Efficient RCCP-Guided Graph Estimation for Time Series
items.summary: We introduce fastC-GC and fastC-GC$^*$, computationally efficient methods for time-series graph estimation using the two-test rule motivated by Reichenbach's common cause principle (RCCP) and the conditioning sets of causalised Granger causality (c-GC and c-GC$^*$). The methods use standardized data, ridge-residual correlation, and complete circular shift enumeration evaluated by Fourier transforms. Shared precision calculations and Schur downdates avoid repeated regression fits. On a single-threaded benchmark, fastC-GC was 68-277 times faster than the compared c-GC implementation, and fastC-GC$^*$ was 192-886 times faster than c-GC$^*$. Across four suites with reference graphs, aggregate mean area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) differed from the corresponding baseline by at most 0.019, but F1 was lower at the selected thresholds in every suite. The computational gains therefore accompany a change in estimator and selected graphs. Among eight methods, Bagged PCMCI+ had the highest mean AUPRC on sparse VAR, an autocorrelated structural process, and DREAM3; CUTS+ led on Lorenz-96. Wind-tunnel and river-discharge applications illustrate differences between inferred graphs without establishing causal accuracy. We prove the computational identities and a restricted population adjacency result for fastC-GC$^*$. Causal interpretation requires the stated graphical assumptions; validity of the implemented tests additionally requires a suitable shift-invariant null law. Empirical null rejection rates informed the conditional threshold $β= 0.005$, without establishing general test validity or graph-wide error control.

items.title: Rewarding Noise: Incentives in Decentralized A/B Testing
items.summary: Many firms that run A/B tests struggle with low statistical power, increasing the risk that launch decisions are driven by noise rather than true impact. We argue that in decentralized organizations, low power can reflect misaligned incentives: product teams choose what and how to test on a customer-facing experience to maximize their private reward, while the experience owner sets evaluation rules and launch criteria to optimize the experience. We formalize this interaction via a principal-agent model and show that evaluating tests using raw impact estimates creates a reward to sampling noise. Correctly calibrated posterior-mean evaluation removes this reward and creates a local incentive to reallocate toward fewer, more precise tests of more ambitious ideas. Using data on A/B tests run at Amazon, we document patterns consistent with these model predictions. After an Amazon experience shifted to posterior-mean-based evaluation in 2024, test volume declined while both precision and the dispersion of true impacts increased, more than doubling signal-to-noise ratios. Our results highlight that A/B testing methodologies can shape not only measurement and launch decisions, but which tests are pursued in the first place.

items.title: On dynamic price formation in the course of capital reallocation driven by differential rates of profit: strict conservation of value supports Karl Marx's theory
items.summary: We develop a three-sector model in which Marx's aggregate equalities (total price equals total value; total profit equals total surplus value) restrict a sequence of fully realized states during capital reallocation and technical diffusion. Anchoring one sector's profit rate to the contemporaneous average selects a trajectory without modeling pricing intentions. Before innovation, capital inflow lowers the receiving sector's price and excess profitability along calibrated stable paths, without a demand function. Stability is predictable from value and technical data; near a stable equalization, the receiver's profit rate falls even where its price rises. A labor-saving, capital-intensifying innovation creates temporary extra surplus value and revalues committed capital. At constant real wages the final uniform rate rises, as Okishio predicts; when rising wages keep exploitation constant, it falls.

items.title: On the Use of Design-Based Simulations
items.summary: Design-based simulations hold outcomes fixed and generate variation by resampling treatment assignment or shocks. They can be used in both methodological and applied work to assess inference procedures. However, their informativeness for these uses is not straightforward. We show that, when treatment effects are nonzero, these simulations can be misleading about spatial or serial correlation in clustered experiments, difference-in-differences, and shift-share designs. We analyze alternatives and formalize how these simulations can reveal features of the error distribution despite holding outcomes fixed. Finally, we consider limitations in the use of design-based simulations to select among different inference methods in applied work.

items.title: Hosting is not capturing: an exposure-capability framework and Hungary's electric-vehicle battery bet
items.summary: How should a dependent economy respond when a polycrisis turns economic integration from a source of efficiency into a surface of vulnerability? This paper develops the exposure-capability framework, which maps a country's strategic options along two dimensions - the concentration of its external dependence and the depth of its productive capability - and yields four ideal strategies. It applies the framework to Hungary's large-scale bet on electric-vehicle battery manufacturing, asking what the concentrated exposure purchased: movement toward a higher position in the battery value chain, as a catch-up gamble, or the reproduction of the country's existing position under a new product, as dependent entrenchment. Using a firm-level panel of Hungary's largest companies for 2010-2024, it tests four hypotheses and examines the conditions attached to the support that financed the investments. The sector has expanded enormously, but its value capture neither rises beyond the recovery from construction losses nor shifts up the chain: production remains concentrated in the lowest-value stage, matures only to the level of comparably young foreign-owned firms, and does not cover its own costs. The support that financed it required investment volume, revenue and employment retention; capability-relevant criteria entered the decree as considerations rather than conditions, and a capability-contingent instrument within the same scheme went unused. On the evidence to 2024 the bet is a lateral substitution at constant quality, in which battery-cell fabrication replaces automotive assembly at the same dependent position. Hosting the green transition's supply chain, the case shows, is not the same as capturing its value.

items.title: Demand Estimation with Unobserved Stockout Substitution: Exact Likelihood Maximization
items.summary: When a product is sold out, customers who prefer it may buy a substitute or leave without purchasing. Efficient demand estimation in this setting is challenging when inventory is observed only at replenishments, because the stockout times, and hence the products available to each customer, are unobserved. Estimating demand efficiently under stockout substitution has been a challenging problem since Anupindi et al. (1998), and it has become more pressing as the scale of such problem instances grows thanks to innovations in retailing such as unmanned stores. We provide a complete solution to this problem for the multinomial logit (MNL) model, the most widely used model of customer choice. Using a continuous-time representation of the purchase process developed in Zhou et al. (2026), we show that the exact likelihood and its gradient are one-dimensional integrals, no matter how many products, customers, or stockouts there are. Both can be evaluated at a cost linear in the numbers of products and periods. Our method estimates demand for 2,000 products from 2,000 selling periods in under ten minutes.

items.title: Climate change, sea level rise, and the agricultural revolution
items.summary: We test various hypotheses for the invention and spread of agriculture: higher temperatures, increased seasonality, carbon dioxide fertilization, sea level rise, and technological progress on the extensive margin. We successfully replicate Matranga (QJE 2024). His seasonality hypothesis survives alternative data, estimators, and competing hypotheses. Population density played a role in the invention of agriculture, while spatial diffusion was important for its spread. Sea level rise and climate change had a minor effect on the population density of the areas that first adopted agriculture. Extrapolating a logit model for the invention of agriculture, some now-submerged areas in the Persian Gulf, Mediterranean, and Yellow Sea were suitable for early agriculture. Over time, technological progress was the main factor in extending agriculture's extensive margin.

items.title: A polyhedral characterization of worker-quasi-stable matchings
items.summary: We provide the first polyhedral characterization of worker-quasi-stable matchings in the classical one-to-one matching model. By modifying the classical stability constraints, we introduce a convex polytope and prove that it is integral. Consequently, its extreme points coincide exactly with the incidence vectors of worker-quasi-stable matchings, demonstrating that worker-quasi-stability preserves the geometric tractability of standard stability.

items.title: TRACE: Governing AI-Assisted Research with Principles from Computer Science
items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has made it easier than ever to produce research outputs. Adding an agentic tool to a research team's work potentially extends the team's capabilities but calls for an active approach to organizing the research process. The pressing question, therefore, is how research teams should organize their work with this technology. We contend that the question is not new: software engineering and security research have long studied how teams of people working with machines keep control of projects with many contributors. We distill principles from the practices these literatures report and transpose them to AI-assisted research. The principles form TRACE: Track records, Review against sources, Accept independently, Control transitions, and Evaluate corrections. Together, the five principles give researchers a common basis for remaining in control while integrating AI into their workflows. By bounding units of work and attending to how each is shaped, they can help researchers pace AI-assisted work to human attention rather than to the speed at which AI produces content. We also introduce TRACE-OS, an operating system for AI-assisted research projects. It puts the principles into practice through shared instructions, tools, and records that fit researchers' existing workflows. With TRACE, we aim to join a conversation about the governing principles through which the research community can benefit from AI. We contend that a simple enough and useful standard can contribute to harnessing AI capabilities, allowing teams to delegate parts of their work to AI, while also building trust within teams and the broader research community.

items.title: Algorithmic Monoculture in Machine Learning-based Site-Specific Fertilizer Recommendation
items.summary: Machine learning recommendations are often evaluated one model at a time, despite deployment across interconnected decision makers. For continuous NPK fertilizer prescriptions, correlated errors can aggregate across farms and generate systemic costs. A model of shared and farm-specific recommendation errors links expected social loss to model adoption shares; the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index characterizes concentration effects when common model errors are independent and predictive risks are equal. A covariance-generalized formulation captures the dependence between model families. A two-model threshold characterizes when privately optimal monoculture is socially dominated, and a convex portfolio rule limits average private predictive regret. Nine model families across five Moroccan cereal systems provide a benchmark-based calibration. Under illustrative parameters and a 10% regret cap, accuracy-constrained diversification lowers modeled social loss in all five systems by 10.89-41.53% (mean 19.41%). Uniform allocation reduces modeled loss in this setting, but breaches the regret cap in every crop. Correlation sensitivity shows that highly dependent model errors attenuate the benefits of diversification. These counterfactual outcomes are not estimates of agronomic or monetary welfare; the framework identifies adoption architecture and error dependence as ecosystem-level evaluation variables.

items.title: A Semiparametric Real-Time GARCH Model with Nonstationary Variance
items.summary: We propose a semiparametric real-time GARCH (SRT-GARCH) model that combines a smooth deterministic long-run volatility component with a stationary short-run process driven by contemporaneous return innovations. The model accommodates gradual changes in unconditional variance while allowing short-run volatility to respond directly to current information rather than relying solely on lagged observations. We derive the variance normalization, conditional moments, and closed-form conditional density of the model. For estimation, we develop a two-step procedure that combines kernel smoothing with conditional Gaussian maximum likelihood. Under Gaussian innovations and mild regularity conditions, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the short-run parameter estimator. The analysis exploits geometric moment contraction to control serial dependence and shows that estimating the long-run component adds a positive semidefinite rank-one adjustment to the oracle covariance matrix obtained when the long-run component is known. The resulting asymptotic covariance matrix admits a plug-in estimator that requires neither lag truncation nor additional tuning parameters. Monte Carlo simulations show good finite-sample performance of the estimator and the associated inference procedure. Applications to FTSE~100 returns and U.S. natural gas futures show that allowing for a time-varying long-run component improves forecasting relative to the parametric RT-GARCH benchmark, while the additional real-time feedback mechanism provides more pronounced gains in the natural gas application than in the FTSE application. The proposed model also delivers competitive one-step-ahead Value-at-Risk forecasts.

items.title: Characterizing Maximum Nash Welfare: Envy-Freeness and Proportionality
items.summary: When allocating indivisible goods, the maximum Nash welfare rule is known to be the unique welfarist rule satisfying envy-freeness up to one good. We strengthen this characterization by showing that envy-freeness up to one good can be replaced by substantially weaker fairness requirements: envy-freeness up to $k$ goods or proportionality up to $k$ goods, for any fixed $k$. Our characterization holds even for profiles with identical goods.

items.title: Evaluating A/B Testing Methodologies via Sample Splitting: Theory and Practice
items.summary: We develop a theoretical framework for sample splitting in A/B testing environments, where data for each test are partitioned into two splits to measure methodological performance when the true impacts of tests are unobserved. We show that sample-split estimators are generally biased for full-sample performance but consistently estimate sample-split analogues of it. We derive their asymptotic distributions, construct valid confidence intervals, and characterize the bias-variance trade-offs underlying sample-split design choices. We validate our theoretical results through simulations and provide implementation guidance for A/B testing products seeking to evaluate new estimators and decision rules.

items.title: Aggregative Efficiency of Bayesian Learning in Networks
items.summary: When individuals in a social network learn about an unknown state from private signals and neighbors' actions, the network structure often causes information loss. We consider rational agents and Gaussian signals in the canonical sequential social-learning problem and ask how the network changes the efficiency of signal aggregation. Rational actions in our model are log-linear functions of observations and admit a signal-counting interpretation of accuracy. Networks where agents observe multiple neighbors but not their common predecessors confound information, and even a small amount of confounding can lead to much lower accuracy. In a class of networks where agents move in generations and observe the previous generations, we quantify the information loss with an aggregative efficiency index. Aggregative efficiency is a simple function of network parameters: increasing in observations and decreasing in confounding. Later generations contribute little additional information, even when generations are arbitrarily large and agents observe arbitrarily far into the past.

items.title: Sybil-Proofness of Generalized Adaptive Clinching and Implications for Blockchain Mechanism Design
items.summary: The adaptive clinching auction of Dobzinski, Lavi, and Nisan (FOCS'08) is a cornerstone of mechanism design with budget-constrained bidders, and it has since inspired a broad range of extensions to substantially richer market settings. Adaptive clinching enjoys compelling guarantees: it is Pareto optimal, and truthful bidding is a dominant strategy whenever budgets cannot be overreported. In many real-world environments, however, identities are cheap to create, making resilience to Sybil attacks an additional requirement. Whether the guarantees of adaptive clinching survive when a bidder can split its budget across fake identities has remained open. We introduce a generalized framework for adaptive clinching and prove that it satisfies Sybil-robust incentive compatibility: a bidder cannot benefit from splitting into any finite number of identities with arbitrary value reports, provided their aggregate reported budget does not exceed the bidder's enforceable true budget. Sybil resilience thus joins the list of ideal properties of adaptive clinching. Our work is motivated by practical problems in decentralized finance, where automated market makers (AMMs) are among the most widely used applications. We design a new AMM mechanism that extends classical adaptive clinching in two ways: it supports a two-sided market and protects against two-sided strategies, and it allows the supply function to depend on the auction state. Its one-sided special case is captured by our generalized adaptive clinching framework, and our proof techniques show that the full two-sided mechanism simultaneously satisfies Sybil-robust incentive compatibility and a relaxed notion of Pareto optimality. We argue that these guarantees are essentially the best possible via impossibility results. More broadly, our work reveals new connections between classical algorithmic game theory and modern decentralized blockchains.

items.title: Valid Post-Contextual Bandit Inference
items.summary: Contextual multi-armed bandits (CMAB) are increasingly used as adaptively sampled experiments, after which researchers test hypotheses about treatment effects. We derive the Hájek-Le Cam limit experiment for multi-armed contextual bandits under equal-arms (weak-signal) asymptotics. It is Locally Asymptotically Quadratic, but not a (mixed) Gaussian shift experiment. Girsanov's theorem gives it a structural representation in stochastic differential equations. Together with a general weak convergence result, this yields the asymptotic null distribution and local asymptotic power of often-used test statistics. Two kinds of nuisance parameters threaten size control: the common reward level of the arms of interest and the rewards of the arms not of interest. The first threat is removed by translation-invariant sampling. We propose Regularized Translation-Invariant (RTI) versions of Thompson, tempered-greedy, tempered-(Lin)UCB, and exploration sampling. The second threat calls for appropriate pivots. The structural representation of the limit experiment is key to overcome the inferential challenges arising from adaptive sampling. Simulations corroborate the theory.

items.title: Mediated Disclosure
items.summary: We introduce a mediator to a communication setting with verifiable (hard) evidence and characterize precisely when mediation can induce every obedient outcome--every type-contingent distribution of actions that the receiver is willing to follow--including the outcome that delivers the sender's commitment (Bayesian persuasion) payoff. For both type-independent and general preferences, it is necessary for each type to have a message he alone can send. This is also sufficient for type-independent preferences, whereas the general case also requires a particular alignment of the types' utilities. We also rank evidence structures by the distributions of actions conditional on the sender's type that they can induce at (mediated) equilibrium, through garbling conditions analogous to Blackwell's comparison of experiments.

items.title: Invariant Modeling for Joint Distributions
items.summary: A common theme underlying many problems in statistics and economics involves the determination of a systematic method of selecting a joint distribution consistent with a specified list of categorical marginals, some of which have an ordinal structure. We propose guidance in narrowing down the set of possible methods by introducing Invariant Aggregation (IA), a natural property that requires merging adjacent categories in one marginal not to alter the joint distribution over unaffected values. We prove that a model satisfies IA if and only if it is a copula model. This characterization i) ensures robustness against data manipulation and survey design, and ii) allows seamless incorporation of new variables. Our results provide both theoretical clarity and practical safeguards for inference under marginal constraints.

items.title: Bias Correction and Inference for Panel Quantile Regression
items.summary: We develop a large-$n$, large-$T$ theory for the unsmoothed fixed-effects quantile regression estimator, paralleling Hahn and Newey (2004) for smooth nonlinear panel models. An exact rank-score identity for the profiled criterion, with a convexity argument, delivers the leading incidental parameter bias of the slope estimator, of order $T^{-1}$, in closed form. When $n$ and $T$ grow at the same rate, the estimator is asymptotically normal but in general not centred, and conventional intervals are invalid. Admissible growth of $n$ relative to $T$, up to $n=o(T^3)$, depends on the regularity of the conditional error densities. A split-panel jackknife removes the leading bias throughout this range and yields valid inference. In serially dependent panels whose dependence decays geometrically or polynomially, the bias acquires a term from the dependence between regressors and errors of different periods, the jackknife remains valid with contiguous but not with interleaved half-panels, and clustered standard errors are valid.

items.title: The Theory of Strategic Evolution: Three Principles of Strategic Replicators
items.summary: Strategic replicators combine evaluated choice and reproductive transmission. An agent chooses among alternatives; the consequences of those choices influence continuation or reproduction; and successors receive organization that shapes later choices. Artificial intelligence makes this combination salient when agents have authority to create, configure, or retire software instances. This paper organizes the general logic around three principles: situated choice, reproductive transmission, and institution-mediated coupling. The principles are constitutive rather than predictions of growth or improvement. A common representation distinguishes carriers, inherited records, decision owners, and the mechanisms that allocate consequences. Actual parent-descendant attribution yields a selection-transmission identity. Separate compatibility results characterize when utility-maximizing choices also maximize a reproductive criterion. Gode and Sunder's zero-intelligence traders reveal the role of institutions: enforced properties can hold across different decision procedures, while aggregate efficiency alone determines neither individual gains nor descent. A worked market-rent-entry model connects institutional profits to actual offspring, with its occurrence-level ancestry bridge checked in Lean. A direct-deployment example then shows evaluated preferences undergoing selection without presupposing that every chooser values reproduction. Formal appendices develop games with endogenous players, deployment-induced tipping, endogenous electorates, and the production of institutions, with models, proofs, and examples. The paper and its supporting formal artifacts are a prototype kernel with a generative function: an instrument for constructing models of strategic replication. The results are formal; their application to deployed populations and their empirical implications remain to be tested.

items.title: Sharp Testable Implications of Encouragement Designs
items.summary: This paper studies a potential outcome model with a continuous or discrete outcome, a discrete multi-valued treatment, and a discrete multi-valued instrument. We derive sharp, closed-form testable implications for a class of restrictions on potential treatments where each value of the instrument encourages towards at most one unique treatment choice; such restrictions serve as the key identifying assumption in several prominent recent empirical papers. Borrowing the terminology used in randomized experiments, we call such a setting an encouragement design. The testable implications are inequalities in terms of the conditional distributions of choices and the outcome given the instrument. Through a novel constructive argument, we show these inequalities are sharp in the sense that any distribution of the observed data that satisfies these inequalities is compatible with this class of restrictions on potential treatments. Based on these inequalities, we propose tests of the restrictions. In an empirical application, we show some of these restrictions are violated and pinpoint the substitution pattern that leads to the violation.

items.title: Many Hands Make Light Work: Long-Term Effect Inference for the Experiment Reservoir
items.summary: The surrogate index method is the modern standard for estimation of long-term effects in a designed experiment using only short-term outcomes. This method relies on the surrogacy and comparability assumptions which may be violated in practice leading to estimation bias. We propose a new method called Experiment Reservoir Surrogate (ERS) which leverages a reservoir of historical long-term experiments that is common in large-scale experimentation platforms. ERS avoids the surrogacy assumption by predicting the long-term average treatment effect directly, and relaxes the comparability assumption by matching to similar historical experiments, without requiring every experiment in the reservoir to be comparable to the target experiment. Moreover, ERS is memory-efficient, as it only requires aggregate data for each time period, instead of raw individual-level data. We theoretically justify the improved efficiency of ERS and demonstrate the improvement empirically on a reservoir of experiments from the online platform DoorDash.

items.title: Nonlinear Drivers of Macroeconomic Tail Risk: A Threshold Stochastic Volatility-in-Mean VAR with Regime-Dependent Leverage
items.summary: The tails of macroeconomic outcomes can respond differently from the centre of their distribution to aggregate shocks. We demonstrate this via a threshold stochastic-volatility-in-mean VAR with regime-dependent leverage. The model allows interactions between the endogenous variables and their volatility, contemporaneous level-volatility dependence, and regime-specific propagation. We estimate the model using a long-run U.S. data set, finding evidence for three inflation-based regimes. We identify business-cycle, financial, macroeconomic-uncertainty, and financial-uncertainty shocks and decompose their contributions to growth- and inflation-at-risk. Business-cycle shocks dominate the median response of GNP growth but account for a substantially smaller share of growth-at-risk. In contrast, uncertainty makes a material contribution to both growth- and inflation-at-risk.

items.title: Training for Alignment
items.summary: We propose a simple model of training an agent with an endogenous bias. A principal chooses in which states to train the agent and what actions to prescribe in these states. In response, the agent updates their bias and then acts optimally given their new bias in untrained states, while following their training in trained states. The agent chooses their new bias to minimize a weighted average of their loss under their initial and final biases. Training can thus generalize to untrained states via the agent's bias updating. We characterize optimal training, which involves \emph{over-correction} in trained states and \emph{generalization-aware} (non-greedy) selection of training states. If only a small share of states can be trained, greedy state selection is approximately optimal, but over-correction remains essential. If any bias function is possible, or if the principal evaluates training robustly over bias functions that admit the possibility of full alignment, the value of training generalization vanishes, and greedy training becomes optimal. With a more pessimistic objective, \emph{under-correction}, or even no training at all, may be optimal. The principal benefits from the agent's preferences being more flexible (\emph{corrigibility}) when the set of possible biases is known and contains full alignment, but otherwise corrigibility can be harmful. Applications include socialization in organizations and families, and AI post-training and recursive self-improvement.

items.title: Distribution-Matching Posterior Inference for Incomplete Structural Models
items.summary: Distribution-matching posterior inference (DMPI) extends the minimal econometric interpretation to generalized posterior inference and model comparison for incomplete structural models. It combines a structural-parameter prior with exact Dirichlet-multinomial scores comparing empirical and model-implied distributions of selected population moments. Ensemble size controls structural discipline, and annealed sequential Monte Carlo computes posterior and generalized evidence. In New Keynesian Phillips Curve simulations, a stochastically singular model remains useful under moderate discipline despite failing as an exact representation. In a U.S. three-equation New Keynesian DSGE application, restoring full rank raises or lowers generalized evidence depending on the structural innovation added.

items.title: Asymmetric Rationality: Protocol Design and Behavioral Anomalies
items.summary: We study how asymmetric rationality in strategic interactions can generate seemingly anomalous patterns of belief updating and behavior. A boundedly rational receiver designs a finite-state decision protocol to learn from a fully rational, privately informed, and biased sender who controls the flow of information. The receiver must allocate scarce memory between learning and incentive provision. We identify a simple class of protocols sufficient for optimal design and show how their structure generates information disengagement, indecision, and polarization. The receiver hesitates before deciding but becomes unresponsive to further evidence afterward. Identical receivers following the same protocol can reach opposing decisions despite receiving the same sequence of signals, with the probability of disagreement remaining bounded away from zero as their payoffs approach the optimum. These behaviors, which might otherwise appear erratic or psychologically driven, arise from the strategic use of limited memory.
